News.title: 'I spent night at Travelodge and woke up covered in 100 bites – people say I look diseased'
News.content:
'I spent night at Travelodge and woke up covered in 100 bites – people say I look diseased'

Travel blogger Hannah Stephenson has managed to largely avoid bugs during her trips to Asia and Africa, but she was left with more than 100 bed bug bites during a night at a Travelodge

View 5 Images Hannah Stephenson was left covered in bites (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

A woman who spent a night at a Travelodge hotel woke up covered in more than 100 bed bug bites that she says have left people fearing she has a disease.

‌



Travel blogger Hannah Stephenson, 31, had been expertly dodging creepy crawlies while travelling around Asia and Africa, but it was a night in Cambridge that proved her undoing.

‌



She was staying at the Newmarket Road branch of the budget hotel firm on July 26 after a day out with a friend.

‌



Hannah woke the next day feeling itchy before discovering her arms were covered in red spots.

She soon discovered blood stains and black dots on her pillow before finding bed bugs crawling in the bedding.

The horrified customer soon discovered more bites appearing across her chest, back, face and legs.

‌



View 5 Images Hannah says people think she has a disease (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

She complained to reception but alleged she was simply told to contact Travelodge's customer services by email. They assured her that hotel room would not be let that night.

Travelodge has since apologised to Hannah for the "distressing" incident and claim they have "resolved the matter to her satisfaction".

‌



They also confirmed there were bed bugs in Hannah's room and claim they are retraining housekeeping at the hotel.

Hannah, from Bassingbourn, Cambridgeshire, said: "I was horrified and shocked. I didn't expect it from a Travelodge, I always thought they are pretty reliable. The swelling has gone down. Now it looks like I have chicken pox.

"People have been horrified, they've said I look like I have a disease. Everyone is saying how bad it looks."

‌



View 5 Images Hannah found bed bugs crawling over the sheets (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

Hannah admits the incident left her "embarrassed" to attend her cousin's wedding earlier this month. She was forced to cover up the bite marks with foundation while she also switched outfits to a dress with long sleeves - not ideal given the current hot spell.

She added: "I felt really embarrassed going to a wedding. They're on my hands, which are hard to cover up, I feel very self-conscious. People are going to think I'm dirty or something.

‌



"I don't usually wear foundation but I went to buy one to cover up for the wedding, I couldn't wear my original outfit which had no sleeves."

Hannah, who has travelled in Asia and Africa, says she's never experienced anything like it anywhere else in the world.

View 5 Images The blogger has managed to avoid creepy crawlies during her travels (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

‌



She called 111 who advised her to visit a pharmacy, where she was given steroids and antihistamines to tackle the bites.

But she is still scratching after a week while the incident is making her want to avoid hotels - especially other Travelodge branches.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson’s experience and recognise how distressing an incident like this can be.

‌



"The safety of our customers is our priority and we maintain stringent, expert-led measures to prevent and manage pest issues, including training our housekeeping colleagues to be vigilant and to spot early signs wherever possible.

View 5 Images Hannah doubts she will ever stay in a Travelodge again (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

"Bed bug activity affects the wider hospitality sector and is completely unrelated to hygiene or cleanliness standards.

Article continues below

"In the rare instance that an issue is reported in one of our hotels, we immediately take affected and surrounding

rooms out of service for inspection and treatment by independent pest control experts. We have apologised directly to Ms Stephenson and resolved the matter to her satisfaction."

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover' when he was general secretary
News.content:
Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.

A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".

Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".

The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.

The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body.

"Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph.

"No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school.

It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

News.title: The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding
News.content:
For months we drew a blank in our hunt for Luka.

And then we had our first breakthrough.

One of those listed in the book, who we tried calling again, finally answered the phone.

He had been the guard for Luka's apartment block, he told us, and eventually agreed to give us the number for someone he said had been Luka's personal bodyguard - a man we are calling Mahmoud.

It took weeks to secure an interview with Mahmoud. Meetings would be scheduled but he would not show up, or he would request a meeting in a private space such as a car or apartment, which our reporter judged too much of a risk.

They eventually met at a hotel one night, just before midnight. Broad-shouldered and physically imposing, Mahmoud seemed to be considering every answer carefully before he spoke.

He told us he was angry with Luka for leaving him behind when the regime fell. As word had spread in December 2024 that Assad's rule was on the brink of collapse - with rebels advancing on the capital - Luka had said he would stay and defend Damascus, Mahmoud told us. But by the early hours of the next morning, Luka had disappeared, taking a large sum of money with him from the office safe, Mahmoud said.

Mahmoud refused to share any contact details for Luka or his family, but did give us a number for Luka's driver, who he believed had driven the former spy chief out of the capital that night.

This man proved even harder to reach.

When he answered the phone, his voice was nervous and unsteady. He repeatedly insisted he was just a driver, and knew nothing of Luka's activities. Multiple meetings with us were never kept, and eventually he stopped replying.

We turned our attention to Luka's possible escape routes, including neighbouring Lebanon - where the Iran-backed group Hezbollah had close links with the Assad regime.

One senior source in the Lebanese government told us he understood Luka had passed through Lebanon on a "good Russian passport but with a different name", before flying out to Russia.

We managed to find a man, now based in Lebanon, whose name was listed in Luka's contacts book, but under a number that no longer worked. He is one of many wanted by the new Syrian government, because of his close association with the Assad regime.

This man, who we cannot identify, said he had a number for Luka.

We saw it, and realised it had a Russian country code.

Russia was a key backer of the Assad regime, and in the days after his fall, Assad released a statement confirming that he had fled there. Many of his inner circle were believed to have followed him.

Back in Luka's apartment in Damascus, we had found clues that Luka also had strong links to Moscow - awards from Russia's foreign spy service, and even a New Year's card addressed to him from a senior Russian official.

Now, the Russian telephone number for him suggested we finally had proof that he was - as we had predicted - in Russia.

News.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
News.content:
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

News.title: Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
News.content:
Temperatures on Saturday will begin to climb above average again, reaching the mid- to high 20s Celsius in most of England and Wales.

It will be cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland at 17 to 21C with more cloud, a bit of rain and a blustery wind.

By Sunday and into next week temperatures will rise even further with many parts of the UK exceeding their heatwave threshold temperature of 25 to 28C, depending on location.

With this hotter weather expected to last well into the week, many locations will have the three consecutive days needed to declare the fifth widespread heatwave of the year.

It has already been a remarkable summer in the United Kingdom with multiple records broken.

July has been the sunniest month on record for the UK, as well as the driest July on record for England and Wales.

There have so far been 33 days this year when temperatures have exceeded 30C in the UK. Next week, it is likely the record of 34 days, set in 1995, will be broken.

For the first time ever, a temperature of 35C has also been recorded somewhere in the UK on the three consecutive months of May, June and July.

It is possible August will join that list by the end of next week as some forecast models suggest 35C in central and south-east England.

News.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
News.content:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

News.title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back and 'a bit more real'
News.content:
Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.

The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention â "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.

He's right â digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.

There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18â30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.

So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?

For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".

She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.

"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.

That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids â where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image â are also popular on socials right now.

With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.

"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.

"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."

News.title: How a former GB Olympian curbed his porn problem - and the signs and steps to recovery
News.content:
Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn.

"Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do was open those sites," he revealed.

By age 12, he was regularly visiting what he calls "hardcore" sites. As his career progressed - which included representing his country in the Olympics - he was watching adult content several times a day.

Now aged 30, the Olympian has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset.

"You can't be the person who is trying to quit porn. You have to be someone who doesn't watch porn, and that takes a lot of work," he said.

So how can you spot when a porn habit has become unhealthy, and how can you tackle it?

Although it has become a common phrase, "porn addiction" is not an officially recognised condition in its own right.

"We know a lot of people have a problem with porn," explains sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves, who says the matter has become more prevalent among clients at his private practice.

But experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction" â like someone might experience with drugs, for example â and how best to deal with it.

Researcher Campbell Ince, from Australia's Monash University, says the vast majority of clinicians now agree people can suffer from "problematic porn use", but there is still a lot to figure out about its causes and treatments.

This means there is no definitive list of symptoms or treatments available to those worried they may be addicted.

Some clinicians approach it as a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a condition recognised by the World Health Organization.

This is sexual behaviour that "feels out of control, is causing significant distress, and despite repeated attempts to control it, they can't," explains psychotherapist Dr Paula Hall, who works privately at the Laurel Centre, a sex and porn addiction centre, and also runs a not-for-profit service.

The NHS does say, external it is possible to be addicted to "just about anything", including sex.

News.title: Police officers investigated over handling of sex offender who murdered two women
News.content:
Levy, from Tottenham, north London, was found guilty at the Old Bailey on Friday of two counts of murder, two counts of rape, grievous bodily harm with intent, and non-fatal suffocation.

He was remanded into custody ahead of sentencing on 12 August.

The IOPC later confirmed its investigation began in January following a voluntary conduct referral from the Metropolitan Police and remains ongoing.

It added that issuing misconduct or gross misconduct notices does not necessarily mean disciplinary proceedings will follow.

The watchdog is examining the management of Levy over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 on sexual assault charges up to his arrest in September 2025.

Levy had been released from prison on licence in February 2023 and was briefly returned to prison in May 2024 after being accused of rape and breaching his licence conditions but was not charged.

On Friday, he was convicted at the Old Bailey of two murders, rape and other charges including grievous bodily harm with intent, and non-fatal suffocation against the surviving woman.

The jury, which was given a majority direction in the trial, found him guilty on all counts.

During his trial jurors heard Levy had a string of convictions for attacking women dating back to July 2018, including one carried out against a prison officer in 2022.

An IOPC spokesperson said: "We are examining whether action could or should have been taken to prevent his reoffending, and if all officers involved in his management followed policies, procedures, and training.

"We are also assessing whether any learning, whether individual, force-wide, or nationally, or other changes should be implemented in light of the events under investigation."

News.title: Police failings revealed as sex offender left free to murder and attack women
News.content:
His first victim was attacked was on a busy Tube in central London.

Levy boarded and positioned himself directly in front of the woman, before leaning his elbow on her. She moved away.

A few minutes later, she felt something touch her, over her clothes, on her vagina. Such was the force Levy used, that she felt like it was an attempt to push his fingers inside her through clothing.

She grabbed Levy's hand and asked what he was doing, but he did not respond.

When other passengers asked if she was all right, Levy protested his innocence.

"What are you talking about - look my hand is covered," he said, pointing to the jumper draped over his arm.

Levy then called her "crazy" and "stupid" and got off the tube at Westminster station.

The woman got off at the next stop, upset and crying.

She went on to report the assault to BTP. There was CCTV available of Levy, but police did not identify him. He would only be linked to the case two years later, after more women had been attacked.

A year after his first Tube assault, he assaulted three more women in quick succession and was arrested.

After being assaulted herself, the first of those three victims then filmed Levy sexually assaulting a second, unidentified woman, travelling in the same carriage.

The first woman immediately reported what had happened to BTP and provided the footage. Levy assaulted a third woman a week later.

After he had been questioned and had denied the three offences, BTP officers said they did not have enough evidence to charge, and he was released on bail.

The subsequent BTP investigation was full of delays. It was weeks before identity parades were arranged, and BTP did not approach the CPS for six months.

When it did, in May 2025, a CPS team had to scramble to make an emergency charging decision overnight, because BTP had again arrested Levy and wanted him in court the next day. This was highly unusual - BTP had known about the initial offences for six months.

In a statement, BTP Assistant Chief Constable Charlie Doyle said: "It is clear that opportunities to expedite the investigation were missed and we have amended our procedures to address these issues to ensure that repeat offenders are dealt with expeditiously and that linked offences are prioritised more effectively."

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
News.content:
The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment.

"Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said.

"The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

News.title: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college
News.content:
AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.

North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.

No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was rapedâ¦ by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up.

"We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves.

"I don't want anyone who has the ambition and talent to join our armed forces to be deterred, so it's contingent on us to make sure that we've got our act together," he added.

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".

Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.

Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

News.title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
News.content:
Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and Pink, has died at the age of 69.

A statement, external released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

News.title: Police make further arrests as Thetford disorder continues
News.content:
More arrests have been made over disorder linked to anti-immigration protests that saw crowds attempt to storm the homes of suspected asylum seekers and a police officer "seriously bitten".

Asylum seekers were removed from properties in Thetford on Thursday for their own safety, Norfolk Police said.

Two men in their 40s were arrested as protests in the market town continued for a third night, and a woman was arrested on Friday in relation to an assault on a police officer, bringing the total number detained to six.

Protesters attempted to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living on Tuesday and Wednesday night, when officers were also "subjected to significant aggression".

News.title: Brothers jailed for killing man and injuring his son while racing cars home
News.content:
Following sentencing, Rhys' wife Caroline Jenkins, also known as Carrie, said in a statement she often wondered what difference it would have made to her family's future "if we'd hugged a little tighter and a little longer" when she waved them off that day.

She said, for her son, life "without a dad who was involved in everything you did is a hard adjustment" and it "carried an element of PTSD".

Carrie said Ioan was emotionally and physically scarred by the crash.

"It's impossible to convey the full impact Rhys' death had on us," she said, and there remains a "massive hole left in our lives by his unnecessary death".

Ioan, who broke both arms, and suffered a fractured rib and perforated bowel, said he wished his dad was still here to "watch me grow up and be my dad".

Rhys' youngest son, Gruff, was six when the crash happened.

In his own victim impact statement, he said he was in bed when police arrived to tell his mum what had happened.

After being told his dad had died, he said: "I ran out of the house. I didn't know where I was going. It was the worst feeling of my life."

The court was told Umar Ben Yusaf's car was not directly involved in the crash, but the "competitive" nature of his driving with Abubakr Ben Yusaf contributed significantly.

Judge Timothy Petts said the trauma the Jenkins family had been through in the last 21 months was "difficult for me to summarise".

"You have all been suffering with your own devastating grief but also trying to deal with the practical consequences of Rhys's death and Ioan's injuries.

"It has been an horrendous time for all of you," he told them.

Petts said to Umar and Abubakr Ben Yusaf that he was satisfied they were racing each other.

"Both of you were constantly riding your luck at high speed, completely unnecessarily, and eventually it ran out with appalling consequences.

"Rhys Jenkins never stood a chance because you were so close to him when you lost control. He was driving perfectly properly and did nothing wrong. He had no time to avoid the collision."

Sgt Sara John, from Dyfed-Powys Police's serious collision investigation unit, said: "The sentences passed today cannot undo the tragic loss suffered by Rhys's family."

She added she hoped the outcome "provides them with some closure as they begin to move forward with their lives, which have been changed forever".

"The actions of Abubakr and Umar Yusaf on that day were catastrophic. Their choice to drive in the manner they did shows their utter disregard towards other road users."

News.title: Ann Widdecombe investigators reopen probe into ‘arson attempt’ at Nigel Farage’s home
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Counter-terror police probing the alleged murder of Ann Widdecombe have reopened a year-old investigation into a “firebomb” attack at Nigel Farage’s house, it has been reported.

A “lit incendiary device” was posted through the Reform UK leader’s mailbox in Greater London in April 2025, the Telegraph said.

Mr Farage earlier described the alleged attack as an “outright arson attempt”.

He said that he was not in at the time, and he found the damage when he returned home.

“Luckily it had burned itself out on the porch,” he told the Telegraph in April this year.

The Metropolitan Police and Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said that they investigated an “attempted burglary”, but no arrests were made.

open image in gallery Ann Widdecombe was allegedly murdered on 8 July ( PA Archive )

The case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

Since it was reopened, CTP London has identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by them at the time”.

The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct, is now investigating the “conduct” of a CTP London staff member, following an allegation that the employee “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry” related to the attempted burglary.

Ms Widdecombe, a Reform UK spokesperson and former Conservative minister, died on 8 July.

Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with her murder. He has not yet entered a plea.

At a hearing at the Old Bailey, it was alleged that Ms Widdecombe was hit 21 times with a hammer.

open image in gallery Nigel Farage said that he was the victim of an ‘outright arson attempt’ in 2025 ( PA Wire )

Senior national co-ordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.

She added: “Given the nature of this matter and the significant public interest in the investigation into Ann Widdecombe’s death, it was of critical importance for us to provide this update.”

CTP London said it made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the police watchdog on Friday.

An IOPC spokesperson said on Friday: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today.

“The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025.

“Counter Terrorism Policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.”

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Man City reject Rodri bid, Arsenal identify Vinicius Jr alternatives, Man Utd done deal
News.content:
Why Arsenal Want Bruno Guimaraes So Badly

Rodri looks set to leave Manchester City amid interest from Barcelona and Real Madrid. The World Cup winning captain is into the final year of his contract and favours a move to Barca – though an initial offer of £38m has been rejected.

Arsenal were dealt a blow in one of their summer transfer pursuits as Vinicius Jr has signed a contract extension with Real Madrid. The Gunners have moved on from targeting the winger and have reignited their interest in Atletico Madrid’s Julian Alvarez while PSG’s Bradley Barcola is also on their list.

In more positive news, Bruno Guimaraes has completed a medical at Arsenal ahead of his £75m move from Newcastle United. The 28-year-old midfielder is now expected to be announced as a new Gooner on Friday ahead of Arsenal’s pre-season fixtures this weekend. The deal represents a key piece of business of Mikel Arteta ahead of Arsenal’s title defence.

Liverpool, meanwhile, also want to sign Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain and have also lined up his teammate Ibrahim Mbaye in what could be a double swoop for Andoni Iraola’s side. The European champions may be willing to let them go especially following Maghnes Akliouche signing from Monaco.

Elsewhere, Manchester United have added to their ranks by bringing in a teenage midfielder and they are exploring their options at left-back with Lewis Hall reportedly now set on a move to Old Trafford, but Newcastle are determined to stop the exodus and insist he is not for sale.

September is one of the best months to steal away for a holiday, particularly in southern Europe where it’s still very much summer.

Go hiking along Italy’s southern coast, or soak up the sun on a Greek or Spanish island. If you want to go further afield, the delicious flavours of Mauritius are waiting to be tasted.

Closer to home, drive a slow boat through the Cambridgeshire Fens, or explore the peaceful Suffolk countryside.

If you’re in the mood for something special, take over a gorgeous villa in the South of France, or have a romantic honeymoon in Slovenia and Venice.

Wherever you decide to go on holiday in September, these ideas will give you some inspiration.



Greece

open image in gallery Paxos is located just south of Corfu ( Getty Images )

Enjoy summery temperatures at the end of September in this delightful two-bedroom villa in Paxos. Villa Somnium sits above Marmari Beach near Loggos, and you’ll have your own pool as well as a lovely terrace. GIC the Villa Collection has a week available from 28 September for £1,419.50pp, based on two sharing, including flights, car hire and welcome pack. The second bedroom is in a gallery above the sitting room, and the price for four people travelling would be £1,174.50pp.



Spain

open image in gallery Pollença is famous for the 365 Calvari Steps ( Getty Images )

If you’ve been putting off that big family and/or friends gathering during the summer, now’s the time to snap up this five-bedroom villa in Mallorca for September. Just a few minutes’ drive from Pollença, C’an Pontarro is an immensely stylish country house surrounded by lush vegetation. Lounge by the outdoor pool after cooking in the summer kitchen’s built-in barbecue and lunching on the covered terrace. Vintage Travel has availability from 5 September from £4,448 for a week’s rental, or save more if you can wait till 26 September and pay from £2,698.



Cambridgeshire

open image in gallery Narrowboat on the River Great Ouse and River Nene ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Enjoy a slower pace of life on a narrowboat holiday through the Cambridgeshire Fens, where life doesn’t go any faster than 3mph. Try this four-night taster that starts in Ely and lets you meander along the Ouse through Wicken Fen towards Cambridge. Black Prince Holidays has a four-night break in September aboard a 58ft narrowboat that sleeps four from £1,284, down from £1,426. This includes tuition, towels, linen, insurance and car parking, but fuel is extra.



Mauritius

open image in gallery Grand Baie sits on the northwest coast of Mauritius ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

September is still dry season in Mauritius, with temperatures in the high 20s. At Veranda Grand Baie Hotel & Spa, it’s easy to keep cool in the hotel’s pools as well as the clear waters of Grand Baie lagoon on the island’s north-western side. Away Holidays has a week’s holiday (with an overnight flight) in September from £985pp, including flights and breakfast.



Italy

open image in gallery Otranto is a historic coastal town in the Puglia region ( Getty Images )

Get to know the beauties of coastal Puglia on this five-day self-guided walk with Ramble Worldwide. You’ll start in Otranto and make your way down to Gagliano del Capo and eventually Lecce, stopping for refreshing swims and wanders round fishing villages while your luggage is being transported for you. Departures in September start at £639pp and include breakfast, luggage transfers, route notes and maps. Flights are extra.



Suffolk

open image in gallery Halesworth is a market town in north-eastern Suffolk ( Getty Images )

If you’re up for rambles in the Suffolk countryside, make the very cute Holly Cottage your base. This three-bedroom 17th-century cottage is in the tiny hamlet of Huntingfield (which has a pub), about a 10-minute drive from Halesworth. Two of the three bedrooms are doubles, and exposed beams, a wood-burning stove, country kitchen, plus an enclosed garden for a dog make the cottage a cosy bolthole. Booked through Rural Retreats, it costs £722 for a three-night break in September.



And if you want to splash out…

Slovenia/Italy

open image in gallery Portorož is a famous Slovenian seaside resort ( Getty Images )

If you’re planning a honeymoon, or any other romantic holiday, this tailor-made Hidden Hearts of Slovenia and Venice by Completely Slovenia should shoot up your list. You’ll soak up the romance of Venice before heading to Portorož on Slovenia’s Adriatic coast. A session in the Sečovlje Salt Pans Spa in the national park and a carriage ride on Lipizzaner horses follow before you go glamping in Lake Bled. Then gorgeous Ljubljana and a thermal spa resort before the final night in a luxury spa hotel. This eight-day holiday starts at £5,000pp, down from £5,500pp, and includes flights, transfers, luxury boutique accommodation, breakfasts, selected dinners, entrance fees, boat rides, selected spa treatments and a professional photo session.



France

open image in gallery Cannes is famous for its film festival ( Getty Images )

Bastide Splendide certainly lives up to its name. This sumptuous five-bedroom stone villa above the Bay of Cannes is the place to gather up to 12 people and bask in sublime views. Outside it’s all traditional provençal stone, while inside there’s more of a Scandi feel to the light interiors. Relax in the pool or on the various tree-shaded terraces tumbling down the slope. All five bedrooms are en suite, and one has a small twin that leads off it. CV Villas has availability from 12-19 September for £12,016, down from £15,019.



Mary Novakovich is editor at large at 101holidays.co.uk

News.content:

Audience members who saw Amanda Knox’s controversial comedy show at Edinburgh Fringe on opening night say that it is both “respectful” and “genuinely funny”.

Knox, who was falsely imprisoned in 2009 for the murder of her roommate Meredith Kercher, performed her new show Cartwheel on Friday night following unsuccessful calls for it to be pulled from the line-up.

Kercher, an exchange student from the University of Leeds, was killed aged 21 in Perugia, Italy in 2007.

Knox was convicted in 2009, along with her then-boyfriend Raffaele Sollecito, of Kercher’s murder and sexual assault.

She was released from prison in 2011 and cleared by Italy’s Supreme Court in 2015.

The show’s title refers to a story that the now-39-year-old did cartwheels in the police station following Kercher’s death.

open image in gallery Meredith Kercher (right) with her sister Stephanie Kercher ( Family handout )

Kercher’s sister Stephanie Kercher earlier called for Cartwheel to be cancelled, claiming that it “normalises and trivialises violence against women”.

More than 6,000 people signed a petition demanding it be pulled from the Fringe line-up.

However, people leaving the show on Friday night said it was both “powerful” and “respectful”.

One audience member said: “I think that [Knox] has every right to tell her story and to deal with her own grief and pain and what’s been taken from her in her own way.

“She was profoundly respectful to the victim of the crime. She said that she never got the chance to express her own grief about what had happened, because as soon as the crime had happened, she was put in this position of having to defend herself. So I think that was important for her.”

The man said Knox was also “genuinely funny”.

open image in gallery Amanda Knox spent two years in prison for Meredith Kercher’s murder ( AFP/Getty )

Audience member Nigel, from London, also found it to be respectful.

“I thought it was really authentic – [Knox] came across as quite powerful and carried the room,” he said.

“There was a lot of clapping and standing at the end, and a lot of laughter all the way through.”

Nigel added: “I thought it was an opportunity for her to tell her story in a very different environment.”

He also said that Knox refers to Kercher in the show as someone who she had known as a friend.

A man from Glasgow, who did not wish to be named, said the show is more about storytelling than it is about comedy.

“I was a wee bit hesitant about going along because I knew that there was controversy, and I understand Meredith Kercher’s family being concerned – I’ve got total sympathy for that – but having seen the show, there’s nothing in that show that is, you know, like offensive or demeaning to Kercher,” the man said.

“It’s trailed as a stand-up comedy, but it’s not a stand-up comedy show. There’s elements of humour in it, but it’s more about her story.”

open image in gallery More than 6,000 people signed a petition calling for the show to be cancelled ( Getty )

A woman, from Edinburgh, who also did not want to be named, said the show is emotional, and nearly moved her to tears.

“The one very moving part was where she talks about her friend, her flatmate, Meredith, and that almost brought tears to my eyes,” she said.

“It was a very small part of the show, but it was basically the guilt that she actually feels about being here.”

Overall, the woman said the show was more about being a mother than it was about Kercher’s murder.

In a statement posted on Instagram, Knox said: “Cartwheel is a show about motherhood, raising a daughter in a world that is unfair and dangerous for women, and what it costs to be the kind of mother who tells her the truth about that.

“Neither the author of this petition nor anyone who signed it has seen Cartwheel.

“The petition contains many false assumptions and completely mischaracterises the show.

“Cartwheel honours Meredith Kercher’s memory and calls out the violence that was done to her and to me.

“A petition to cancel a show no one has seen on the grounds of false accusations intended to shame and vilify a wronged woman into silence is not an argument against Cartwheel.

“It’s a fairly precise description of what Cartwheel is about and why it deserves to exist.

“And the Edinburgh Fringe is the perfect place for a show like this.”

News.title: Ship swaps and missed stops: How river cruise lines are dealing with low water levels
News.content:

Droughts and heatwaves across Europe have reduced water levels in some of the continent’s most prominent rivers, which has restricted where cruise ships can visit.

Levels were close to their lowest on the Danube River around Budapest earlier this month and have hit the lowest levels since 1996 in Romania.

Other European rivers such as the Rhine are facing similar issues. The Rhine’s depth dropped to 53 centimetres near Frankfurt last week.

This makes it harder for cruise ships to dock. Brands such as Uniworld, Viking and TravelMarvel have had to change embarkation points, and cancel or reroute sailings, as a result.

Cruise Critic executive editor Chris Gray Faust was among passengers affected on Uniworld’s SS Emilie river cruise on the Danube earlier this month.

She told The Independent: “I knew that it was likely that my cruise, slated to sail from Vienna to Nuremberg, would have some issues.”

The low water on the Danube in Germany meant the ship couldn’t go any further than Vilshofen so passengers missed three stops: Deggendorf, Regensburg and Nuremberg, the disembarkation point.

Instead, the ship added a stop in Linz and offered Bavarian Forest and Regensburg excursions as bus tours from Vilshofen.

open image in gallery SS Emilie is among ships affected by low water levels on the Danube ( Uniworld )

Any excursion that turned into a full day trip came with €30 (£25) towards lunch, as usually passengers would be able to return to the ship to eat.

Ms Gray Faust told The Independent: “I chose to do both bus trips. I’ll admit, while one bus trip is doable, multiple bus trips – one day after another – is not ideal. But there were no alternative onboard activities added.”

Passengers who were due to fly home from Nuremberg disembarked the ship a day early. They were put up in a nice hotel and given €50 (£42) each for dinner. Airport transfers were arranged the next day.

She said: “Generally, other passengers reacted to the changes on our itinerary in a positive way. They would have preferred the trip to go as planned, but most felt Uniworld handled it well. The itinerary before us, from Belgrade to Vienna, had even more changes, and I understood that people were quite unhappy about that one, which required more bus time.”

Ms Gray Faust adds that this isn’t just a summer problem. She said: “Water levels in Budapest have been sitting within inches of the 2018 record low this year, and other lines – Viking, Avalon, AmaWaterways, Scenic, Tauck – have all been managing similar disruptions on the same stretch of river.

“It's worth knowing that low water in summer, and high water in spring, are both realistic possibilities on these rivers, regardless of which line you sail.”

Uniworld said in a statement: "River conditions can change throughout the season, and Uniworld's teams work in close coordination with local authorities and regional partners. With more than 50 years of experience operating on Europe's waterways, Uniworld remains focused on adapting as needed while delivering the exceptional service, immersive excursions and seamless travel experiences guests expect."

With temperatures set to remain high in August, there could be more disruption to come.

Emma Guse, a river cruise specialist with travel agent Travelmation, says she currently has clients on the Danube who were unable to embark on their cruise in Budapest as planned but instead had to board the ship at a different port, approximately 60 miles away.

She told The Independent: "Bus transportation was then required the following day for excursions in the city. This is unfortunate as sailing into and docking in the heart of these grand cities is an important part of the experience.”

“Moving into August, I do have clients whose itineraries may be impacted by river levels, but this is why it is crucial to set expectations and encourage a flexible spirit, which is always important in travel.”



How cruise lines are responding to low water levels

Cruise lines are used to navigating different water levels but the prolonged heatwave has created extra challenges this summer.

Chris Pitchford, founder of the World of Cruising research site, told The Independent: “This year is certainly worse than usual. Cancellations have so far been kept to a minimum, and cruise lines have reacted with itinerary and ship changes to keep disruption to a minimum.

“Budapest – a main starting point for Danube cruises – is currently a problem area, with ships struggling to dock in the city.

“In some cases, guests have been told that their cruises will start at a nearby port where water levels are higher or that they will begin their trips with a hotel stay in Budapest before being transferred to their ship by coach.”

A Uniworld statement to The Independent said adjustments may include itinerary modifications or alternative travel arrangements to help passengers continue with their route.

The cruise line highlighted that sailings in France, Italy and Portugal are operating as scheduled.

open image in gallery People stand on the usually-submerged banks of the Danube in Romania ( AP )

Another way that cruise lines tackle changing water levels is through ship swaps.

Cruise lines such as Viking and Riviera Travel position ships across different stretches of affected rivers to ensure passengers can complete their journeys.

In June, guests on Viking’s Rhine Getaway from Amsterdam to Basel had to swap ships due to low water levels. This involved a 24-hour stay on the ship in Koblenz before a five-hour bus to Strasbourg to embark on another river ship.

A spokesperson for Viking said its captains monitor water levels and implement operational adjustments as needed, adding: “Viking strategically deploys sister ships on the same itineraries in opposite directions.

“When river conditions require it, Viking may implement a ship swap, allowing guests and their luggage to transfer to their exact same stateroom on an identical sister ship positioned on the other side of the affected section of river. This approach helps preserve itineraries and reduce disruptions to the guest experience.”

Cancelling a cruise is always a last resort, said Riviera Travel.

A statement said: “To give our on board teams and guests extra support, members of our head office team are also flying out to join sailings where needed.

“We are keeping guests updated daily, and thanks to the extraordinary dedication of our teams on the water and our guests’ fantastic spirit of adventure, feedback from those currently travelling remains overwhelmingly positive.”

open image in gallery Low water levels have also affected traffic on the Danube in Serbia ( AP )

Passengers should keep an eye on changes to their cruise before and during the sailing.

Paul Melinis, a managing director at Travelmarvel, highlights that river cruise itineraries are always subject to navigational conditions.

He said it is important to choose an experienced brand that can cope with changes, adding: “Extreme weather is something the industry has always had to manage and, with hotter summers becoming more frequent, being prepared and able to adapt quickly is more important than ever.

“The best advice I could share with anyone due to travel is to stay in close contact with their river cruise operator or travel agent.”

What are your rights if a river cruise is disrupted?

A cruise line will typically offer refunds or credit to rebook if a sailing is cancelled.

However, changes during the sailing may be covered by the booking’s terms and conditions, meaning itinerary changes will not necessarily be claimable against.

Taking out travel insurance that includes cruise cover can be useful in this situation as it may cover you for prepaid activities that you can no longer attend or if you miss a flight due to a delay.

Some cruise travel insurance policies may even let you pay for extras such as insufficient or excessive water levels.

Jacqueline Mondelli, chief marketing officer for insurance platform Squaremouth, said: “There are key differences in the level of protection offered by the cruise line you have booked with, standard travel insurance policies and a cruise insurance plan. A cruise insurance plan offers the most protection in this case, as it covers factors such as insufficient water levels.”

Passengers are facing travel chaos at Bristol airport after a runway defect suspended operations for hours leading to cancellations and delays.

Passengers were left stranded on Friday after the airport’s runway was closed at around 6pm. It remained shut, with no flights coming in or out, until 8am on Saturday, but operations have now resumed.

Though the runway has reopened, passengers are now facing hours of delays, with multiple flights affected.

An updated statement on the airport’s website said: “Flights have resumed at Bristol Airport this morning. There will be some disruption to some flights today and customers are advised to refer to their airlines with any flight queries. We apologise for any inconvenience caused.”

Earlier, the airport said that it had suspended operations to assess and repair a “defect on the runway.”

If you have been affected by the runway closure at Bristol airport, please get in touch by emailing daniel.haygarth@independent.co.uk

Among the many flights to be delayed this morning, according to the airport’s online departures board, are the 5.55am service to Faro, which is scheduled to take off at 10.40am, and the 6.20am flight to Menorca, which is expected to depart at 11.30am.

Cancelled or delayed flights: What are my rights to a refund? Check here

Paul Smith, who was due to fly to Glasgow on Friday for his son's 20th birthday but had to cancel the holiday, told the BBC: "The communication, advice and support for passengers has been really poor”.

Mr Smith said there were no announcements for more than an hour on Friday and claimed that he was only getting information from EasyJet staff in the departure lounge.

On X, responding to a passenger asking if flights have been cancelled today, airline Jet2 said: “Our flights have not been cancelled. They are currently delayed, and are expected to fly later today when the runway re-opens.”

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.title: The best luxury hotels in the Cotswolds
News.content:
From gracious old farmsteads and magnificent manor houses to an ancient coaching inn creaking with Tudor character, the top luxury hotels in the Cotswolds combine a wonderful sense of history with contemporary style and outstanding modern British cuisine. Whether near picturesque Broadway in the north of the region or close to Bath in the south, location is a key attribute to them all: some offer serene escapes in acres of their own rolling parkland; others sit amid superb gardens; and several take over classic honey-stone villages that look as if they have been beamed in from a halcyon era of the past.

They all excel in providing creature comforts, whether crackling fires by kick-back sofas, canopy beds with soft throws, or suites with terraces and hot tubs. Facilities are top-notch too, ranging from beautiful bars and quiet terraces to blissful spas with inviting pools and even an opportunity for equine adventures. News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”
