To an 11-year-old, carrying alcohol home every morning and evening may feel like work. But the line between carrying and consuming can be dangerously thin.

Ade’s first sip came from his father. Chibuike’s first taste came from an adult while carrying out an errand. Their stories show how adults can make informed choices about alcohol, adults have already made the choice for them. And that is the heart of the crisis.

The question is no longer only why children drink. It is also who gives them the first drink, who sends them to buy it, who sells it to them, who watches them consume it, and who looks away. For a country that repeatedly describes its children as the leaders of tomorrow, the answers may determine what kind of tomorrow Nigeria will have.

Vanguard News

World.title: Ukraine’s Zelensky visits Russian ally Serbia for talks
World.content:
Ukraine President, Zelensky

President Volodymyr Zelensky was making his first official visit to Serbia — a rare European country still closely aligned with Moscow — on Saturday as Ukraine seeks to bolster international support in the face of intensifying Russian strikes.

Zelensky was to hold talks with his counterpart Alexander Vucic at the presidential palace on Saturday, after another intense bombardment of Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight killed at least three people and wounded seven.

Diplomacy is at a standstill more than four years after the start of Russia’s large-scale offensive against Ukraine and the two countries are ramping up long-range strikes, causing a growing number of civilian casualties.

Moscow has significantly upped its attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent months, typically firing salvos of hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles in short blitzes, with Ukraine pleading for more US-made Patriot interceptors.

Kyiv, in turn, has been firing record numbers of drones at Russia.

A senior Ukrainian official earlier described Zelensky’s visit to Moscow’s traditional ally Serbia as “a slap in the face for the Russians”.

Serbia is historically close to Russia and Vucic has refused to sanction Moscow, a move that has irked the EU and slowed Belgrade’s path to joining the bloc.

Zelensky had dinner on Friday with Vucic, who repeated this week that he will not change his mind on sanctions, ahead of the talks.

“We will discuss expanding economic ties between our countries, relations with the European Union, other areas that can benefit our nations, and security issues,” Zelensky said on X.

The pair are also due to address the media.

Zelensky — who has toured much of the world seeking support since Russia’s 2022 invasion — has not visited Serbia since he became president in 2019.

Although heavily dependent on cheap Russian gas and one of the rare European leaders to still visit Moscow, Vucic has also supplied non-military aid to Kyiv.

The Kremlin has accused Serbian firms of selling munitions to Ukraine, a claim Vucic has repeatedly denied.

Vucic went to Ukraine for a regional summit in 2025 and visited Kyiv this year. He has promised assistance to Ukraine but avoided signing a formal declaration of support in the war.

The overnight attacks on Kyiv killed three people, including a child, in the Brovary district northeast of the city, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration, wrote on Telegram.

Falling debris from the attacks damaged houses and vehicles and caused a fire in a non-residential building, he said.

Three people in the area were also wounded, while a further four were wounded from the overnight attacks in Kyiv.

Ukraine’s state emergency service shared photos of a destroyed building in flames, saying the attack in the village of Pukhivka destroyed a two-storey house and two cars and sparked a fire in a warehouse.

An AFP reporter in the capital heard a dozen explosions as Ukraine’s air force warned of the “threat of ballistic weapon use from the north”.

AFP

World.title: Inspector Omogbai: Doing policing with motherly love
World.content:
File image.

By Adesina Wahab

She got enlisted in the Nigeria Police Force, NPF, 24 years ago and has risen through the ranks to become an Inspector in the Traffic Department. Justina Omogbai, a mother of five, was recently recognized and honoured by the management of Trinity University, Sabo, Yaba, Lagos during their second Registry Week and Lecture. They gave her a Certificate of Recognition and an undisclosed amount of money for her tireless efforts at ensuring students in public schools in that axis get to school on time and are properly dressed.

Read Also:25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker

After observing that some students are fond of loitering around when they ought to be in school, Omogbai turned herself to a chief whip, ensuring that they get to school early enough for their studies. Like a football referee, she would put a whistle in her mouth and clutch a cane, not to beat any student, but to scare them to do the right thing – get to school early enough. She has also become a Madam Santa Claus to some of the students she assists occasionally with writing materials, shoes, uniforms among others.

To know the depth of the sacrifices she makes, one needs to have an idea of how much a police inspector earns monthly in the country.

According to the Consolidated Police Salary Structure, CONPOSS, an Inspector of Police in Nigeria earns an estimated monthly basic salary between N167,000 and N254,000, depending on their precise sub-rank and grade level. The Inspector rank is divided into sub-categories which dictate the exact take-home pay: Inspector of Police (IP) II: N67,000 per month, Inspector of Police (IP) I: N254,000 per month.

On what prompted her service to humanity, she said, “I was posted to Sabo, Yaba in 2021 and I have been in the service for 24 years. Everywhere I have worked in Lagos, I have always tried to distinguish myself. These pupils and students are our future leaders and we must do everything possible to lead them aright. They can be governors, President, Ministers or anything God has purposed for them in the future. Whenever I see them pass by without dressing properly, I feel for them. I also went to a public school and our parents took great care of us. We wore Cortina shoes to school and dressed well. Nobody wore slippers to school.

“But now, some children don’t dress well to school, they will wear torn uniforms or not minding to wash those uniforms. And they go to school very late too. You will see a child that is supposed to be in school by 7.45am just strolling there by 8.30am or even 9am. Majority of them I see at food vendors’ places, or where they would meet to discuss sports and other issues. So, I said what kind of life is this? Because a wayward child today possibly started like that. So, I decided to take it upon myself to start to caution them. That they should not do such things but to have focus in life.”

But with five children of her own, and with the current economic situation in the country, surely it is an arduous task living comfortably, not to think of serving in loco parentis to some children one does not know their parents. But Omogbai would not be deterred. She has kind words for her husband, an Air Force personnel for being her pillar of support.

“It was difficult for me when I started, some of my colleagues were telling me whether I have taken adequate care of my own children. I have five children. When I talk to those children, I will draw them close and advise them.

“There are 10 public schools in this axis that I take care of their students. Some of them do come to me to seek advice on issues or tell me what they are going through at home or in school. I do encourage them. I used to tell them that though I am not their biological mother, I am still a mother figure to them. Whenever I collect my salary, I used to dedicate part of it to their welfare. I buy socks, shoes, writing materials etc for them. I am glad that my husband also supports me, as without his support, I won’t be able to do those things.”

Is she not behaving like a dog which wants to keep guard in two different apartments? Will one duty, precisely, her official duty, not suffer neglect, since she has turned herself to a timekeeper for the students? Explaining, she said she found a way of not letting her zeal for community work stand in the way of her official duty.

“As a traffic officer, when I get to my point of duty, I will control the traffic to ensure free flow. Also, there are other officers with me including LASTMA people. After ensuring that the traffic is flowing, then I can move down to begin to look out for where the children normally stay to loiter. I have my whistle and I will blow it. Once I do that, the students will begin to run and move in the directions of their schools. Though I used to carry I cane, I never used it. The children fear me and when they hear the whistle, they know it is me and will do the right thing by heading to their schools.”

With the thinking in some quarters that discipline has taken flight from our schools, the police inspector emphatised with teachers, expressing the feeling that they are surely overwhelmed with the number of students they cater to and handle.

As a law officer and a mother, one would expect her to have a tough approach to raising children, but Omogbai believes that raising children is not all about shouting or beating them, “but talk to them like a parent and they will understand.”

In the course of her community voluntary work, she said there has not been any reason to recommend taking any of the students to a remand home. “If they have issues with their teachers or school authorities , I do intervene and help to settle such,” she stated.

On the part her background plays in her attitude to life, she noted her desire has been to positively impact others anytime and anywhere she goes.

“I was born and raised in the barracks, the Air Force Base and I am married to an Air Force personnel. I want to make a difference in the lives of people, children, widows and anybody who comes my way and I am in the position to help. I never knew people were watching me. All of a sudden, somebody just told me they needed my attention at Trinity University and I asked whether I have done anything wrong and he said no, that they saw my good works and truly I enjoy doing the work. When you do good, God has a way of rewarding you.

I am overwhelmed with the recognition given me by Trinity University. You could see that I was unable to talk, I shed tears of joy. I just started thanking God.”

The motherly Police Inspector had encomium poured on her by the Vice Chancellor of Trinity University, Prof. Clement Kolawole and the Registrar, Mr David Oyejide, who described her as a positive influence on the young ones, who could learn the art of kindness and assisting others from her.

Omogbai, who has received recognitions and has been honoured by different groups and individuals, is an example of proving wrong those who don’t believe that nothing good can come out of Nazareth of the Nigeria Police Force.

World.title: Imo 2027: Can Uzodimma break 27-year-old jinx?
World.content:
Gov Hope Uzodimma of Imo State

By Emmanuel Iheaka

SINCE the return to democracy in 1999, no governor of Imo State has produced a successor. The first governor of the state in the current republic, Chief Achike Udenwa, failed to install a successor at the end of his two-term of eight years in 2007.

Successive governors of the state have emerged through either what could be described as ballot revolution or powers from above.

By the time the dust of the 2007 governorship election in the state settled, Chief Ikedi Ohakim of the now defunct Progressive Peoples Alliance, PPA, had been declared the new helmsman of Imo. Ohakim would later be ousted in 2011, in what could be described as one of the biggest political upsets in the current republic in the state.

Eccentric Rochas Okorocha led a people-centred movement to displace Ohakim. But again, Okorocha failed to install a successor, when what majority saw as a selfish bid to crown his son in-law, came crumbling like a pack of cards.

Former Speaker, House of Representatives, Chief Emeka Ihedioha, had the shortest stay on the governorship saddle of the state, following his sack by the Supreme Court, which paved the way for the incumbent, Senator Hope Uzodimma.

Can Uzodimma break the jinx by producing a successor? Time will tell. However, there are early indications that the opposition will literally be fighting the battle of their life in the bid to maintain the history of the state, in not allowing any governor to produce a successor. Though the state government and the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, have distanced themselves, the early attacks on opposition parties leave no one in doubt that it is not going to be a walk in the park for those opposing the APC.

Pre-poll violence

About a week ago, thugs reportedly disrupted a meeting of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, in Owerri Municipal, in which a Senatorial candidate of the party, Uche Onyeagucha, was addressing party members.

Few days after the incident, the Young Progressives Party, YPP, and the All Peoples Party, APP, reported an attempt to break into their secretariats and destruction of their billboards at about midnight.

The Imo State Chairman of YPP, Michael Anyanwu, said he got a distress call at about 3:00am on the fateful day, alerting him of the attack. Anyanwu vowed that his party would fight on.

“I got a distress call by security guards on ground that between the hours of 3 and 4am, some unidentified men in an unmarked Sienna vehicle came to our party secretariat, vandalised our signages and wanted to make entry into the party secretariat, if not that our security guards had to create panic alert which made them to disperse.

“This is not campaign signage, this is just to show landmark. I wonder why we will be targeted. Are they trying to silence opposition parties in Imo State?

“I have gone to the police to make an entry. We are law-abiding party; we are not going to be cowed by anybody”, the chairman submitted.

Attack stage-managed – APC

The ruling APC has dismissed the said attack as stage-managed, and warned the opposition to play by the rules.

In a statement, the state Publicity Secretary of the APC, Onwuasoanya Jones, said there were indications that the purported attack might have been stage-managed.

APC stated that it is not threatened by the existence of any opposition party in the state and urged the opposition to play by the rules.

“The All Progressives Congress in Imo State is not threatened by the existence of any political Party and would not go outside the law and established democratic methods in ensuring that we maintain our unassailable popularity and acceptability with Imo people.

“Our Party frowns at any act of violence and disorderly behaviour and we encourage all opposition parties in the state to play by the rules by working towards convincing Imolites with logical arguments and verifiable records about why their parties might deserve the consideration of Imo people, rather than resorting to crude and unlawful strategies in order to draw attention.

“While these parties might consider this as Disruptive Advertising or Marketing strategy, we must warn them to ensure that they follow the law in carrying out their activities and marketing their political parties to the populace, as any attempt to disturb the peace of the state or cause panic will be reported to the appropriate authorities for necessary investigations and actions”, the party had submitted.

Speaking to Vanguard, APP which has become a major opposition party in the state, however, appears unperturbed and unruffled. Cajetan Duke, former Publicity Secretary of the party in Imo, and now the Chief Press Secretary to the leader of the party, Chima Amadi, insisted that APC is exit-bound in the state. According to Duke, the recent actions of the APC follow the known last minute pattern of actions of previously ousted ruling parties in the state.

“APP has demonstrated enough readiness for the 2027 general elections in Imo. APC is aware that APP is the party to beat in Imo. APP is now the largest number one opposition party in Imo. We have two National Assembly members. That’s an indication of strength and acceptability.

“What is happening in Imo has become a panic-reaction pattern by governments. In 2011, the PDP government was very hostile to Imo people because they realised the people had rejected them, to the point the government prevented APGA from holding a rally at the stadium. At a time, Rochas had to hold the rally on the streets of Owerri. What was the resultant effect of it, the people spoke through the ballot.

Panic mood

“In 2019, the outgoing government went into that panic mood and became hostile to the opposition. When they realised the people had left them, they decided to weaponise the government against the opposition. At the end of the day, the people stood their ground.

“Today, the APC in Imo knows that the 2027 election is about the people trying to take back their destiny in their hands. The people are looking for credible alternatives and they have found that in APP.

“You cannot intimidate people who have made up their minds. We have seen governments come and go. We know the behavioural tendencies of a government that is exit-bound. Imo people should remain resolute and law abiding. The darkest part of the night is the hour next to dawn. Guard your PVC, our votes will count”.

Another major opposition party in the state, the African Democratic Congress, ADC, told Vanguard that it was battle-ready for the APC.

State Publicity Secretary of the party, Macdonald Amadi, claimed that ADC has captured the nooks and crannies of the state .

“My party has come to save Nigeria from hunger and starvation; provide basic health, quality education, and infrastructure. Our party is rooted in rule of law, and abhors violence and election rigging.

“If there is any party that is prepared to rule in Imo, it is ADC. Our party has sold itself to the people of Imo in all the nooks and crannies of the state. We are ready for the 2027 general elections.

“Our party is against blackmail and running down individuals. ADC believes in constructive criticism and holding governments accountable by getting them to pursue policies aimed at ensuring the welfare of the people.”

Uzodimma’s scorecard

There is a seeming consensus that the Uzodimma administration has done well in road construction and rescuing the state to a large extent, from the insecurity that ravaged it for years. But not a few point to the apparent neglect of the education sector, with many school buildings in decrepit condition. There is also what analysts describe as the disconnect between Uzodimma and the people, owing to what they term the governor’s elitist disposition.

The APP led by the energetic Chima Amadi, and House of Representatives member, Ikenga Ugochinyere, has been vociferous in its criticism of the Uzodimma administration.

The ADC, led by Emeka Ihedioha, has however, not been that loud. The surprising appearance of the erstwhile House of Representatives Speaker at the recent celebration of Imo at 50, where he received an award from Uzodimma, had sparked speculations and permutations about the 2027 political intrigues.

The NDC doesn’t seem to have a definite governor aspirant at the moment. But one can easily guess that the former Chairman of the Nigeria Electricity Regulatory Commission, Dr. Sam Amadi, will fill in the gap.

Whatever be the case, the forthcoming 2027 off-circle governorship election in Imo will be a clash of the titans that will either rewrite or retain the political history of the state.

World.title: US court orders halt to White House ballroom construction; Trump reacts
World.content:
(FILES) A view of the ongoing construction of a helipad (L) and ballroom (R) at the White House, as seen from the Washington Monument observation deck in Washington, DC on July 23, 2026. An appeals court on August 7, upheld a US judge’s order to halt construction on President Donald Trump’s prized White House ballroom, but issued a two-week delay to enforcement for a possible Supreme Court appeal. (Photo by Kent Nishimura / AFP)

An appeals court on Friday upheld an order halting work on Donald Trump’s prized White House ballroom, enraging the US leader and setting up another Supreme Court battle over the limits of presidential authority.

The US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit, which had allowed construction to continue while it considered the case, agreed with a lower court that such a massive White House overhaul required the explicit consent of Congress.

It stayed its own decision for two weeks to give Trump time to ask the Supreme Court to intervene.

The Republican president lashed out after the 2-1 ruling, calling it “horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful.”

The two judges in the majority were appointed by Democratic presidents, while the dissenter was nominated by Trump himself.

The president vowed in a lengthy social media post to immediately appeal to the Supreme Court.

“This decision, made after much of the work has been done and paid for, is a National Security Threat at the highest level. It is also a National Disgrace,” Trump said in another post on his Truth Social platform Friday night.

Trump initially touted the construction of the ballroom as being necessary to host galas, but has since repeatedly pointed to the concurrent addition of an underground military bunker and other security features.

– East Wing –

Under the district judge’s initial order, work was to be allowed to continue only on a limited set of structures, including those that were underground.

“This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom,” the majority wrote Friday.

“What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the Constitution and laws require.”

Trump, who has repeatedly complained that the White House lacks sufficient space for grand galas such as state dinners, unilaterally ordered construction of the massive ballroom.

Work on the project began last year with the sudden demolition of the White House’s entire historic East Wing.

Since then, photos have shown significant work on a basement complex, with some concrete walls rising up above ground.

Trump has insisted that the ballroom will be privately financed, but media reports in June showed that significant taxpayer funds were going to the project, which could cost as much as $600 million.

While the White House initially cited a $200 million price tag for the project, it quickly doubled the estimate to $400 million.

The ballroom is just one of Trump’s pet projects to leave his mark on Washington by the time he leaves office in 2029, along with a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other parks, as well as the construction of a gigantic arch.

Several of the projects have similarly faced legal challenges, but the ballroom project would be the first to reach the Supreme Court.

AFP

World.title: Salvation in the bus!, by Stephanie Shaakaa
World.content:
There is a peculiar talent that governments sometimes acquire after years in office. It is the ability to mistake the symptom for the disease, to become so captivated by the manageable inconvenience that the genuine emergency fades into the wallpaper. Nations reveal themselves not only by the crises they endure, but by the crises they choose to confront. Some spend decades strengthening schools, courts and hospitals because they understand that institutions outlive administrations. Others become fascinated by the theatre of governance, where visible action is mistaken for meaningful progress.

The recent controversy surrounding the Federal Road Safety Corps amendment bill and its provision on preaching, hawking and trading inside commercial vehicles belongs to that familiar theatre. Whether the clause merely restated an existing prohibition or represented a fresh legislative impulse is almost incidental. The real story was never a preacher standing in the aisle of a commercial bus. It was our astonishing ability to invest enormous public energy in a question that sits comfortably on the margins while the centre continues to collapse.

If anyone wishes to understand why that instinct has become so deeply Nigerian, they should spend a single morning inside a commercial bus.

A woman climbs aboard carrying two bags of tomatoes. To everyone else, they are groceries waiting to become sales. To her, they are school fees, cough syrup, transport fare and, if the day is kind, a piece of meat in the evening pot. She settles into a cracked seat and instinctively draws the bags closer, knowing that tomatoes bruise almost as easily as profit.

Around her sits a country held together by quiet endurance. An elderly man keeps opening a brown envelope to reassure himself that the hospital test results are still inside. Across from him, a university graduate studies the reflection on the dark screen of his phone, silently rehearsing answers for interviews that rarely become employment. A young mother rocks a sleepy child while calculating how long she can postpone buying another tin of infant formula. Beside the window, a mechanic with grease permanently worked into his fingernails sleeps with the heavy exhaustion of someone who has mistaken survival for rest.

Nobody asks another passenger’s name. It is unnecessary. In a Nigerian commercial bus, introductions are a luxury. Everyone arrives carrying a private burden, and everyone leaves with it. The conductor slaps the body of the bus.

“One more! One more!”

It is the oldest fiction in public transportation. There is never one more. There are always four.

The engine coughs awake and the bus joins the slow procession of a city already bargaining with itself. Hawkers drift effortlessly through the traffic selling bottled water, handkerchiefs, chargers and biscuits. Office workers weave between vehicles with the urgency of people who know that lateness in Nigeria is often punished more severely than incompetence. Somewhere ahead, a broken-down tanker has converted an ordinary road into a lesson in collective patience.

Inside the bus, the country’s parliament is already in session.

“My landlord says the rent is going up again.”

“My son graduated two years ago. He’s still looking.”

“Rice was cheaper last week.”

No one raises a voice. Hardship rarely requires volume. It simply settles into the empty spaces between ordinary conversations.

The woman with the tomatoes says nothing. She is occupied by a mathematics that no university teaches. If she sells everything before noon, she can restock tomorrow. If prices rise again, she will buy fewer baskets. If her youngest daughter’s cough refuses to disappear, medicine will compete with school fees. If nothing unexpected happens, and in Nigeria that is always the most expensive assumption, perhaps tomorrow will resemble today.

Then the bus crashes into a pothole.

The tomatoes lurch forward. She catches them before they spill into the aisle. The old man instinctively shields his envelope. The graduate grips his phone. For a brief moment, every passenger reaches for the one fragile thing that cannot afford to break.

At the next junction, a man rises from the back seat with a small Bible in his hand. His faded blue shirt has survived too many washings to remember its original colour. He smiles, clears his throat and begins softly. “My brothers and sisters…”

Half the passengers already know how the story will unfold. Some bow their heads. Others continue staring through the window. The conductor keeps demanding exact change with unwavering commitment. The preacher speaks quietly about gratitude, uncertain journeys and the dangerous confidence of believing tomorrow has already made promises to us.

When he finishes, he thanks the passengers, returns to his seat and becomes anonymous once again.

The bus moves on, carrying not merely commuters, but a republic in miniature.

In Part Two, I’ll pivot from this bus journey to the deeper political argument, showing why the real issue was never the preacher at all, before ending with a much more haunting conclusion built around the tomato seller. I think that’s where this version can rise from excellent to genuinely memorable.

The bus offers a useful education for anyone trying to understand the country’s political imagination. A visitor spending his first day in Nigeria would leave with a catalogue of obvious national anxieties. He would see roads that consume more hours than distance should permit. He would hear conversations shaped by inflation, unemployment, rising rents and shrinking purchasing power. He would notice that almost every passenger is carrying a calculation invisible to everyone else, forever adding, subtracting and postponing. He would reasonably conclude that these are the questions occupying the full attention of those entrusted with governing.

Then he would discover that one of the loudest public arguments concerns what should happen when someone begins preaching before the conductor has finished collecting transport fare.

The bewilderment would be understandable. No society should object to conversations about courtesy in shared public spaces. Commuters deserve peace if they want it. Those who preach, trade or entertain inside commercial vehicles should exercise consideration for people who may be carrying grief, exhaustion or simply a desire for silence. Civilised societies are built on mutual respect.

But proportion matters. The measure of a government’s seriousness is not whether it can regulate the small inconveniences of everyday life. It is whether it can summon the imagination and discipline to confront the larger forces that make those inconveniences feel unbearable in the first place.

The woman carrying tomatoes does not board that bus wondering whether someone might preach before she reaches her destination. She wonders whether she will sell enough before the afternoon heat softens the fruit. The graduate is not consumed by the possibility of an unsolicited sermon. He is wondering whether another week will pass without the telephone call that changes his life. The elderly man is thinking about test results, not public order. Their burdens are older than the debate. They will almost certainly outlive it.

That is the danger of symbolic politics. It creates the reassuring appearance of movement while leaving reality stubbornly where it has always been. It is easier to regulate behaviour than to repair institutions, easier to draft another rule than to rebuild an economy, easier to police the visible than to confront the slow, patient failures that quietly shape a nation’s destiny.

History is full of governments that became remarkably efficient at organising appearances while neglecting foundations. They announced campaigns as factories closed. They enforced order as public confidence dissolved. They perfected the language of action while ordinary people perfected the art of endurance.

Nigeria has never lacked regulations. It has too often lacked the institutions that make regulations meaningful. Perhaps that is why the commercial bus feels less like public transport than a moving census of deferred dreams. Every morning it gathers strangers whose lives would never otherwise intersect and reminds us that the country’s greatest common language is not ethnicity, religion or politics, but quiet perseverance. The accountant, the trader, the mechanic, the graduate and the widow may vote differently and pray differently, but they all understand the arithmetic of survival.

That is also why the preacher is not really the central figure in this story. The tomato seller is. She never interrupted the sermon because survival had already become her liturgy. She needed no microphone to testify. Her gospel was written in prices that rose faster than her earnings, in children whose appetites ignored inflation, and in the fragile hope that tomorrow’s market might be kinder than today’s.

When the bus finally reached her stop, she lifted her bags with the same care she had shown when she boarded, stepped into the morning and disappeared into the crowd. The preacher’s words remained inside the bus. Her work continued outside it. Perhaps that is where every public policy should ultimately be judged. Not by the applause it attracts, the headlines it generates or the impression of decisiveness it creates, but by a far simpler question. When the woman carrying the tomatoes gets off the bus, is her journey towards dignity any shorter than it was before?

If the answer is no, then we may have regulated another symptom while leaving the disease untouched. Everything else is conversation. She still has tomatoes to sell.

World.title: 2027 Presidency: Rivers people will decide who wins — Reuben Abati; Rufai Oseni disagrees
World.content:
Federal Capital Territory (FCT) minister, Nyesom Wike

*No, Wike will actualise his boast, will deliver Tinubu – Rufai Oseni

By Juliet Umeh

The political temperature ahead of the 2027 general election rose another notch this week as comments by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, that Rivers State was already secured for President Bola Tinubu triggered a heated debate on ARISE Television’s The Morning Show.

Read Also: Tinubu’s EFCC directive over Osun govt’s account sparks fresh questions over agency’s independence

The programme also examined claims by Catholic leaders that the Presidency should pay closer attention to the realities facing Nigerians, with the show’s anchors disagreeing over whether President Tinubu is being shielded from public opinion.

The controversy followed Wike’s declaration during his media chat in Abuja that politicians eyeing Rivers State for the 2027 presidential election should “forget it,” insisting that the state belongs politically to President Tinubu.

“I am telling you, let nobody make a mistake. The only person that can win Rivers State is Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu,” the minister declared, describing himself as “a political realist.”

The remarks immediately generated reactions on social media, with many users arguing that such comments could discourage voters and undermine confidence in the electoral process.

On ARISE Television, Ayo Mairo-Ese urged Nigerians not to interpret Wike’s comments as a foregone conclusion, describing them as political posturing intended to unsettle opponents.

“What he was doing is what we call mind games. It is ‘political big speak’. It is psychological warfare,” she said.

According to her, regardless of political influence, elections are ultimately decided by voters.

“Wike has one vote, just like every other Nigerian. The people of Rivers State will determine who emerges as the winner.”

She, however, warned that influential political figures should exercise caution because statements suggesting that election outcomes have already been determined could deepen voter apathy.

She also challenged the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, to strengthen public confidence by conducting elections that leave no room for manipulation.

“INEC has to demonstrate that every vote counts and that elections are free, fair and credible,” she added.

But co-anchor Rufai Oseni disagreed sharply with Mairo-Ese’s interpretation, arguing that Wike’s remarks should not be dismissed as mere political posturing because they reflected what many Nigerians already perceive about the country’s electoral system.

Oseni argued that the minister’s confidence was rooted in his political influence and controversies surrounding the 2023 presidential election in Rivers State where figues declared didn’t tally with the ones on IREV which he said the BBC pointed out in a special report on Ngeria. Although he said that Wike’s statements reinforced public distrust in democracy, he was ready to bet with anybody that Wike’a claims would come to pass.

“With due respect, he is not saying what he has not done. He is saying what he has done,” Oseni said, citing reports that questioned aspects of the 2023 election in Rivers and recalling Wike’s own claims about his dominance of the state’s political structure.

He argued that pretending such fears do not exist would only deepen public cynicism, insisting that many Nigerians already doubt whether elections truly reflect the will of the people.

“We keep saying we don’t want voter apathy, but many people already believe the process is a charade already,” he said.

He maintained that many Nigerians already believe the electoral process is compromised and that journalists should confront that perception rather than dismiss it in the name of encouraging voter participation.

Dr. Reuben Abati, however, rejected Rufai’s position, insisting that no politician has the constitutional authority to determine electoral outcomes.

“Wike is just like every other Nigerian qualified to vote. He has only one vote,” Abati said.

“He cannot sit today and announce the outcome of the 2027 election in Rivers State.”

Describing Wike’s position as “a trip of delusion,” Abati stressed that only INEC is empowered by law to declare election results.

He urged Rivers voters not to surrender their democratic rights because of political pronouncements.

“The people of Rivers State have the right to go out and make their own informed choice,” he said, adding that those who attempt to undermine the electoral process should be held accountable.

The discussion later shifted to criticism of the Tinubu administration by Catholic leaders following recent comments by Archbishop Emeritus Cardinal John Onaiyekan and Monsignor Obiora Ike.

While some commentators suggested that those around the President were shielding him from the realities confronting Nigerians, Rufai disagreed.

“There is no way the President will not know about all these things. He knows,” he said.

According to him, President Tinubu has repeatedly responded to public criticism during meetings with religious leaders and traditional rulers, showing that he is fully aware of the hardship facing citizens.

“The issue is not awareness. The issue is whether the government’s narrative is landing with Nigerians,” he argued.

He noted that although the administration continues to defend its economic reforms, many Nigerians remain unconvinced because of rising hardship, insecurity and the high cost of living. Abati took a different view, defending the right of religious leaders to speak on national issues. He said the Catholic Church has historically challenged governments whenever it considered it necessary in the public interest.

“The Catholic Church has a reputation for speaking its mind. They are not in the business of opposing the government for the sake of it,” he said. He added that the government should see such interventions as constructive criticism rather than hostility.

“What we want in Nigeria is a prophetic Church that defends the interest of the people and speaks truth to power.”

The exchanges reflected growing national anxiety over electoral credibility, governance and public trust ahead of the 2027 general election, with the three analysts offering sharply different interpretations of whether Wike’s declaration was merely political bravado or a reflection of deeper concerns about Nigeria’s democratic process.

World.title: Tense Osun Poll: Vote Buying Worries INEC
World.content:
*CSOs flag 13 high-risk LGAs, appeal for police neutrality

*Kudos, knocks trail Tinubu’s directive to unfreeze state’s account

*Police assure Nigerians of peaceful, credible governorship election

Adedayo Akinwale, Sunday Aborisade and Linus Aleke in Abuja and Yinka Kolawole in Osogbo

Ahead of the August 15 governorship election in Osun State, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) yesterday expressed concern over the growing threat of vote buying, warning that the practice could undermine the credibility of the poll if not decisively checked by security agencies.



This comes as Civil Society Concerns on Election Security in Osun urged the Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies to remain neutral and professional during the state governorship election.

Also yesterday, reactions continued to trail President Bola Tinubu’s Thursday’s directive ordering the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to return to court and vacate the order freezing the Osun State Government’s bank accounts, with political parties, civil society organisations and security agencies expressing divergent views over the development.



While the Inter-Party Advisory Council (IPAC) in Osun State and the opposition Accord Party commended the President’s intervention as a demonstration of respect for democracy and the rule of law, the Civil Society Legislative Advocacy Centre (CISLAC) warned that the directive could undermine the operational independence of anti-corruption institutions.

The House of Representatives Minority Caucus said the directive issued by the President to the EFCC was due to massive public outcry and not by respect for the rule of law.



Also, the Inspector-General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Disu, yesterday assured Nigerians that adequate security arrangements had been put in place to ensure a peaceful, free, fair and credible governorship election.

Speaking on INEC’s level of preparedness, a senior official of the Commission who spoke to THISDAY on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to comment publicly on the election, said while the electoral body was fully prepared for the exercise, vote buying remained one of its biggest concerns given the heightened political atmosphere in the state.



The official disclosed that the commission had completed virtually all critical preparations for the election, including the deployment of election materials, training of personnel and testing of its electoral technology.

“As far as INEC is concerned, I can confidently say we are over 90 per cent prepared for the election,” the official said.

He revealed that INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, recently led a comprehensive readiness assessment in the state, which involved six National Commissioners, directors, senior officials and technical staff.



According to him, the exercise, which lasted about five days, involved a thorough review of every aspect of the commission’s preparations, including a mock accreditation exercise to test the effectiveness of the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS).

The official, however, stressed that INEC alone could not guarantee a credible election, saying the success of the poll would depend on the conduct of security agencies, political parties and their supporters.



He described the political environment in Osun as “quite tense,” urging all stakeholders to exercise restraint and uphold the rules of engagement.

“Our biggest concern is vote buying, which we fear could be widespread. We want the Nigeria Police and other security agencies to remain professional, impartial and above board in enforcing the law.



“Vote buying is prohibited under the Electoral Act. It is a criminal offence and one of the greatest threats to the integrity of Nigeria’s electoral process. Anyone arrested for the offence should face the full weight of the law,” the official added.

Meanwhile, the Civil Society Concerns on Election Security in Osun has urged the Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies to remain neutral and professional during the state governorship election.



The group made the call yesterday, during a press conference at the Nigeria Police Force Headquarters in Abuja.

Executive Director Samson Itodo, who spoke on behalf of the group, warned that public confidence in the electoral process would depend largely on how security personnel conduct themselves before, during and after the poll.



“This is the last major election to be held ahead of the 2027 general election. Therefore, it has a lot of significance, and it’s a unique opportunity to inspire public trust, not just in the management of the election, but election security.

“The public would want to see institutions demonstrate neutrality so they can have confidence in those institutions,” Itodo stated.

He warned that the level of pre-election violence and political tension recorded in parts of Osun State could undermine public trust and confidence if not effectively addressed.



He disclosed that findings from Yiaga Africa’s election observation and risk assessment showed that 13 of Osun State’s 30 local government areas have been classified as high-risk due to recurring violent incidents and heightened political tension.

These he said included Irewole, Osogbo, Boripe, Obokun, Ife North, Ife Central, and parts of Ijesaland.

He added. “Our comprehensive assessment and monitoring process shows that there have been about 34 known fatalities across incidents recorded between 2025 and June 2026.”



In the meantime, reactions have continued to trail President Tinubu’s directive ordering the EFCC to return to court and vacate the order freezing the Osun State Government’s bank accounts ahead of the August 15 governorship election.



IPAC, in a statement issued yesterday by its Caretaker Committee Chairman, Odesola Oluseye Titus, described President Tinubu’s directive to the EFCC as a demonstration of respect for democratic principles and the rule of law.

The council said the President’s action had reinforced confidence in Nigeria’s democratic institutions and should serve as a guide for all agencies involved in the electoral process.



Commending Tinubu for directing the anti-graft agency to vacate the court order, IPAC also praised the President’s insistence on the independence and professionalism of law enforcement agencies.

Quoting Tinubu’s position that anti-corruption agencies should discharge their statutory responsibilities “independently, professionally, without fear or favour or political interference,” the council described the President as “the father of the nation.”



It urged INEC, the Nigeria Police Force, the Nigerian Army and other security agencies to emulate the President’s example by performing their constitutional responsibilities impartially.



According to IPAC, the President’s directive should guide the conduct of all agencies involved in the forthcoming governorship election, stressing that security agencies and electoral officials must act professionally to sustain public confidence in the electoral process.

The council also appealed to political actors to respect the rules of engagement and urged eligible voters to come out en masse on election day, expressing confidence that every vote would count.



However, the opposition Accord Party demanded the immediate resignation of the Chairman of the EFCC, Ola Olukoyede, insisting that he should be held accountable for approving what it described as the unconstitutional freezing of the Osun State Government’s bank accounts.



Speaking at a world press conference in Abuja, the party’s National Chairman, Chief Maxwell Mgbudem, commended President Tinubu for what he termed a timely intervention that prevented a constitutional crisis.

He, however, argued that the EFCC chairman had embarrassed the President, damaged Nigeria’s democratic image and brought the anti-corruption agency into disrepute.

Mgbudem said if Olukoyede failed to resign voluntarily, President Tinubu should remove him from office to restore public confidence in the Commission.



The Accord chairman also called for the immediate release of about 60 of the party’s members allegedly detained in Abuja, Osun and Nasarawa States, saying their continued detention could heighten political tension ahead of the election.

He further urged INEC to conduct a free, fair and credible governorship election, describing the Osun poll as a critical test for Nigeria’s democracy ahead of the 2027 general election.



In a sharp contrast, the Executive Director of CISLAC and Head of Transparency International Nigeria, Auwal Musa Rafsanjani, criticised the President’s intervention, warning that directing the EFCC to seek the lifting of the court order could weaken the operational independence of anti-corruption institutions.



Addressing journalists in Abuja, Rafsanjani argued that while governance should not be unnecessarily disrupted, presidential intervention in specific enforcement actions created a dangerous precedent.

According to him, the EFCC derives its powers from the law and should be allowed to investigate and prosecute economic crimes professionally and without political interference.

He maintained that if the Commission took an inappropriate decision, the proper avenue for redress remained the judiciary rather than executive intervention.

Rafsanjani also stressed that lifting the restriction on the state’s accounts should not signal the end of investigations into the alleged diversion of public funds, insisting that anyone found culpable should face prosecution regardless of political affiliation.

In the meantime, the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, assured Nigerians that the Nigeria Police Force had concluded comprehensive security arrangements for the August 15 governorship election.

Hosting civil society organisations in Abuja ahead of the poll, the IGP said the Police had no preferred candidate or political party and remained committed to ensuring that the lawful choice of the people prevailed.

He disclosed that adequate personnel and operational assets had been deployed across Osun State, while intelligence gathering and threat assessments had been intensified in collaboration with INEC, the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES) and other stakeholders.

Disu warned that anyone involved in vote buying, ballot box snatching, voter intimidation, thuggery or any other electoral offence would be dealt with in accordance with the law, irrespective of political affiliation.

He also urged political parties and their supporters to conduct themselves peacefully, stressing that elections should be contests of ideas rather than violence and intimidation.

The Police boss encouraged eligible voters to come out without fear to exercise their constitutional rights, assuring them that the Force would provide a secure environment throughout the electoral process.

The political atmosphere in Osun also became more charged yesterday as the All Progressives Congress (APC) asked Governor Ademola Adeleke to apologise to President Tinubu and the Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, for accusing them of influencing the EFCC’s action against the state government.

The party maintained that while the President objected to the timing of the account freeze, he did not exonerate the Osun State Government from the allegations being investigated by the anti-graft agency.

The House of Representatives Minority Caucus said the directive issued by the President to the EFCC was due to massive public outcry and not by respect for the rule of law.

It added that the move exposed deep contradictions and a deliberate plot to intimidate the Osun State Government ahead of next week’s gubernatorial election.

Its Leader, Hon. Fredrick Agbedi and the Spokesman of the caucus, Hon. Afam Ogene in a statement issued yesterday, said the President’s directive exposed “a government at war with itself,”.

The caucus pointed out that while EFCC Spokesman, Mr. Wilson Uwujaren, stated on national television on Thursday that the freezing of Osun’s account was done “without a valid court order”, the President’s statement later same Thursday afternoon directed the Commission to go to court to “vacate the order.”

The caucus noted: “So, which is it? Was there a court order or not?. Is the President not aware of what his own appointees are saying and doing?

“Has the President lost control of his army of sycophants who behave like lords over the people? Or are they simply trying to hide an illegality that has already been exposed?”

The Caucus also accused the President’s senior aides of being the first to circulate and defend the EFCC’s initial press release supporting the EFCC overreach.

The Caucus described the August 5 EFCC action as the latest in what they termed a sustained campaign of intimidation against Osun by the APC-led Federal Government.

The caucus decried that for months, the federal government had illegally withheld and seized statutory allocations due to Osun Local Governments, describing it as economic strangulation aimed at crippling governance at the grassroots ahead of elections.”

It noted: “ The gestapo-style arrest and detention of the Secretary to the Osun State Government, Teslim Igbalaiye and others over flimsy accusations is a direct attack on the institution of the state government.”

Also yesterday, the World Bishops Council (Africa Chapter) and the Religious Engagement (Christianity) Committee working for Governor Adeleke’s re-election endorsed the governor for a second term, describing him as “a man of destiny” who had promoted peace and religious harmony in the state.

The groups urged voters to re-elect Adeleke and announced a seven-day fasting and prayer programme for peaceful elections and the governor’s victory.

In another development, the Imole Campaign Council dismissed an alleged oath-taking video circulating on social media and purportedly linked to Governor Adeleke, describing it as a desperate smear campaign orchestrated by the APC.

The council insisted that Adeleke neither authorised nor participated in any oath-taking exercise, maintaining that his re-election bid was anchored on his performance in office and the goodwill of the people rather than intimidation or superstition.

World.title: Senior Goldman Sachs Executives Visit Dangote Industries Limited, Laud World-class Refinery
World.content:
* Dangote targets $100bn annual revenue by 2030

*Goldman Sachs hails scale, quality of refinery

Sunday Ehigiator

Senior executives from leading global investment banking and financial services firm, Goldman Sachs have toured the Dangote Industries Limited’s integrated petroleum refinery, petrochemicals and fertiliser complex in Lagos.

The delegation, led by Co-Chief Executive Officer of Goldman Sachs International and Global Co-Head of Investment Banking, Anthony Gutman, visited the Dangote Petroleum Refinery & Petrochemicals, Dangote Fertiliser Limited and supporting infrastructure during a recent visit to Nigeria.

Speaking after an extensive tour of the 700,000 barrels per day refinery, the Goldman Sachs executives remarked, “It is extraordinary what Mr. Dangote and the whole organisation have achieved. The ambition, the scale of the project, the quality of the project and the culture of the people is very impressive.”

Responding, the President and Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, said the refinery and associated industrial facilities demonstrate the transformative potential of long-term investment in Africa, adding that the Group’s growth ambitions extend well beyond its current strategic plan.

“No matter how we try to explain what we have built, you cannot fully appreciate it until you see it. But this is only the beginning. We need to look beyond 2030. The next phase of our journey will include new investments and acquisitions as we continue to scale the business,” he was quoted to have said.

Dangote said detailed internal modelling had reinforced management’s confidence that the Group’s target of generating US$100 billion in annual revenue by 2030 was achievable. He noted that the projections were based on conservative assumptions and had strengthened the company’s conviction that it could pursue an even more ambitious long term growth strategy.

He added that the level of employee participation in the recent private placement of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery reflected strong internal belief in the company’s growth strategy and prospects.

The Goldman Sachs team included Adib N. Zouein, Co Head of EMEA Emerging Markets Regional Sales and Head of the Middle East and North Africa region for Global Banking & Markets Public; Ryad Yousuf, Global Head of FICC Sales Strats and Structuring; and Jimi Adesanya, Head of Sub Saharan Africa Sales (excluding South Africa).

They were received by Aliko Dangote; Group Vice President, Oil & Gas, Devakumar Edwin; Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery & Petrochemicals, David Bird; Group Executive Director, Oil & Gas, Fatima Aliko Dangote; Chief of Staff to the President/CE, Ibrahim Dikko; Group Chief Branding and Communication Officer, Anthony Chiejina; Group Chief Economist, Dr Hassan Mahmud; and Group Chief Strategy Officer, Aliyu Suleiman, among others.

The visit came a few days after Aliko Dangote held discussions with Canada’s Prime Minister, Mark Carney, on opportunities to strengthen investment partnerships and deepen economic cooperation between Canada and Africa.

The meeting focused on expanding investment opportunities in Canada and exploring how the Dangote Group, alongside other African investors, could contribute to Canada’s economic growth. Both leaders also exchanged views on Canada’s Africa Strategy and the importance of promoting stronger two-way trade and investment flows between Canada and African countries.

Dangote had also emphasised the growing potential for collaboration between African and Canadian businesses, noting that closer economic ties would unlock new opportunities for job creation, innovation, industrial development, and long-term prosperity.

“Strategic partnerships between Africa and Canada have immense potential to drive sustainable growth and create value for both regions. There is a strong case for increasing investment, fostering innovation, and building mutually beneficial commercial relationships,” Dangote had said.

World.title: US Appeals Court Blocks Trump’s $400m White House Ballroom Project
World.content:
Oluchi Chibuzor with agency report



A United States federal appeals court yesterday ordered Donald Trump’s administration to stop construction on a $400 million ballroom on the site of the White House’s demolished East Wing, dealing the Republican leader a major setback in a case testing his presidential authority.



“Each ‌President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House,” and cannot fundamentally reshape it without congressional approval, Reuters quoted the Washington-based U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to have said in a 2-1 opinion.

The order upheld a preliminary injunction won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued last year after the administration tore down the East Wing and began building a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom without seeking authorization from Congress.



“Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” the panel’s majority wrote.

The appeals court placed its ruling on hold for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Trump, who has increasingly claimed that the ballroom project was a security necessity, referred to the structure as a “military center” in a post on Truth Social on Friday and said the administration would appeal to the Supreme Court. He called the decision “horrendous” and politically motivated and said it left him, other White House officials and visitors exposed to attack.



“This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety,” Trump wrote. He said the ballroom plan includes bomb shelters, medical facilities, shielding from drones and missiles and other security features that are “all tied together as one big, expensive, and very complex unit.”



National Trust President Brent Leggs said in a statement that the ruling marked “a great day for our country and for the American people’s right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish, including the White House.”

Trump appealed after U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, an appointee of Republican former President George W. Bush, twice blocked above-ground construction on the site while allowing underground work to continue.

The ballroom plan, which the administration has described as necessary for large formal functions and to preserve the safety of the White House, is the grandest ‌of several Trump efforts to reshape central Washington’s landscape of government buildings and national monuments.



A judge in a separate lawsuit recently said Trump’s name was illegally added to the exterior of the Kennedy Center performing arts venue and ordered its removal.

In the ballroom case, Justice Department attorney Yaakov Roth said during D.C. Circuit arguments on June 5 that the courts have no role in weighing the privately funded project. He said the National Trust’s “architectural preference” should not take precedence over national security concerns, claiming evidence that the former East Wing left thepresident and others in the White House vulnerable to attack.



The Democratic-appointed judges in the appeals court’s majority — Circuit Judges Patricia Millett and Brad Garcia — said their order does not permanently bar construction of a ballroom, but halts above-ground work during the lawsuit and until the White House secures approval from Congress.



National security arguments “are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card,” the opinion said.

“The bold assertion that the Executive can act with utter lawlessness, destroying treasured national landmarks and harming the interestsof individuals, and that no court can stop it flouts our constitutional order,” the judges wrote.

Circuit Judge Neomi Rao, whom Trump appointed during his first term, said in her dissent that the trial judge’s injunction blocking the project “is beyond the proper province of the federal courts” and that construction should be allowed to continue.



“The district court seized supervision of construction at the White House, and my colleagues affirm this judicial overreach,” Rao wrote.

World.title: Extend Pay Rise for Military to Other Security Agencies, Rewane Tells FG
World.content:
· Reveals electronic payment transactions rose to N122.98trn in July

· Projected to hit N126.7trn in August

Nume Ekeghe

The Managing Director and Chief Executive of Financial Derivatives Company (FDC), Mr. Bismarck Rewane, has called on the federal government to extend the recently approved increase in the salary of military personnel to other security agencies, warning that excluding them could create distortions within the country’s security architecture.

This is as the economist also revealed that the value of electronic payment transactions in Nigeria increased by 5.54 per cent month-on-month to N122.98 trillion in July 2026, up from N116.52 trillion recorded in June. He projected that the figure would climb further to N126.70 trillion in August, as seasonal spending and the continued adoption of digital payment channels lift transaction values.

Rewane, while weighing in on the increase in emoluments, in a presentation he made at the August edition of the Lagos Business School (LBS) Breakfast Session, a copy of which was obtained by THISDAY yesterday, argued that following the federal government’s approval of a comprehensive wage review for personnel of the Nigerian Army, there should be a corresponding salary adjustment for the Nigeria Police Force, Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) and other security agencies to maintain equity and morale across the security services.

The wage review approved for the Nigerian Army provides for an 80 per cent increase for lower-ranking personnel, 50 per cent for officers from warrant officers to colonels, and 30 per cent for officers from colonels to generals, with the total cost estimated at N924 billion.

While acknowledging the importance of improving the welfare of military personnel, Rewane warned that the policy would inevitably have wider implications for the public and private sectors.

He said the salary adjustment would affect wage relativities across the public service and place pressure on private sector employers to review compensation packages.

“The knock-on effects will affect the rest of the public sector and the relativity factor for the private sector,” he stated.

He further cautioned that higher wages without a corresponding increase in productivity could fuel inflation, estimating that the adjustment could add between two and three percentage points to inflationary pressures.

“This will push wages higher without productivity. Inflation is bound to increase by a minimum of two to three per cent,” he noted.

Rewane stressed that fairness demanded a compensating salary review for all other security agencies.

“There must be a compensating review of all other security agencies and armed forces, including the Police and Civil Defence,” he said.

He, however, warned that such an expansion of the wage review would significantly increase recurrent expenditure across all tiers of government.

According to him, extending similar salary adjustments across the security services would lead to “a ballooning of government revenue expenditure at all levels,” further tightening fiscal conditions.

The economist urged policymakers to balance the imperative of improving the welfare of security personnel with measures that enhance productivity and strengthen government revenue in order to avoid worsening inflationary pressures and fiscal deficits.

Meanwhile, the report presented at the LBS showed that the Nigeria Instant Payment (NIP) platform remained the dominant payment channel, accounting for the bulk of transaction values. NIP transactions rose by 4.89 per cent to N109.59 trillion in July from N104.48 trillion in June.

The report also showed that the Nigeria Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT) platform recorded the fastest growth among the major payment channels, with transaction values surging 18.03 per cent to N6.48 trillion from N5.49 trillion in June. Point-of-Sale (PoS) transaction values increased by 5.56 per cent to N6.65 trillion, while cheque transactions rose modestly by 4.35 per cent to N264 billion.

Looking ahead, FDC projected that electronic payment transactions would expand further to N126.70 trillion in August. NIP transaction value was expected to rise to N112.21 trillion, while PoS transactions are forecast to jump sharply to N7.97 trillion as consumer spending strengthens during the holiday period. Although NEFT transactions are expected to moderate slightly to N6.29 trillion, overall electronic payment activity is projected to remain resilient, reinforcing the steady transition towards a cashless economy.

The latest monthly performance mirrors the longer-term expansion of digital payments highlighted in the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) 2025 Annual Report and Statement of Accounts.

According to the apex bank, the value of electronic payment transactions increased by 26.07 per cent to N3, 458.77 trillion in 2025, while transaction volume rose by 2.62 per cent to 47.88 billion transactions.

The CBN attributed the growth to stronger consumer preference for digital payment channels, expanding e-commerce activity and continued improvements in payment infrastructure.

It stated: “Analysis of retail payments showed notable changes between 2024 and 2025. The volume of e-payments transactions increased by 2.62 per cent to 47,879.73 million in 2025, compared with 2024. The value of transactions also rose by 26.07 per cent to N3, 458.77 trillion.

“The increases reflected user preferences, adoption of digital channels, growth in e-commerce, and infrastructure improvements.”

At the recent launch of the Payments System Vision 2028 (PSV 2028), CBN Governor, Mr. Olayemi Cardoso, had reaffirmed the apex bank’s commitment to achieving 95 per cent financial inclusion and enabling “faster-than-a-blink” digital transactions through sustained reforms of Nigeria’s payment ecosystem.

World.title: 2027: PDP, 15 APC Guber Aspirants Negotiate Power-sharing in Kwara
World.content:
.Cracks deepen in Kwara APC as PDP drafts Saraki to woo aggrieved members ahead of 2027

.Kwara APC reconciliation committee submits report, hails support of gov AbdulRazaq, party exco

Chuks Okocha in Abuja and Hammed Shittu in Ilorin

The Kwara State chapter of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the 15 aggrieved gubernatorial aspirants of All Progressives Congress (APC) in the state have commenced negotiations on the sharing of elective positions ahead of 2027 elections.

With political permutations ahead of the 2027 general elections gathering momentum, the Kwara State PDP has also moved to capitalise on the growing discontent within the ruling APC, mandating former Senate President, Bukola Saraki, to begin talks with aggrieved members of the party.

As part of efforts to put its troubled house in order which engulfed the party after the conduct of the party primaries in the state, the Kwara State APC Reconciliation Committee yesterday submitted their report to the State Working Committee of the party.

The parley according to THISDAY checks might not be unconnected with the recent resolutions of the PDP leadership to meet the aggrieved 15 APC gubernatorial aspirants towards fostering political understanding ahead of the forthcoming elections.

At the meeting of the aggrieved gubernatorial aspirants held in Ilorin on Thursday, they had pledged their commitment to the electoral victory of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu come 2027, but vowed not to work for the success of the APC in the state.

However, the PDP and the 15 aggrieved gubernatorial aspirants have set up a committee on how to share the elective positions before the final closure of the portal of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Sources close to the two groups told journalists in Ilorin yesterday, that the PDP camp was said to have presented six members of the state House of Assembly, two senatorial tickets and two House of Representatives slots to the 15 aggrieved gubernatorial aspirants’ camp.

On the part of the 15 aggrieved APC gubernatorial aspirants, the group was said to have demanded 10 slots of the members of the state House of Assembly, two senatorial tickets and two House of Representatives tickets from the PDP.

Speaking at a press briefing in Ilorin, spokesperson of the coalition and former Senator, Yahaya Oloriegbe, alleged that the governor’s leadership had sidelined many stakeholders and deepened divisions within the party.

He warned that unless the APC national leadership intervenes, the lingering crisis could undermine the party’s electoral prospects in the 2027 general elections.

According to Oloriegbe, the Oto Ge Progressives was formed to protect the principles of fairness, inclusiveness and transparency, alleging that many party faithful had been excluded from critical political decisions.

He also claimed that members of the coalition had been subjected to intimidation and pressure to support what he described as a predetermined succession arrangement.

The coalition insisted that candidates for elective offices must emerge through transparent and democratic processes rather than through the influence of any individual, urging the APC leadership to urgently address the grievances before they escalate.

Seizing on the apparent cracks within the ruling party, PDP stakeholders at a two-day strategic meeting in Ilorin authorised Saraki to commence consultations with members of the APC’s G15 bloc and other political groups as part of efforts to expand the party’s support base ahead of the next general elections.

The decision was contained in a communiqué jointly signed by the Kwara PDP Chairman, Adamu Bawa, and the State Secretary, Abdulrahman Kayode, following the meeting attended by party leaders, former political office holders, aspirants, women and youth representatives.

The communique said, “At the meeting, His Excellency, Dr. Abubakar Bukola Saraki appreciated all aspirants and stakeholders for the serious sacrifices they made before, during and after the 2026 party primaries, and for their commitment to the unity and growth of the PDP in Kwara State.

“After extensive deliberations, the stakeholders unanimously resolved as follows: stakeholders passed a vote of confidence on our National Leader, His Excellency, Dr. Abubakar Bukola Saraki, for his consistent leadership, political sagacity and unwavering commitment to the PDP and the people of Kwara State.

“Noting that the PDP in Kwara State is already strong and united, the meeting mandated His Excellency, Dr. Abubakar Bukola Saraki to proceed with engagements with members of the Kwara APC’s G15 and other political parties, with the objective of further strengthening the PDP and expanding its base ahead of future elections.”

The meeting also resolved that all stakeholders, aspirants, and candidates must be prepared to set aside personal ambitions and individual interests in the greater interest of the party.

Meanwhile, the APC had on 3rd of July 2026 set up the five-member committee, chaired by retired Col. AbdulWahab Ademola Lawal(rtd) to resolve internal disputes following the party’s primary elections.

Presenting the report at the party’s Secretariat in Ilorin, Col. Lawal, appreciated the governor and the party executives for their trust and for giving them an enabling environment to operate.

He said the committee had invited all the aggrieved members in the course of their findings and provided them with a level playing ground to ventilate their grievances – a step he noted aided their work.

He said that the committee, however, got assurances of the members to remain in the party and to “not go back to Egypt.”

“I want to say that on the mandate given to us we received the blessings of His Excellency (Governor AbdulRazaq), and the Party Chairman made it clear to us that: “please allow everybody to vent their anger and sentiments and also do what is needful,” he said, adding that the report will go a long way to resolving the disagreement.

“We made it clear to them that this is a family affair; no one is outside the family. All of us are together and in a family. But there are bound to be disagreements and therefore they should see us as mediators,” Lawal said.

The state APC Chairman Prince Sunday Fagbemi, thanked the committee for their effort, and pledging that the state leadership of the party will do everything humanly possible to do justice to the report.

He described Col. Lawal as highly disciplined and a diplomat par excellence, adding all members of the committee are people of integrity.

“When we go through the report of the committee, we will do all that is humanly possible to make sure we remain as a family.

“We are appealing to all that are aggrieved to await the actions that will be taken after the presentation of the committee’s report,” Fagbemi said.

Other members of the reconciliation committee are the Assistant Comptroller of Immigration, AIG Ahmed Abbas, Engr. Musa Yeketi, Dr. Oluwatoyin Opawoye and Hajia Kubura Kassum.

World.title: Woro Community Rescued Victims Arrive Kwara
World.content:
Hammed Shittu in Ilorin

The rescued victims abducted during the deadly February 3, 2026 attack on Woro community in Kaiama Local Government Area of Kwara State have arrived in Ilorin, Kwara state capital.

The victims numbering 163 were rescued on Wednesday August 5, 2026, by security forces after spending six months in captivity.

THISDAY checks revealed that the rescued victims arrived Ilorin, the state capital late Thursday night.

Sources told THISDAY that the affected rescued victims were received at the Nigerian Army’s 2 Division, Sobi Barracks, Ilorin.

They said the affected rescued victims were said to have been moved to an undisclosed location where they spent the night.

It would be recalled that the victims were abducted when armed bandits invaded the community earlier this year, killing scores of residents and whisking away many others into the forest, triggering widespread outrage and intensified security operations.

Following sustained military operations and coordinated efforts by security agencies, the victims regained their freedom and were transported from Niger State to Ilorin.

The rescued victims are expected to be officially handed over to Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq.

Their arrival marks a major breakthrough in the month-long efforts to secure the release of the abductees, while authorities continue to verify the number of those rescued and provide necessary care and support.

World.title: COAS Charges Troops to Uphold Professionalism as Army Expands New Formations
World.content:
.Troops arrest 4 Lakurawa terrorists, recover livestock in Sokoto

Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Chief of Army Staff (COAS), Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has charged soldiers graduating from Exercise RESTORE HOPE X to uphold the highest standards of professionalism, discipline and operational excellence as they prepare to serve in the Nigerian Army’s newly established divisions, formations and units.

This was as the troops of 8 Division Garrison of the Nigerian Army have apprehended four suspected Lakurawa terrorists while selling six cows at the Darussa Village market in Gudu Local Government Area of Sokoto State.

Speaking at the graduation ceremony of the Advanced Infantry Training Programme at the Nigerian Army Training Centre (NATC), Kachia, Kaduna State, the COAS described the exercise as the flagship of the Army’s post-basic infantry training framework, designed to sharpen combat proficiency, strengthen the warrior ethos and prepare soldiers for the realities of contemporary military operations.

According to a statement by the Acting Director of Army Public Relations, Colonel Appolonia Anele, Shaibu said the graduation coincided with the Army’s ongoing force expansion and capability enhancement following President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s approval for the restructuring of the Service. He noted that many of the graduands would form the nucleus of the newly established divisions, formations and units.

The Army Chief urged the soldiers to justify the investment in their training by demonstrating professionalism, sound judgement and unwavering commitment to mission accomplishment.

He also called on them to remain physically fit, mentally agile and technologically proficient while upholding the rule of law, protecting human rights and strictly observing the rules of engagement.

Earlier, the Chief of Training (Army), Major General Valentine Okoro, described Exercise RESTORE HOPE X as a critical component of the Nigerian Army’s training architecture, saying it had consistently produced combat-ready soldiers through realistic operational scenarios, leadership development and counter-insurgency training while strengthening institutional capacity across Army training establishments.

Meanwhile, a security source told the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) yesterday that the four Lakurawa terrorists suspects were engaged in trading livestock suspected to have been rustled.
