Brazil’s latest second-quarter reports offered four different readings of the economy. Diagnostic-services group Fleury converted expansion into sharply higher profit. Insurance distributor Wiz Co absorbed regulatory disruption. Onshore producer PetroReconcavo protected its operating margin despite lower volumes. Energisa’s growing utility platform, meanwhile, was overwhelmed at the bottom line by financial and extraordinary accounting effects.

Company Q2 profit / loss Year on year Main signal Fleury R$221.9m / US$43.5m +45.7% Broad-based growth Wiz Co, adjusted consolidated R$101.0m / US$19.8m −13.5% Consigned-credit pressure PetroReconcavo R$202.7m / US$39.7m −14.9% Price offset lower output Energisa, reported −R$40.0m / −US$7.8m From R$490m profit Financial and accounting drag

Fleury Converts Expansion Into a 46% Profit Jump

Fleury delivered the clearest positive report. Net income increased 45.7% to R$221.9 million (US$43.5 million), while net revenue rose 14.4% to R$2.31 billion (US$452.8 million). EBITDA reached R$612.9 million (US$120.1 million), up 15.2%, with a 26.5% margin.

Growth extended across consumer diagnostics, hospital services and newer healthcare businesses. The company cited integration of acquisitions, organic expansion and efficiency gains. Net margin improved to 9.6%, showing that the revenue increase was not absorbed by the larger operating footprint.

The board also approved R$217.8 million (US$42.7 million) in interest on equity. The near-quarterly-profit distribution signals confidence in cash generation, although Fleury must keep acquisition integration and leverage disciplined as it continues combining organic and purchased growth.

Wiz Co’s Two Profit Measures Move in Opposite Directions

Wiz Co reported consolidated adjusted net income of R$101.0 million (US$19.8 million), down 13.5%. Net revenue excluding commissions fell 18.0% to R$235.3 million (US$46.1 million), and consolidated adjusted EBITDA declined 19.2% to R$152.8 million (US$30.0 million).

The weaker consolidated comparison reflected regulatory changes affecting payroll-deducted credit and a tougher environment in parts of the Bmg and BRB distribution network. Issued insurance premiums fell about 10% to R$879.7 million (US$172.4 million), while credit and consortium sales volume dropped 10.1% to R$3.3 billion (US$646.8 million).

Profit attributable to the controlling company tells a different story: it rose 8.4% to R$53.6 million (US$10.5 million). That figure excludes the portion belonging to minority investors and should not be confused with consolidated adjusted profit. Inter Seguros reached a record result, partially offsetting pressure elsewhere in the portfolio.

PetroReconcavo Protects Margin as Production Falls

PetroReconcavo’s statutory net income fell 14.9% to R$202.7 million (US$39.7 million) from R$238.1 million (US$46.7 million). Net revenue was almost flat at R$807.9 million (US$158.4 million), while EBITDA increased 6% to R$396.1 million (US$77.6 million).

The EBITDA margin widened to 49.0% from 46.4%. Improved commercial terms for oil sold from the Potiguar asset and stronger realized pricing helped offset a 12% decline in average gross production to 24,100 barrels of oil equivalent per day. Free cash flow turned positive at R$74 million (US$14.5 million), from a R$99.9 million (US$19.6 million) outflow a year earlier.

Adjusted net income, which removes mark-to-market effects from hedges and related deferred tax, was lower still at R$104.6 million (US$20.5 million), down 33%. The board approved R$100 million (US$19.6 million) in interest on equity, but restoring production will be more important than quarterly derivative gains for sustaining future distributions.

Energisa’s Operating Growth Fails to Reach the Bottom Line

Energisa posted a consolidated net loss of R$40 million (US$7.8 million), reversing a R$490 million (US$96.0 million) profit in Q2 2025. The reported result included extraordinary accounting effects tied to the agreed sale of five transmission companies to Taesa and the resulting reclassification of those assets.

The recurring picture was also weak, though not loss-making. Adjusted recurring profit fell 80% to R$88 million (US$17.2 million), mainly because net financial expenses increased. Adjusted net revenue rose 4% to R$7.25 billion (US$1.42 billion), and recurring adjusted EBITDA edged 1% higher to R$1.95 billion (US$383.0 million).

Transmission, distributed generation and natural gas made positive EBITDA contributions, partially offsetting softness in electricity distribution and holding costs. Energisa approved R$251.5 million (US$49.3 million) in dividends, equivalent to R$0.50 per unit, for payment on August 24.

What the Four Reports Say About Brazil

Fleury’s result points to resilient private healthcare demand and successful consolidation. Wiz shows how quickly regulatory changes can disrupt fee-based financial distribution. PetroReconcavo demonstrates that stronger pricing can protect margins without solving declining field output. Energisa shows the burden that high financing costs can place on capital-intensive utilities even when operating revenue grows.

Investors should therefore look beyond the headline profit comparisons. The next tests are Fleury’s return on acquired capital, Wiz’s adaptation to new credit rules, PetroReconcavo’s production recovery and Energisa’s ability to reduce the financial drag on its expanding regulated asset base.

Consolidated adjusted profit fell 13.5% to R$101.0 million (US$19.8 million) as payroll-credit regulatory changes and weaker activity at some distribution partners reduced revenue and EBITDA.

Better oil-pricing and commercial terms lifted its EBITDA margin to 49.0%, but lower production, financial effects and other below-EBITDA items left statutory profit 14.9% lower.

World.title: Eztec Q2 Profit Falls 21% to US$22M; Launches Jump 58%
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Profit declined. Net income fell 21.0% to R$110.4 million (US$21.6 million). —Revenue contracted. Net revenue dropped 16.0% to R$376.7 million (US$73.8 million). —The margin remained high. Gross margin was 39.7%, compared with 40.7% a year earlier. —Launches accelerated. Q2 launch value rose 57.8% to R$773.0 million (US$151.5 million). —Net sales grew. Eztec’s share of net sales increased 18.2% to R$577.6 million (US$113.2 million). —A dividend was approved. The R$26.2 million (US$5.1 million) distribution equals about R$0.09 per common share.

Eztec’s income statement weakened just as its development engine accelerated: the quarter brought lower profit and revenue, but the strongest first-half sales and launch volumes in the company’s history.

São Paulo developer Eztec entered the second half of 2026 with a deliberately larger pipeline. That expansion did not prevent a year-on-year earnings decline in the second quarter, but it changed the meaning of the result: current revenue reflected the timing of project recognition, while sales and launches pointed to future delivery volume.

The Rio Times previously covered Eztec’s record first-half operating preview. The newly released financial statements add the missing earnings, margin, cash-flow and dividend detail, which is the focus of this report.

Profit and Revenue Fell From a Strong Comparison

Net income was R$110.4 million (US$21.6 million), down 21.0% from roughly R$139.8 million (US$27.4 million) in Q2 2025. Net revenue declined 16.0% to R$376.7 million (US$73.8 million). The bottom line nevertheless remained supported by Eztec’s financial income, including returns on its cash position and interest on customer receivables.

Gross margin eased one percentage point to 39.7% from 40.7%. Construction-cost savings and a land sale helped protect the margin despite lower recognized revenue. For a homebuilder, this measure matters because it captures both pricing discipline and whether cost inflation is being contained across long construction cycles.

Metric Q2 2026 Year on year Net income R$110.4m / US$21.6m −21.0% Net revenue R$376.7m / US$73.8m −16.0% Gross margin 39.7% −1.0 pp Launch value, Eztec share R$773.0m / US$151.5m +57.8% Net sales, Eztec share R$577.6m / US$113.2m +18.2% Net sales speed 14.8% −0.4 pp

Record First-Half Activity Builds the Backlog

Eztec launched three projects during Q2 with a combined company-share gross development value of R$773.0 million (US$151.5 million), 57.8% above the prior-year quarter. The largest was GranResort in São Caetano, followed by Azzure Resort Life in Osasco and a third phase of Reserva São Caetano Bosque.

The first-half total reached R$1.70 billion (US$332.8 million), up 53.5% and the company’s highest launch volume for any first half. Eztec kept its 2026 launch guidance at R$2.5 billion to R$3.5 billion (US$490.0 million to US$686.0 million), leaving a wide range for the timing of second-half projects.

Net sales rose 18.2% in Q2 to R$577.6 million (US$113.2 million). For the first half, net sales climbed 47.3% to R$1.27 billion (US$249.8 million), also a record. Sales of completed inventory grew 42% over the six-month period, an important sign because converting finished units releases capital that can be recycled into new developments.

Inventory Growth Is Both Opportunity and Risk

Total inventory increased 21.8% year on year to R$3.31 billion (US$649.4 million), reflecting the faster launch pace. Completed inventory nearly doubled to R$1.21 billion (US$236.2 million) and represented 36.4% of the total. Those ready units can generate cash quickly when sold, but they also expose the company to carrying costs if mortgage rates or buyer confidence weaken.

Quarterly cancellations rose 40.9% to R$97.5 million (US$19.1 million), broadly in line with the greater sales volume but still worth monitoring. The net sales speed of 14.8% was slightly below 15.2% a year earlier and well below the first quarter’s 18.2%.

Eztec consumed R$5.5 million (US$1.1 million) of cash in Q2, compared with R$59.7 million (US$11.7 million) of cash generation a year earlier. Excluding dividends paid during the quarter, however, operating cash generation remained positive. The distinction matters as the company funds more construction sites simultaneously.

Dividend Preserves the Payout While Capital Needs Rise

The board approved R$26.2 million (US$5.1 million) in interim dividends, equivalent to R$0.09456614033 per common share. Shareholders of record on August 13, 2026, are entitled to the payment; the shares trade ex-dividend from August 14, and payment is due by August 28.

The payout is modest relative to quarterly profit, which gives Eztec room to retain capital for construction while maintaining its record of shareholder distributions. Future dividend capacity will depend on the conversion of the larger sales backlog into recognized revenue and cash.

What to Watch Next

Revenue recognition. Strong first-half sales need to translate into higher reported revenue as construction milestones are reached.

Completed inventory. Faster sales of ready units would release cash and reduce carrying risk.

Gross margin. Holding close to 40% would show that launch growth is not being purchased through weaker pricing.

Cash conversion. The enlarged pipeline must generate enough cash to fund construction without undermining dividends or balance-sheet flexibility.

World.title: Alupar Q2 IFRS Profit Near Triples to US$82M; Regulatory Profit Falls
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —IFRS profit surged. Net income attributable to Alupar shareholders rose 187.6% to R$416.6 million (US$81.7 million). —Regulatory profit moved the other way. The regulatory measure fell 14.6% to R$159.0 million (US$31.2 million), from R$186.1 million (US$36.5 million). —Operating revenue expanded. Regulatory net revenue grew 10.3% to R$946.1 million (US$185.4 million). —EBITDA rose more slowly. Regulatory EBITDA increased 6.5% to R$724.7 million (US$142.1 million), and its margin declined to 76.6%. —Leverage improved. Net debt to EBITDA fell to 3.2 times from 3.4 times a year earlier, despite higher absolute debt. —A dividend was approved. Alupar will distribute R$69.2 million (US$13.6 million), equal to R$0.21 (about US$0.04) per ALUP11 unit.

Alupar’s headline profit boom and its underlying earnings decline are both correct: IFRS project accounting lifted the statutory result, while the regulatory view showed how interest costs still constrain recurring cash earnings.

The second quarter reinforced Alupar’s core strength as a power-transmission developer and operator, but it also demonstrated why investors cannot read a single profit number in isolation. The Brazilian utility reports both IFRS and regulatory results, and the two frameworks produced opposite year-on-year directions.

IFRS and Regulatory Profit Tell Different Stories

Under IFRS, net income attributable to Alupar shareholders reached R$416.6 million (US$81.7 million), up 187.6% from R$144.9 million (US$28.4 million) in Q2 2025. The statutory framework recognizes construction revenue and the remeasurement of contractual assets in transmission concessions, so earnings can move sharply as projects advance and discount assumptions change.

The regulatory view, which is closer to the cash-generation profile of operating concessions, produced attributable profit of R$159.0 million (US$31.2 million). That was 14.6% below R$186.1 million (US$36.5 million) a year earlier. Higher financial expenses and inflation-linked debt weighed on this measure even as operating revenue and EBITDA increased.

Neither figure is inherently wrong. IFRS is the statutory accounting result and captures the economic value created during construction. Regulatory accounting strips away much of that timing effect and is therefore often more useful for assessing the recurring capacity of mature transmission and generation assets to service debt and pay dividends.

Metric Q2 2026 Year on year IFRS attributable profit R$416.6m / US$81.7m +187.6% Regulatory attributable profit R$159.0m / US$31.2m −14.6% Regulatory net revenue R$946.1m / US$185.4m +10.3% Regulatory EBITDA R$724.7m / US$142.1m +6.5% Regulatory EBITDA margin 76.6% −2.7 pp Net debt / EBITDA 3.2× From 3.4×

Transmission Remained the Quality Core

Regulatory net revenue increased 10.3% to R$946.1 million (US$185.4 million), while regulatory EBITDA rose 6.5% to R$724.7 million (US$142.1 million). The margin fell to 76.6% from 79.3%, showing that costs and the changing project mix absorbed part of the revenue gain.

Transmission delivered the most dependable performance. Regulatory revenue in the segment rose about 15%, and EBITDA increased 12.7%, with a margin still close to 90%. Annual permitted revenue adjustments and the commissioning of new assets supported the expansion.

That predictability is central to Alupar’s investment case. Transmission concessions receive contracted availability-based revenue rather than depending primarily on the amount of electricity transported, which reduces exposure to power prices and demand swings. The trade-off is heavy upfront investment and a long period of debt-funded construction.

Debt Grew, but Operating Coverage Improved

Net debt reached about R$9.49 billion (US$1.86 billion), roughly 5% above the prior-year level. Even so, net debt to EBITDA improved to 3.2 times from 3.4 times because operating cash earnings grew faster than indebtedness.

More than 60% of the debt is indexed to Brazil’s IPCA inflation measure. That structure matches the inflation-linked revenue of many concessions over time, but it can create quarterly pressure when monetary correction raises financial expenses before tariff adjustments fully flow through earnings.

Most maturities remain long term and are housed within operating or construction-stage subsidiaries whose payment schedules are designed around each project’s cash generation. Investors should nevertheless watch whether the new-project pipeline continues improving consolidated EBITDA fast enough to keep leverage moving down.

Dividend Confirms Cash Distribution Despite the Split

The board approved R$69.2 million (US$13.6 million) in interim dividends. The payment equals R$0.07 (about US$0.01) per common or preferred share and R$0.21 (about US$0.04) per ALUP11 unit.

Shareholders recorded on August 13, 2026, will be entitled to the distribution. The securities trade ex-dividend from August 14, and payment is due by October 6. The modest quarterly payout reflects the balance between shareholder remuneration and the capital needs of a large transmission-development program.

What to Watch Next

Regulatory profit. The key test is whether financial expenses stabilize enough for operating growth to reach the bottom line.

Project commissioning. New transmission assets must move from construction accounting into recurring permitted revenue on schedule.

Leverage. A further decline from 3.2 times would show that the expansion cycle is strengthening rather than stretching the balance sheet.

Dividend capacity. Future distributions depend more on regulatory cash generation than on volatile IFRS construction gains.

IFRS net income attributable to Alupar shareholders rose 187.6% to R$416.6 million (US$81.7 million).

Why did Alupar’s regulatory profit fall?

Regulatory profit declined 14.6% to R$159.0 million (US$31.2 million) as higher financial expenses offset stronger transmission revenue and EBITDA.

Why are Alupar’s IFRS and regulatory profits so different?

IFRS recognizes construction revenue and contractual-asset remeasurement, while regulatory reporting more closely reflects recurring cash earnings from operating concessions.

What was Alupar’s leverage?

Net debt to EBITDA improved to 3.2 times from 3.4 times a year earlier, although absolute net debt rose to about R$9.49 billion (US$1.86 billion).

How much dividend did Alupar approve?

Alupar approved R$69.2 million (US$13.6 million), equal to R$0.07 per common or preferred share and R$0.21 per ALUP11 unit.

World.title: ALLOS Q2 Attributable Profit Jumps 53% to US$60M
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Attributable profit accelerated. Net income attributable to controlling shareholders rose 53.0% to R$308.1 million (US$60.4 million). —Profit measures differ. Consolidated net income was R$340.8 million (US$66.8 million), up 11.9%, while the company’s ex-straight-line-rent measure was R$294.0 million (US$57.6 million), up 57.7%. —Revenue outpaced mall sales. Net revenue excluding straight-line rent rose 11.6% to R$732.3 million (US$143.5 million), while shopping-center sales increased 3.4% to R$10.5 billion (US$2.06 billion). —Services drove the mix. Service revenue climbed 39.6% to R$115.9 million (US$22.7 million), helped by media campaigns and airport expansion. —Cash earnings advanced. Funds from operations reached R$340.8 million (US$66.8 million), 12.0% above the prior-year quarter. —Leverage stayed contained. Net debt remained at 1.7 times trailing EBITDA, and the average debt spread improved to CDI plus 0.57%.

ALLOS’s quarter was less about a boom in tenant sales than about extracting more value from a mature portfolio: services, media and cost discipline lifted earnings even as same-store sales slowed.

Brazil’s largest listed shopping-center platform produced broad earnings growth in the second quarter, but the quality of that growth matters. Traditional mall operations remained resilient rather than spectacular, while newer service businesses and lower administrative costs widened the company’s sources of profit.

Three Profit Numbers, Three Different Views

ALLOS reported consolidated net income of R$340.8 million (US$66.8 million), an 11.9% increase from a year earlier. The portion attributable to controlling shareholders reached R$308.1 million (US$60.4 million), up 53.0%. That attributable figure is the cleanest legal-accounting measure for shareholders and anchors the headline.

The company also highlighted net income of R$294.0 million (US$57.6 million), 57.7% higher year on year, in its management presentation excluding the effect of straight-line rent. Straight-line accounting spreads contracted rent increases across a lease term, so the exclusion is intended to show a cash-oriented operating view. It must not be confused with either consolidated or attributable statutory profit.

Funds from operations, a commonly used real-estate cash-earnings metric, increased 12.0% to R$340.8 million (US$66.8 million). FFO per share rose 11.9% to R$0.68 (US$0.13), with share repurchases helping per-share growth track slightly differently from the absolute result.

Metric Q2 2026 Year on year Net revenue, ex-straight-line rent R$732.3m / US$143.5m +11.6% Adjusted EBITDA, ex-straight-line rent R$525.4m / US$103.0m +10.5% Consolidated net income R$340.8m / US$66.8m +11.9% Attributable net income R$308.1m / US$60.4m +53.0% FFO R$340.8m / US$66.8m +12.0% Shopping-center sales R$10.5bn / US$2.06bn +3.4%

Services Grew Faster Than Rent

Net revenue excluding straight-line rent increased 11.6% to R$732.3 million (US$143.5 million). Adjusted EBITDA on the same basis rose 10.5% to R$525.4 million (US$103.0 million), leaving the margin at 71.7%. The slight margin compression shows that revenue grew marginally faster than operating earnings, but administrative savings limited the pressure.

Service revenue was the standout, climbing 39.6% to R$115.9 million (US$22.7 million). The Helloo media business benefited from World Cup campaigns, a multiplatform project and expansion in airports. That growth is strategically important because it reduces ALLOS’s dependence on fixed and percentage rents alone.

Net operating income from the malls reached R$601.3 million (US$117.9 million), up 3.8%, with a 91.8% margin. Excluding Shopping Tijuca, where recovery costs and insurance effects continue to distort comparisons, NOI growth was stronger and the margin was closer to the prior-year level.

Mall Demand Remained Resilient, Not Rapid

Total shopping-center sales rose 3.4% to R$10.5 billion (US$2.06 billion). Same-store sales grew 2.4%, while same-store rent advanced faster. Management attributed part of the sales slowdown to the Easter calendar and football World Cup games, which changed traffic patterns and shortened shopping periods.

Occupancy remained high at 96.2%, and tenant affordability indicators stayed controlled. That matters because high occupancy protects rental cash flow even when shoppers’ spending growth softens. The quarter therefore supports the argument that well-located physical retail can remain relevant alongside e-commerce, especially when malls combine shopping with food, services and entertainment.

ALLOS also continued developing digital channels. Its platform’s gross merchandise value reached R$1.6 billion (US$313.6 million), up 31%, while sessions rose 12% to 17 million. The value is not booked like mall rent, but the traffic and transaction data can support media sales and loyalty programs.

Low Leverage Provides Room for Capital Returns

Net leverage held at 1.7 times EBITDA. The company had roughly R$3.39 billion (US$664.5 million) in cash, while its average debt spread improved to CDI plus 0.57%, from CDI plus 0.75% a year earlier. A R$1.0 billion (US$196.0 million) real-estate receivables issuance in April helped extend maturities and lower the average cost.

The interest-rate environment remains the principal external risk because nearly all debt is linked to Brazil’s CDI benchmark. The same exposure also creates upside if rates fall: lower CDI would reduce interest expense without requiring additional mall traffic or rent growth.

Capital expenditure totaled R$89.3 million (US$17.5 million), focused on maintenance, revitalizations and selected expansions. ALLOS maintained its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of R$2.17 billion to R$2.24 billion (US$425.3 million to US$439.1 million) and kept its capital-return plans in place.

What to Watch Next

Core mall sales. Investors need to see whether same-store sales reaccelerate after the calendar and World Cup effects fade.

Service margins. Media and digital revenue are growing quickly; the next test is whether they sustain group margins as they scale.

Shopping Tijuca normalization. Insurance proceeds and recovery costs must be separated from recurring NOI to show the asset’s underlying trajectory.

Interest rates and capital allocation. Falling CDI would support FFO, while asset sales, buybacks and distributions determine how that cash reaches shareholders.

More: Brazil news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was ALLOS’s Q2 2026 attributable profit?

Net income attributable to controlling shareholders was R$308.1 million (US$60.4 million), up 53.0% year on year.

Why are several different ALLOS profit figures reported?

Consolidated net income, profit attributable to controlling shareholders, the ex-straight-line-rent management measure and FFO answer different accounting or cash-flow questions and should not be treated as interchangeable.

How much did ALLOS’s revenue grow?

Net revenue excluding straight-line rent rose 11.6% to R$732.3 million (US$143.5 million).

How did ALLOS’s shopping centers perform?

Total shopping-center sales increased 3.4% to R$10.5 billion (US$2.06 billion), same-store sales rose 2.4% and occupancy remained high at 96.2%.

What was ALLOS’s leverage in Q2 2026?

Net debt remained at 1.7 times trailing EBITDA, while the average debt spread improved to CDI plus 0.57%.

World.title: Magazine Luiza Posts US$14M Q2 Loss as Online Sales Fall 12%
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Loss widened. Magazine Luiza reported a statutory net loss of R$72.5 million (US$14.2 million), versus R$24.4 million (US$4.8 million) a year earlier. —Adjusted earnings also stayed negative. The adjusted loss was R$50.4 million (US$9.9 million), reversing a small R$1.8 million (US$0.4 million) profit. —Channels diverged. Physical-store sales grew 10.3%, while total e-commerce sales fell 11.9%. —Margins held. Adjusted EBITDA reached R$708.8 million (US$138.9 million), down 2.5%, with the margin unchanged at 8.0%. —Cash remained substantial. Total cash was R$5.8 billion (US$1.14 billion), with adjusted net cash of R$806 million (US$158.0 million).

Magazine Luiza’s quarter tells two different retail stories: physical stores regained momentum, but shrinking online sales and heavy financing costs kept the broader group in the red.

The operating result was more resilient than the loss suggests. Gross margin edged higher and the adjusted EBITDA margin held at 8.0%. The problem sits below that line: R$572.3 million (US$112.2 million) of negative financial results exceeded adjusted operating income before financing, leaving the retailer unable to convert stable margins into net profit.

A Wider Loss Despite Stable Operating Margin

The statutory net loss widened to R$72.5 million (US$14.2 million) from R$24.4 million (US$4.8 million). Excluding provisions, restructuring expenses and other nonrecurring items, the adjusted loss was R$50.4 million (US$9.9 million), compared with a R$1.8 million (US$0.4 million) profit in Q2 2025.

Adjusted EBITDA fell 2.5% to R$708.8 million (US$138.9 million), but its margin was unchanged at 8.0%. Gross margin improved by 0.1 percentage point to 30.6%, while selling expenses declined to 18.5% of net revenue from 18.7%. Those figures show expense discipline, but net revenue fell 2.6% to R$8.90 billion (US$1.74 billion).

Metric Q2 2026 Year on year Total ecosystem sales R$14.51bn / US$2.84bn −5.1% Net revenue R$8.90bn / US$1.74bn −2.6% Adjusted EBITDA R$708.8m / US$138.9m −2.5% Statutory net loss R$72.5m / US$14.2m Loss widened Physical-store sales R$5.2bn / US$1.02bn +10.3% E-commerce sales R$9.3bn / US$1.82bn −11.9%

Stores Grew While E-Commerce Retreated

Physical-store sales rose 10.3%, with same-store growth of 9.7%. Management said televisions linked to the football World Cup helped the channel, and June store sales alone grew 18%. Magalu ended the quarter with 1,246 stores.

Online performance moved in the opposite direction. First-party e-commerce fell 11.5%, marketplace sales declined 12.6%, and total online sales dropped 11.9%. E-commerce consequently represented 64.3% of total sales, down five percentage points. Magalu says it protected margins rather than chase unprofitable volume amid higher memory-chip costs and intense platform competition.

Amazon, Credit and AI Are the Recovery Bets

Magalu began selling its own inventory through Amazon Brazil in mid-June and expects a more meaningful sales contribution in the third and fourth quarters. The arrangement gives its first-party assortment another route to customers without requiring the company to subsidize its own marketplace traffic.

Financial services supplied an important cushion. Luizacred earned R$135.3 million (US$26.5 million), with annualized return on equity of 23.5%, while MagaluPay’s financial institution posted R$17 million (US$3.3 million) of net income. The company also said its WhatsApp shopping assistant had surpassed R$100 million (US$19.6 million) in cumulative sales by July.

What to Watch Next

Online stabilization. The main test is whether Amazon distribution and better product availability can halt the double-digit e-commerce decline.

Financial costs. Operating discipline will not restore profit unless the R$572 million (US$112.1 million) quarterly financing burden falls or operating earnings rise.

Store momentum. Investors will watch whether 9.7% same-store growth persists after the World Cup boost.

Cash generation. Magalu generated R$258.8 million (US$50.7 million) in operating cash during Q2 and must preserve that discipline while restarting growth.

The key factors are stabilizing e-commerce, maintaining store growth and margins, expanding profitable financial services, and reducing the burden of financial costs.

World.title: Assaí Q2 Recurring Profit Up 94% to US$67M; Leverage Falls
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Recurring profit surged. Assaí’s recurring pre-IFRS 16 net income rose 93.6% to R$344 million (US$67.4 million). —Tax credits lifted reported earnings. Reported pre-IFRS 16 profit more than doubled to R$537 million (US$105.3 million), including a net nonrecurring benefit from PIS/COFINS credits. —Sales stayed soft. Gross revenue increased 2.4% to R$21.38 billion (US$4.19 billion), while net revenue advanced only 0.9%. —Underlying EBITDA was flat. Adjusted pre-IFRS 16 EBITDA excluding PIS/COFINS credits slipped 0.7% to R$1.07 billion (US$209.9 million). —Leverage fell sharply. Net debt plus discounted receivables declined to 2.37 times adjusted EBITDA, from 3.17 times a year earlier. —Traffic reached a record. Monthly customer visits exceeded 40 million, up 3.4%, even as pressure on household budgets restrained the average ticket.

Assaí Q2 results delivered two very different messages: recurring profit nearly doubled and leverage reached its lowest level since 2021, while comparable sales and underlying EBITDA showed that the operating recovery remains incomplete.

That split makes the balance sheet, rather than rapid store growth, the central investment story. Assaí generated cash, spent less on expansion and reduced discounted receivables. The improvement below EBITDA helped profit, but indebted consumers, high interest rates and trading down continued to weigh on how much each customer put in the basket.

Profit Growth Came From More Than Store Operations

Recurring pre-IFRS 16 net income reached R$344 million (US$67.4 million), up 93.6% from R$177 million (US$34.7 million) a year earlier. Reported pre-IFRS 16 profit was R$537 million (US$105.3 million), an increase of 103.4%. The distinction is important because the reported figure includes tax effects that do not represent ordinary quarterly trading.

Assaí recognized about R$293 million (US$57.4 million) of PIS/COFINS credits tied to prior periods and another R$110 million (US$21.6 million) connected with recurring operations. After taxes, the company excluded R$193 million (US$37.8 million) from the reported profit to arrive at the recurring result. The credits were recorded as a reduction in cost of goods sold, so they also lifted reported gross profit and EBITDA.

The cleaner view therefore comes from the company’s operating measures excluding PIS/COFINS credits. On that basis, adjusted EBITDA was R$1.07 billion (US$209.9 million), down 0.7%, and its margin was broadly stable at 5.6%, compared with 5.7% a year earlier. Profit still benefited from a 25.5% improvement in the net financial result, whose cost fell to R$421 million (US$82.5 million).

Record Traffic, but Shoppers Kept Baskets Tight

Metric Q2 2026 Year on year Gross revenue R$21.38bn / US$4.19bn +2.4% Net revenue R$19.18bn / US$3.76bn +0.9% Same-store sales +0.9% Adjusted for calendar Adjusted EBITDA, excluding credits R$1.07bn / US$209.9m −0.7% Recurring net income R$344m / US$67.4m +93.6% Leverage 2.37x −0.80x

Gross revenue rose 2.4% to R$21.38 billion (US$4.19 billion). Net revenue increased 0.9% to R$19.18 billion (US$3.76 billion), with the gap partly reflecting changes in São Paulo’s tax-substitution regime. Assaí says gross revenue provides the more comparable base because the accounting change affects taxes deducted between gross and net sales without materially changing earnings in reais.

Same-store sales increased 0.9% after adjusting for a negative calendar effect of 1.4 percentage points. Management estimated that World Cup matches alone removed about 1 percentage point, as customers were less inclined to make large stock-up trips and stores closed earlier on match days.

Customer traffic told a stronger story than the sales line. Monthly visits rose 3.4% to more than 40 million, and same-store market share gained 0.3 percentage point. The combination of faster traffic and modest sales growth means the average basket remained under pressure. Assaí described a two-speed consumer economy in which lower-income households switched brands, package sizes and categories to protect constrained budgets.

Deleveraging Is Now the Clearest Source of Progress

Net debt plus discounted receivables fell by R$1.39 billion (about US$271.7 million) over 12 months to R$12.40 billion (US$2.43 billion). The leverage ratio declined to 2.37 times adjusted pre-IFRS 16 EBITDA, from 3.17 times in the second quarter of 2025 and 2.52 times in the first quarter of 2026. Assaí said this was its lowest leverage since the third quarter of 2021.

Part of the improvement reflects tax credits included in the trailing EBITDA denominator, but the company also cut discounted receivables by R$953 million (US$186.8 million) and reduced gross debt. Total cash availability, including undiscounted receivables with next-day liquidity, reached R$7.0 billion (US$1.37 billion).

Free cash flow over the last 12 months was R$2.72 billion (US$532.9 million), 1.3% above the comparable period. Gross capital expenditure fell 45.7% to R$88 million (US$17.2 million) in the quarter. The trade-off is explicit: Assaí is sacrificing expansion speed and preserving cash to lower financial risk after its heavy conversion-store investment cycle.

New Growth Projects Remain Small but Strategic

Assaí is adding growth options without returning to aggressive store expansion. It opened its first two Assaí Farma pharmacies in São Paulo in July and plans 25 units in the state by year-end, with long-term potential for about 250 locations. The company also launched more than 30 private-label products during the quarter.

Digital last-mile sales across platforms grew 237%, with coverage reaching 104 stores. The active customer base of the Meu Assaí app expanded 20%. These projects may improve identification, frequency and margins over time, but they remain secondary to the immediate tasks of restoring stronger comparable sales and maintaining deleveraging.

What to Watch Next

Underlying sales. Investors need to see whether same-store growth accelerates after the World Cup and whether traffic gains translate into larger baskets.

Continued deleveraging. Further progress from the current 2.37 times would confirm that the balance-sheet reset is continuing.

Interest costs. Further debt reduction and lower receivables discounting should determine how much flat operating profit converts into net income.

New business economics. Assaí Farma, private labels and digital sales must eventually contribute revenue and margin rather than only start-up costs.

More: Brazil news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Assaí’s recurring profit in Q2 2026?

Assaí reported recurring pre-IFRS 16 net income of R$344 million (US$67.4 million), an increase of 93.6% from a year earlier.

Why was Assaí’s reported profit higher than recurring profit?

Reported pre-IFRS 16 profit of R$537 million (US$105.3 million) included PIS/COFINS tax-credit effects. Assaí excluded a net R$193 million (US$37.8 million) tied to prior periods from its recurring result.

How much did Assaí’s revenue grow?

Gross revenue rose 2.4% to R$21.38 billion (US$4.19 billion), while net revenue grew 0.9% to R$19.18 billion (US$3.76 billion). Same-store sales increased 0.9% after calendar adjustments.

What was Assaí’s leverage at the end of Q2?

Net debt plus discounted receivables equaled 2.37 times adjusted pre-IFRS 16 EBITDA, down from 3.17 times a year earlier.

What should investors watch in Assaí’s next results?

The main tests are stronger same-store sales, continued deleveraging from 2.37 times, lower interest costs and evidence that pharmacy, private-label and digital initiatives can add profitable growth.

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 7, 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Casa de Francisca — Tirambaço The samba group Tirambaço plays the Porão room at 10 pm tonight, in a restored 1902 townhouse two minutes from Metrô Sé. Seated, properly amplified, and the best-sounding small room in the centre.

Tonight at a Glance — Tirambaço at Casa de Francisca Samba in the Porão room, 10 pm, Metrô Sé. Seated show, book ahead — Ginger and The Peppers at Blue Note Rock, not jazz, at 8 pm on Avenida Paulista. Seated, ticketed, over by midnight — Sara Hebe at Sol y Sombra 13 Argentine rap at 10 pm in Bixiga, free, part of the Flipei literary festival — Amaro Freitas Sexteto at Sesc Pinheiros The night’s real jazz booking, 8 pm at the Teatro Paulo Autran — Barra Funda clubs D-Edge and Clash Club for the late shift. Neither has published tonight’s line-up, so check Instagram before you set off

This is a busy Friday even by São Paulo standards, with more than thirty ticketed and free shows across the city. The weekend on top of it is enormous: Anitta at Parque Villa-Lobos, a free MASP concert, and the SP2B festival opening in Ibirapuera.

São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — August 7, 2026. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Circuit: When to Go Where

8 pm – Pick your seated show. Ginger and The Peppers at Blue Note on Paulista, or Amaro Freitas and his sextet at Sesc Pinheiros if you want the jazz.

10 pm – Tirambaço play samba in the basement room at Casa de Francisca, by Metrô Sé. Book; the Porão is small.

10 pm, the free option – Sara Hebe at Sol y Sombra 13 in Bixiga, part of the Flipei independent-publishers festival that runs until Sunday. No ticket needed.

Midnight – Ride-share to Barra Funda for D-Edge or Clash Club. Neither posts a line-up far in advance, so look at their Instagram feeds first.

Saturday, 4 pm – Alessandra Leão sings Alceu Valença in the vão under MASP, free and outdoors. It opens a season of free Saturday concerts running to November.

Saturday and Sunday – Anitta’s Equilibrivm Tour at Parque Villa-Lobos, gates from noon. Saturday is sold out; Sunday tickets were still on sale at the time of writing.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba and MPB — Casa de Francisca has Tirambaço tonight and a Seresta tribute to Arlindo Cruz tomorrow. Sesc Belenzinho has Demônios da Garoa, the city’s oldest samba group, free in the Comedoria at 8 pm. Where: Casa de Francisca, Sesc Belenzinho

Jazz — Amaro Freitas brings his sextet to Sesc Pinheiros at 8 pm, and the Renato Pestana Quinteto plays JazzB near Metrô República at 9 pm. Blue Note has rock tonight, so go there for the room rather than the genre. Where: Sesc Pinheiros, JazzB

Electronic and clubs — D-Edge in Barra Funda is the city’s long-standing house and techno room, with Clash Club a few streets away for indie and themed nights. Neither publishes its Friday bill far ahead. Where: D-Edge, Clash Club

Forró and northeastern — Canto da Ema in Pinheiros has Janayna Pereira from 10 pm, and Raphaela Santos plays the Centro de Tradições Nordestinas in Limão. Both are dance floors rather than seated rooms. Where: Canto da Ema, Centro de Tradições Nordestinas

Free and festival — Flipei, the eighth Festa Literária Pirata das Editoras Independentes, runs to Sunday across central venues with free gigs including Sara Hebe tonight. El Majadero plays cumbia free at the Centro Cultural Vila Itororó at 7 pm. Where: Sol y Sombra 13, Espaço Cultural Elza Soares, Centro Cultural Vila Itororó

Megashows — Anitta’s Equilibrivm Tour takes Parque Villa-Lobos on Saturday and Sunday, with gates at noon on both days. Arena tickets start at R$200 (US$39.20) full price and R$100 (US$19.60) at the half rate. Where: Parque Villa-Lobos

Pick Your Night

Date night: Casa de Francisca. Eat upstairs from 8 pm, then take a table for Tirambaço at 10 pm in the Porão.

Solo and safe: Blue Note on Paulista. Assigned seating, attentive staff, and Metrô Consolação directly underneath when you leave.

Dance till late: D-Edge in Barra Funda, with Clash Club as the fallback if the bill does not suit. Check both feeds first, and book your ride home from inside.

Meet locals: A Vila Madalena bar crawl along Aspicuelta and Mourato Coelho. Nothing needs booking and the street does the work for you.

Spend nothing: Sara Hebe at Sol y Sombra 13 in Bixiga, or El Majadero at Vila Itororó. Both free, both part of a genuinely good week for free programming in the centre.

Where to Go

Casa de Francisca — Sé/Centro An intimate music house in a 1902 palacete, with a main Salão upstairs and a smaller Porão below. Seated shows, serious sound, and the city’s best room for MPB and samba at close range. Tonight: Tirambaço, samba, 10 pm in the Porão. Also this weekend: Seresta à Arlindo Cruz on Saturday, at 5 pm and 9 pm, also in the Porão. Cost: Ticketed per show, with a dinner menu available before the set. Prices are published with each show on the venue’s own programme page. Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiúva, 22, Sé Website: casadefrancisca.art.br Getting there: Metrô Sé, about five minutes on foot. Take a ride-share home rather than walking through the centre after the show. Good to know: Book ahead; both rooms are small and sell out. Arrive early if you want to eat first.

Blue Note São Paulo — Avenida Paulista The São Paulo outpost of the New York club, in the Conjunto Nacional on Avenida Paulista. Proper seated concerts, decent cocktails, and a crowd that is dressed up without being stiff. Tonight: Ginger and The Peppers, rock, at 8 pm. This is not a jazz night. Also this weekend: Paula Morelenbaum with Moreno Veloso and Jaques Morelenbaum on Saturday, at 8 pm and 10.30 pm. Cost: Ticketed per show and priced by seat; buy through the club’s own site. A service charge is added to food and drink. Address: Av. Paulista, 2073 (Conjunto Nacional) Getting there: Metrô Consolação is directly beneath the building. The avenue is busy and well lit at any hour. Good to know: Book online; seating is assigned. Smart casual.

D-Edge — Barra Funda Open since 2003 and still São Paulo’s best-known electronic club, with a Funktion-One rig and a crowd that treats dancing as the point. Mixed, unpretentious, and reliably late. Tonight: A Friday club night, but the house has not published a line-up we could verify. Check its Instagram or ticket page before travelling. Best time: Thursday to Saturday. Things do not really start before 1 am. Cost: Entry is priced per event; expect roughly R$40–R$80 (US$7.84–US$15.68) and drinks around R$20–R$35 (US$3.92–US$6.86). Drinks go on a comanda card. Address: Al. Olga, 170, Barra Funda Getting there: Metrô Marechal Deodoro, about 10 minutes on foot. Ride-share is the better call on the way out. Good to know: No dress code. Buy online to skip the queue.

Clash Club — Barra Funda A 1930s warehouse on Rua Barra Funda given over to indie, pop and themed parties across two floors. Younger crowd than D-Edge and an easier door. Tonight: A club night is expected but no bill has been published. Look at the venue’s Instagram before you commit to the trip. Best time: Friday and Saturday. Arrive around midnight. Cost: Priced per party; expect roughly R$30–R$60 (US$5.88–US$11.76) on the door and R$15–R$30 (US$2.94–US$5.88) for drinks. Address: Rua Barra Funda, 969 — the street sits on the Barra Funda and Santa Cecília boundary Phone: (11) 3661-1500 Getting there: Metrô Marechal Deodoro, then a short walk or a ride-share. Same approach as D-Edge. Good to know: Casual dress is fine. Advance tickets are usually available online.

Sardosa Bar — Vila Leopoldina A countryside-São Paulo boteco that ran as Bar da Adelaide until October 2025, when it was renamed. Roughly 200 covers between the dining room and a veranda, with a XV de Jaú shirt on the wall giving away where the kitchen learned to cook. Tonight: Open from noon straight through to midnight. Friday is churrasco day, served from noon to 10.30 pm. Best time: Friday and Saturday evenings. The veranda tables go first. Cost: Skewers from R$14–R$16 (US$2.74–US$3.14), a fraldinha with rustic potatoes at R$65 (US$12.74), and the house Caipirinha do Thiago at R$34 (US$6.66). Any caipirinha can be made without alcohol. Address: Rua Carlos Weber, 1750, Vila Leopoldina — not Vila Madalena, and about 25 minutes by car from Avenida Paulista Phone: (11) 97659-0326 Getting there: No metro nearby; take a ride-share. It is a destination in its own right rather than a stop on a crawl. Good to know: No reservations needed for the bar. Go early on a Friday if you want the churrasco.

Bourbon Street Music Club — Moema One of the city’s longest-running live-music rooms, programming blues, jazz, rock and MPB with table service. An older, well-dressed crowd that comes for the band rather than the scene. Tonight: A Friday booking is likely but we could not confirm tonight’s act. Check the club’s programme before you book a table. Best time: Thursday to Saturday, with dinner service before the show. Cost: Ticketed per show and published with each booking. Full dinner menu on top. Address: Rua dos Chanés, 127, Moema Getting there: No metro station within walking distance; ride-share is the practical option. Quiet, safe neighbourhood. Good to know: Reservations recommended. Book by phone or through the website.

MASP — Avenida Paulista Lina Bo Bardi’s museum on its red concrete legs, with a covered public square underneath known as the vão. The free concerts staged there are a São Paulo ritual. Tonight: No concert. The museum’s own evening hours apply; check before making a special trip. Tomorrow: Alessandra Leão sings a set drawn from Alceu Valença’s songbook in the vão at 4 pm, free. It opens the Música no Vão season, which runs on Saturdays through to November with Assucena, Maria Beraldo and Paola Ribeiro to follow. Cost: The vão concerts are free and unticketed. Museum admission is charged separately and priced on the museum’s own site. Address: Av. Paulista, 1578, Bela Vista Getting there: Metrô Trianon-MASP, one block away. Ride-share pickup on the avenue is straightforward. Good to know: For the vão show, just turn up. Go early if you want to be near the front.

Parque Villa-Lobos — Alto de Pinheiros The riverside park that has become São Paulo’s default site for very large open-air shows. Anitta’s Equilibrivm Tour lands here this weekend. Tonight: Nothing on. The park is a weekend fixture, not a Friday one. This weekend: Anitta on Saturday 8 and Sunday 9 August, gates from noon on both days. Saturday has sold out. Cost: Arena from R$200 (US$39.20) full price and R$100 (US$19.60) half price; Front Stage from R$360 (US$70.57) full and R$180 (US$35.28) half. Address: Av. Professor Fonseca Rodrigues, 2001 Getting there: CPTM to Jaguaré, then a walk, or a ride-share booked well in advance. Roads around the park close on show days. Good to know: Gates at midday means a long day outdoors. Take water and sun cover.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Vila Madalena: Tree-lined streets packed with bars, galleries and a young creative crowd. Aspicuelta and Mourato Coelho are the two streets that matter.

Barra Funda: Industrial-chic club district anchored by D-Edge and Clash Club. Safe on the club strip, dead two streets away.

Avenida Paulista: The city’s spine, with MASP by day and Blue Note by night. Busy enough to walk at any hour.

Sé and Bixiga: The historic centre, with Casa de Francisca and the Flipei venues. Go with a destination in mind and ride-share between them after dark.

Moema and Vila Leopoldina: Comfortable residential districts with destination venues rather than crawls. Bourbon Street and Sardosa Bar are the reasons to make the trip.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

D-Edge — A mixed floor with a long-standing queer presence. There is no dedicated gay night, but the room is reliably welcoming.

Clash Club — Younger and more varied, with themed parties that are sometimes explicitly LGBTQ+. Check the venue’s Instagram for tonight’s billing.

Vila Madalena bars — Broadly LGBTQ+ friendly without any dedicated gay bars. Aspicuelta is comfortable on any night.

Money & How Paying Works Dollar figures in this guide use the Banco Central PTAX close of 6 August 2026, R$5.1014 to US$1. Menu and ticket prices attributed to a named venue come from that venue; club door and drink figures are typical ranges rather than quoted tariffs. Comanda card system: clubs such as D-Edge give you a card on entry, charge drinks to it, and settle the total as you leave. Losing it costs a fixed penalty. Couvert artístico is common at seated music venues and is not optional once it is on your bill. Expect roughly R$30–R$60 (US$5.88–US$11.76) where it applies. Cards and Pix are taken almost everywhere, but a few small bars remain cash-only. Carry R$100–R$200 (US$19.60–US$39.20) as a fallback. Tipping: 10 per cent is standard and usually appears on the bill as ‘serviço’. Anything beyond it is optional.

Getting Home Safe

The metro shuts around midnight on a Friday and reopens early on Saturday morning. If you want to use it, leave the venue by 11.30 pm.

99 and Uber both work well across the city. Barra Funda to Paulista after midnight typically runs R$25–R$40 (US$4.90–US$7.84), with surge worst between 2 am and 4 am.

Wait for your car inside the venue or in a lit doorway. Do not stand on an empty street with your phone out.

Avenida Paulista is walkable at any hour. In the centre after dark, move venue to venue by ride-share rather than on foot.

Barra Funda’s club strip is fine, but the streets around it are empty and industrial. Stay on the main drag and go door to door.

More: Brazil news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a comanda card?

It is a plastic card handed to you at the door of a club. You charge drinks to it through the night and pay the total on the way out; losing it means paying a fixed penalty instead.

Is it safe to walk at night?

On Avenida Paulista, yes, and it stays busy until late. In Vila Madalena stick to the main bar streets, and everywhere else take a ride-share between venues.

Do I need to book ahead?

For seated rooms such as Casa de Francisca and Blue Note, yes, and tonight both are small enough to sell out. For clubs, buy online to skip the queue; for bars, just walk in.

World.title: Cincinnati Open Opens This Weekend With Practices, Fan Events and New Attractions
World.content:
The Cincinnati Open will begin welcoming fans Saturday, August 8, several days before the first official matches are played, as one of the biggest tournaments on the North American tennis calendar opens with a full weekend of player practices, fan activities and special events.



The two-day Community Weekend at the Lindner Family Tennis Center in Mason, Ohio, will give fans an early look at players preparing for the ATP and WTA 1000 tournament before qualifying begins Tuesday. The opening weekend is part of the tournament’s continued expansion beyond traditional match days, with organizers placing greater emphasis on player access, practices and activities around the grounds.



For tennis fans, the biggest draw may simply be the chance to watch some of the world’s top players practice from much closer than is normally possible during tournament competition.

Players Take to the Practice Courts

Saturday’s Kids Day will run from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m. and include open player practices, tennis drills, autograph sessions, a scavenger hunt, live music and other activities throughout the grounds. Unlike a normal tournament day, when attention is divided between matches taking place across multiple courts, the opening weekend gives spectators an opportunity to follow players through their final training sessions before competition begins.



That could provide an early look at how some of Cincinnati’s leading contenders are adjusting to the hard courts and summer conditions in Ohio. The tournament field includes many of the biggest names in men’s and women’s tennis, along with a sizable Latin American contingent.

Brazil’s João Fonseca and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo are among the leading Latin American men entered, while Colombia’s Camila Osorio headlines the region’s representation on the women’s side. Practice schedules can change and are normally finalized closer to the sessions, meaning fans hoping to see a particular player will need to monitor tournament updates throughout the weekend.

Red Bull BassLine Makes U.S. Debut

Saturday evening will feature a different version of professional tennis when Red Bull BassLine makes its United States debut on Grandstand Court. The exhibition runs from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m. and combines a quick-fire knockout format with music from a live on-court DJ.



Rather than playing traditional full matches, players compete in shorter contests designed to create a faster and more informal atmosphere than a regular ATP or WTA match. The event has previously been staged in Europe and Australia, with Cincinnati becoming its first U.S. location.



It will be separately ticketed from the daytime Community Weekend activities, although a BassLine ticket also provides access to the tournament grounds earlier Saturday.

Cincinnati Open 5K Starts Sunday

Sunday will begin at 8 a.m. with another first for the tournament: the inaugural Cincinnati Open 5K. The run will take participants through the tournament’s 40-acre grounds before finishing with a post-race gathering. After the race, All Access Sunday will run from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m. and include additional player practices, meet-and-greets, autograph sessions, live entertainment and a Center Court photo opportunity.



The tournament will also feature adaptive tennis activities during the weekend. Fans who want another day focused primarily on training rather than matches will have one final opportunity Monday, August 10, when the grounds reopen from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m. for player practices.

Competitive Tennis Begins Tuesday

The atmosphere will change Tuesday morning when qualifying officially begins. Gates are scheduled to open at 9 a.m. on August 11, with the first qualifying matches beginning at 10:30 a.m. The second day of qualifying follows Wednesday before the men’s and women’s main draws begin Thursday, August 13.

The tournament then continues through August 23, when both singles champions are scheduled to be crowned. Cincinnati occupies an important position on the tennis calendar because it is one of the final major tournaments before the US Open in New York. Players use the event not only to compete for significant ATP and WTA ranking points but also to test their games against elite competition under North American hard-court conditions.

That makes the practice sessions and early rounds particularly useful indicators of player form heading toward the year’s final Grand Slam.

Cincinnati Builds on Record 2025 Tournament

The opening weekend follows a record-setting year for the Cincinnati Open. More than 285,000 people attended the tournament in 2025 following a major redevelopment of the Lindner Family Tennis Center. The venue now includes 31 outdoor courts and an expanded campus designed to accommodate the tournament’s larger ATP and WTA fields.



The Cincinnati Open was subsequently named the 1000-level Tournament of the Year by both the ATP and WTA. This year’s tournament extends the experience even further by opening the grounds before qualifying begins, turning what was traditionally preparation time for players into several days of public access.

For fans, it also means the Cincinnati Open effectively begins before the first official point is played. The Tico Times will be there to provide on-site coverage and photography from Mason beginning August 13, following the tournament’s leading storylines and Latin American players as the field moves toward the US Open.

World.title: Department of the Environment provides update on Fish Kill in the Belize River Valley area
World.content:
Department of the Environment provides update on Fish Kill in the Belize River Valley area

INVESTIGATION INTO THE FISH KILL IN THE BELIZE RIVER VALLEY AREA

Belmopan, Belize. August 7, 2026: The public is hereby informed that, as part of the ongoing investigation into the fish kill in the Belize River Valley area, the Department of the Environment (DOE) has conducted visual observations and water quality assessments from near Banana Bank, upstream of Santander Farms, to the Burrell Boom Village bridge. Significant fish mortality and changes in water conditions were observed particularly along the approximately 17.5-mile stretch between Isabella Bank and Grace Bank. The Department is also assessing discharge points and other activities along and within the vicinity of the river as part of its investigation into the possible source or sources of the event.

On-site water quality testing and sampling have been conducted at various locations along the river. Preliminary field results recorded extremely low levels of dissolved oxygen in areas where significant fish mortality was observed, together with elevated conductivity, chlorophyll-a and turbidity at certain locations. These conditions can adversely affect aquatic life. Samples have been submitted for laboratory analysis to assist in determining the cause of the observed conditions.

As part of the ongoing investigation, the DOE has also collected water samples from the Santander Farms drainage system and at locations downstream for chemical analysis. Fish and sediment samples are also being collected and analysed to assist in determining the cause of the fish mortality and whether contaminants may have contributed to the event.

The Department is additionally reviewing satellite imagery from before and during the event to assess changes in water conditions, land-clearing activities and other factors that may assist in identifying potential contributing sources. Investigations and assessments are also being conducted in relation to other developments, activities and potential discharge points within the wider area.

At this stage, the Department has not determined the source or responsible party associated with the fish kill. The investigation remains ongoing, and any determination will be based on the results of laboratory analyses and the totality of the scientific and technical evidence collected.

The precautionary advisory issued by the Department on August 5, 2026, remains in effect. The public is therefore advised not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from the affected areas and not to use untreated river water for drinking, cooking, food preparation, livestock or pets until further notice. This advisory applies to untreated water taken directly from the river and does not apply to treated potable water supplied by Belize Water Services Limited.

The DOE continues to coordinate with relevant government agencies and other authorities in monitoring the situation and advancing the investigation. The public will be informed as laboratory results and other verified findings become available.

The Department of the Environment remains committed to protecting Belize’s environment, safeguarding our natural resources and public health, and ensuring that all potential sources are thoroughly investigated and that appropriate action is taken where the evidence establishes a breach of Belize’s environmental laws.

END

World.title: Election Season Starts – Poll of UDP convention in the Culture Capital this weekend
World.content:
Election Season Starts – Poll of UDP convention in the Culture Capital this weekend

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News

By Dr. Philip Castillo: Municipal elections are eight months away and the first steps start with party conventions to select Mayoral and councilor candidates. The Opposition UDP will hold its convention this weekend on August 9. The convention will feature two candidates vying for Mayor, and each candidate has his/her respective slate of six councilor candidates. Hence the ballot will have a total of 14 candidates. Only 7 can win.

Castillo Poll # 3 of 2026 presents the findings of a poll conducted in Dangriga over the weekend of August 1st to 3rd. For a municipal election, the target population is the registered voters of that municipality. However for a party convention, that target population deliberately excludes known members of the other party. So for the upcoming UDP convention, the party will not allow known PUP members to vote. That presents a major challenge since ascertaining who is a “known PUP” is a subjective endeavour. This also means that for polling purposes, the actual target population is unknown.

The above, notwithstanding…here goes:

Table 1 – Mayor

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Table 2 – Councilors

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

A poll is a sample randomly drawn from a given population. I’ve already noted the challenges of identifying the target population. Yet another challenge undertaking any poll is that there WILL always be a margin of error. The margin of error relates to the extent to which the mean or the average of the sample (which is known) varies from the mean or the parameter of wider population (which is unknown). This degree of variance is expressed as a plus (+) or minus (-) because the variation can go in either direction. Polling organizations generally use a margin of error of +/- 3 percentage points. This poll had a margin of error of +/- 9%.

Another statistic that must be noted is the degree of confidence. This refers to the extent to which if you draw repeat samples you realistically expect the same results. For this poll the degree of confidence was at 90 %. This means that if the sample was drawn a hundred times, in ninety out of those one hundred times, the expected result would be the very same. Polling organizations generally use a degree of confidence of 95%.

From my projections, I estimate the voting population on Sunday August 9th 2026 to be around 695 voters. However accounting for the margin of error, the voting population could be as low as 9% less than 695. Or as high as 9% above 695. The actual ranges are 633 to 757 .

Tables 1 and 2 above are redone using these numbers to estimate actual votes.

Table 3 – Mayor

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Table 4 – Councilors

Source: Castillo Poll #3 of 2026 (August, 2026)

Accounting for the margin of error, Dayton Sabal, Jamall Swaso and John Sabal are still EXPECTED to win. Elsworth Magdaleno and Albourne Mashall are LIKELY to win. For the sixth and final council seat, probabilistically and because the numbers fall within the range of the margin of error, Marsha Mejia and Cindy Fajardo are favorites BUT Steven Laurie and Francis Marin have a punchers chance.

Dr. Philip Castillo is a development economist and an independent pollster. Send comments to [email protected].

World.title: Santander responds to Belize River fish kill, says factory does not routinely discharge process water into river
World.content:
Santander responds to Belize River fish kill, says factory does not routinely discharge process water into river

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Santander Sugar Group (SSG) has issued a statement amid concerns over the recent loss of aquatic life in the Belize River Valley, saying it is cooperating fully with an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Environment (DoE) and other government agencies.

In a statement issued Friday, August 7, Santander said it is “deeply saddened” by the reported loss of aquatic life and has granted authorities unrestricted access to its facilities and operations. The company did not accept responsibility for the fish kill, and said it welcomes the completion of the government’s investigation.

Santander said its processing facility operates as a closed-loop system in which process water is recovered, cooled where necessary and reused. According to the company, there is no continuous process effluent stream or routine discharge of high-temperature process water from its factory into the Belize River.

The company also stressed that its canals are not connected to Labouring Creek and said its operations account for approximately 12 percent of the agricultural land within the broader watershed.

Santander has faced environmental scrutiny in the past. In 2012, the company’s development was linked to the dredging of a large canal through the Labouring Creek Jaguar Corridor Wildlife Sanctuary, and in 2016 government authorities cited Santander for breaches of its Environmental Compliance Plan following investigations into activities affecting environmentally sensitive areas.

The present investigation, however, remains ongoing, and authorities have not publicly established that Santander caused the reported aquatic deaths. Santander says it will review any findings and recommendations issued by regulators and remains committed to environmental compliance and protection of the Belize River watershed.

World.title: Surviving burn victims from Guardsman fire return home
World.content:
Fabian Brown, one of the two surviving men of four initially injured in a fire returns home after treatment in the US alongside his wife Myeisha (out of frame)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Two of the four men injured in an explosion at a garage adjacent to Guardsman Group-Beryllium Limited headquarters, on South Camp Road, have returned to Jamaica following intensive burn treatment overseas.

Fabian Brown was one of two airlifted back to Jamaica on Friday in the company of his wife, Myesha, who spoke to Observer Online.

“The journey, I must say, has been rough. It has been hard,” she said.

Despite this, Myesha had high praise for those involved in her husband’s care, including the staff of Wellstar Cobb Burn Centre and Trinity Airlines as well as the Burn Foundation of Jamaica and their Crisis Support Charity arm.

She issued an urgent call to corporate Jamaica to put their support behind the foundation.

“I encourage Jamaica, corporate Jamaica, to support the Crisis Support Charity…it’s not just supporting the survivors. It’s not just burned people alone. But overall, if you look at what they have done, they’ve been doing good. And if it wasn’t for them, we would not have been able to leave here and for him to get that thorough care that he needs.”

Guardsman had committed to supporting the men who were injured in the May 27 incident, which firefighters said happened before 9:00 am while welding work was being done on the property.

Brown was airlifted along with Damian Walters and a third man for care overseas after the incident. The fourth man passed away at a local hospital before he could be airlifted. Walters also passed away while undergoing treatment overseas.

READ: Employee injured in Guardsman fire succumbs to injuries

Meanwhile, as Myesha expressed her sorrow at the two deaths, she and Fabian are now preparing for a life that may look significantly different.

“The journey is just beginning. People might think, oh, you get burned, you’re healed. This is a life-changing experience. People need to understand that when you experience burns and you’re recovering, it takes years, and your life will never be the same. The sun, something that we take for granted, you can no longer go in that,” she said.

Despite the challenges, she expressed faith in God and gratitude for her husband’s life.

“Not until you have someone who has been affected severely by burns can you know what that journey is, and I’m thankful, grateful that Fabian is still here with us,” she said.

World.title: Card, Douglas win silver in 100m at World U20 Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Shanoya Douglas parades with the Jamaican flag after winning the silver medal in the women's 100m on Thursday's second day of the 2026 World Athletics Under 20 championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. Douglas, the world leader was beaten by American Maria Maxwell. (Photos: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas won silver medals in the men and women’s 100m on Thursday night at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

It was the first medals for Jamaica at the championships, putting them in ninth position on the medals tables.

Americans Tate Taylor and Mia Maxwell delighted the home fans by winning the double, only the second time athletes from the same country had taken both gold medals at the same under-20 championships after Americans Noah Lyles and Candace Hill achieved the feat in 2016 in Bydgoszcz, Poland.

Card got off to a fast start but was chased and caught by Tate who passed him to win in a personal best 9.94 seconds (0.1m/s), the Jamaican second in 10.05 seconds. South Africa’s Marko Ferreira took the bronze with 10.16 seconds.

Maxwell got the edge over Douglas at the start and held off the Jamaican to the tape, running 11.14 seconds (-0.1m/s). Douglas finished second in 11.17 seconds with Italy’s Kelly Ann Maevane Doualla Edimo third in 11.27 seconds. Theianna-Lee Terrelonge was sixth in 11.37 seconds

It was the first time in 10 years an American won the women’s 100m and snapped the four-championships winning streak by the Jamaicans – Briana Williams in 2018, Tina Clayton in 2021 and 2022 and Alana Reid in 2024.

Also on Thursday, thrower Able Mills failed to record a legal throw in both the women’s discus and shot put finals that were held within two hours of each other.

Mills had thrown distances close to her lifetime bests to qualify for both finals but failed to make a legal mark in either.

Jamaica also failed to qualify any runner in the 400m finals set for Friday afternoon, all four failing to get past their semifinals.

Jabari Matheson who was running his fourth 400m race in two days, placed sixth in his semi-final in 47.29 seconds, the first time he failed to go under the 47.00 second mark at the championships.

Jason Pitter failed to get up to his high standards, and was sixth in his semi-final in 46.50 seconds after he advanced on time from the first round.

Daniellia Dixon was fifth in her semi-final in 53.77 seconds and Shameika McLean, who had run three times since the start of the championships, just failed to get into the final after placing fourth in her semis in 54.24 seconds.

-Paul A Reid
