Poland’s top administrative court has upheld a decision by the finance ministry to withhold state subsidies from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party due to campaign finance irregularities. The decision was welcomed by the government, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that there will be “no money for grifters”. PiS, however, argues that the money is being withheld for political reasons and accuses the authorities of “Russian standards”. Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny oddalił w środę kasacje ws. dotacji i subwencji dla PiS. – Miażdżący dla PiS wyrok podtrzymany! – stwierdził szef MF Andrzej Domański https://t.co/bcL18WbiYf — OKO.press (@oko_press) August 6, 2026 The dispute dates back to August 2024, when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected PiS’s financial report for the previous year’s parliamentary election campaign after identifying around 3.6 million zloty (€838,000) in unauthorised expenditure. As a result, the PKW ordered that PiS should lose 10.8 million zloty from the state subsidies that political parties in Poland receive based on their level of electoral support. The party would normally have received 25.9 million zloty based on its 2023 election result. The decision triggered months of legal wrangling, with PiS arguing that the funding should be restored after the Supreme Court upheld its complaint against the PKW’s decision. However, finance minister Andrzej Domański refused to release the money, saying there were unresolved legal doubts over the ruling. The finance minister has refused to comply with the electoral commission's decision to pay out subsidies to the opposition PiS party He says there are "legal doubts" over the issue. But PiS says he is obliged to pay and will be held criminally responsible https://t.co/ZwIZRqn5tp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2025 Those doubts stem from a broader dispute over the controversial and contested judicial reforms implemented by PiS when it ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. The chamber of the Supreme Court that ruled in PiS’s favour was created as part of those reforms. It has previously been found to not be a legitimate body by both the European Court of Justice and European Court of Human Rights because it contains improperly appointed judges. After the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling, the PKW initially said it would not recognise the decision until the chamber’s legal status was clarified. Two weeks later, however, it reversed that decision and approved PiS’s financial report. Domański still declined to restore the subsidy, arguing that the PKW’s resolution was internally contradictory. While it approved the payments, it also stated that the chamber’s ruling should come from a body recognised as a court and that it was not determining whether the chamber met that standard. PiS challenged Domański’s decision. However, its case was initially rejected by a lower court in June last year, and that decision has now been upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), which is the final court of appeal for administrative issues. The NSA found the minister had acted lawfully in withholding the funding. It also said the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling had no legal effect because it had been issued by a body that was not a properly constituted court, reports news website OKO.press. The ruling was welcomed by Domański, who called it a “crushing blow to PiS” and said that “yet another PiS lie has been exposed”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, wrote on social media: “Just as we said, there is and will be no money for grifters.” Tak jak mówiliśmy, dla przekręciarzy pieniędzy nie ma i nie będzie. https://t.co/4Kqexj6NoC — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 5, 2026 The PKW’s decision to cut PiS’s funds was made after it found that government resources – including from the justice ministry, Government Legislation Centre (RCL) and Research and Academic Computer Network (NASK) – had been used to support the party’s election campaign. However, PiS has always argued that the decision was a political one, implemented at the behest of the new Tusk government in order to undermine the main opposition party. Radosław Fogiel, a senior PiS lawmaker and former party spokesman, said that the new NSA ruling “does not change the essence of the matter: it unlawfully deprives the main opposition party of the subsidy to which it is entitled. World.title: Polish prosecutors end 10-year treason investigation into Tusk over Smolensk air disaster
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! After a ten-year-long investigation, prosecutors have concluded that Poland’s government in 2010 – which was led by current Prime Minister Donald Tusk – was not guilty of “diplomatic treason” in its response to the plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party – which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 and is led by Lech’s twin brother, Jarosław – has always rejected the findings of official Polish and Russian investigations into the crash, which found it to have been an accident. Instead, PiS claims that the disaster, which claimed the lives of 96 people, many of them senior Polish state officials, was caused deliberately by Russia and then covered up with the help of Tusk’s government. However, while PiS launched various investigations during its time in power, it has never substantiated its claims. And prosecutors now say that there is no evidence that diplomatic treason, a crime that carries a potential prison sentence of up to ten years, took place. Uprzednio wygrałem sprawę cywilną z posłem @OficjalnyJK, który w efekcie musiał wpłacić 50,000zł na siły zbrojne broniącej się Ukrainy. Teraz potwierdzenie @PK_GOV_PL: nie było żadnej zdrady dyplomatycznej ani żadnej intencji jej popełnienia. Oczywiście żaden z kłamców… https://t.co/VKZHlF5xkX — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 5, 2026 Wednesday’s announcement by the National Prosecutor’s Office was welcomed by Radosław Sikorski, the current foreign minister, who held the same role in 2010. He condemned the “Smolensk liars”, such as Jarosław Kaczyński, who he suggested had exploited the tragedy for their own benefit. “They brainwashed millions of people, divided families, stirred up hatred within the nation,” he wrote. “They’ll burn in hell for it. But the power, money and satisfaction they gained from spitting on their rivals – that’s theirs.” The idea that Smolensk was an assassination of Lech Kaczyński has been a core part of PiS rhetoric. In 2022, for example, Jarosław Kaczyński said that the decision was made “at the highest level of the Kremlin” and Tusk’s government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”. Smolensk was an “attack decided at the highest level of the Kremlin”, says Jarosław Kaczyński ahead of the 12th anniversary of the crash. Donald Tusk's government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”, he adds https://t.co/5ae0gHJj3B — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 4, 2022 The investigation into diplomatic treason – a crime consisting of acting to the detriment of Poland while authorised to represent the country in relations with foreign states or organisations – was launched in August 2016, less than a year after PiS had come to power. Among the individuals who had formally notified prosecutors of a potential crime was PiS deputy leader Antoni Macierewicz, who from 2015 to 2018 served as defence minister. He has been the foremost proponent of conspiracy theories around the Smolensk air disaster. In their notifications to prosecutors, Macierewicz and the others accused Tusk and other officials of, in their relations with Russia, deliberately choosing a legal basis for an investigation into the crash that was unfavourable to Poland by giving it no real influence over how it was run. However, prosecutors now say that, after ten years in which they questioned 488 witnesses, gathered extensive documentation and requested legal assistance from several countries, they have “concluded that no crime of diplomatic treason was committed”. In a statement explaining the decision, the National Prosecutor’s Office said that the legal basis chosen for cooperating with Russia on an investigation – Annex 13 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation – was, in fact, “the most advantageous solution” for Poland. It ensured the participation of Polish representatives in the Russian-led investigation, including access to the wreckage and crash site. Other legal options would have offered no greater benefits and involved significant risks, concluded the Polish prosecutors. They acknowledged that Russia “subsequently failed to fulfil some of its obligations arising from the adopted procedure”, but said this should have no bearing on assessing the decisions that were previously made on setting up the investigation. The defence ministry will notify prosecutors of 41 suspected crimes linked to a commission established by the former PiS government to investigate the 2010 plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński https://t.co/aEAlmk9lDM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2024 The prosecutors also found that, not only did Polish officials choose the best legal solution, but there was also “no evidence indicating that individuals authorised to act on behalf of Poland, including the prime minister and members of the Council of Ministers, acted with the intent to harm Poland”. Given that the crime of diplomatic treason requires intent, this finding further reinforced the decision to drop the investigation. However, the prosecutors note that their decision can still be appealed. At the time of writing, neither Kaczyński, Macierewicz, nor other senior PiS figures had commented on the prosecutors’ announcement. However, it is likely they will point to the fact that the current national prosecutor was appointed by Tusk’s government after it had removed the previous PiS-era incumbent in a legally questionable move. The Supreme Court has issued a ruling that effectively found that the government unlawfully replaced a senior prosecutor earlier this year However, the justice minister says the ruling has no legal force as it was issued by illegitimately appointed judges https://t.co/9fCE6d18uy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 27, 2024 In 2020, in a separate civil case, a court ordered Jarosław Kaczyński to apologise for accusing Sikorski of “diplomatic treason” in relation to the Smolensk crash. Two years later, after Kaczyński had refused to comply with the ruling and Sikorski published the apology himself, Kaczyński was ordered to pay the costs. In 2024, an investigation by Tusk’s government found that the PiS administration had wasted tens of millions of zloty on a commission, headed by Macierewicz, that was tasked with re-investigating the Smolensk disaster. It notified prosecutors of dozens of suspected crimes relating to the functioning of the commission. Macierewicz, however, accused the government of spreading “lies and disinformation” designed to “protect Putin”. Jarosław Kaczyński has been ordered to pay 700,000 zl (€150,000) to publish an apology to ex-foreign minister @sikorskiradek. Poland has urged the European Union to adopt tougher measures in response to the recent migration crisis in Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. During a special meeting of EU interior ministers on Tuesday, Poland shared its own experience of dealing with “weaponised” migration from Belarus, which prompted the Polish government last year to restrict the right to asylum for people who cross irregularly. 🔵 KOMUNIKAT | Polska przedstawiła swoje stanowisko ws. migracji na nadzwyczajnym posiedzeniu Rady JHA w sprawie ostatnich wydarzeń w Ceucie 🇵🇱🇪🇺 Wiceminister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji @MaciekDuszczyk wziął udział w odbywającym się we wtorek (4 sierpnia br.)… pic.twitter.com/glfyiu5ZW3 — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) August 4, 2026 Last week, tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, most of them by swimming there from neighbouring Morocco. Dozens died while trying to cross. Among those who managed to enter Ceuta, Spain says that the vast majority have been returned to Morocco. The incident prompted expressions of concern from many European leaders, including calls to restrict Spain’s participation in the Schengen free movement zone (despite the fact that anyone leaving Ceuta for the European mainland is subject to identity checks). Among those to speak out was Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who on Friday called on Spain to “follow our example if Schengen is to survive”. Poland has tightened asylum laws, border procedures, and has built effective barriers on its border with Belarus, which is the eastern border of the EU. We have invested billions of euros and engaged thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards. Spain must follow our… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 31, 2026 That was a reference to Poland’s response to a crisis on its eastern border, where since 2021 Belarus has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross irregularly into the EU. Both Poland and the EU have accused Belarus and its ally Russia of deliberately “weaponising” migration in an attempt to destabilise European societies as part of Moscow and Minsk’s broader “hybrid threats” against the EU. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has restricted the right to asylum, invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, and has deployed thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards there (who have also been given expanded rights to use firearms). A court has ruled that Poland's recently introduced partial suspension of the right to asylum is justified and lawful. It rejected a complaint by a Sudanese man who had been denied the right to claim asylum after crossing irregularly from Belarus https://t.co/jx3s1AxRgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2025 On Saturday, Tusk and 21 other EU leaders jointly signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. While they welcomed Spain’s cooperation with Morocco to send most of the migrants back, they also called for an extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers to “agree on a coordinated European response, including the rapid mobilisation of available EU instruments and the necessary support to Spain”. At that meeting, which took place on Tuesday, Poland’s interior ministry said that it had expressed the view that “illegal entry into the European Union should automatically exclude the possibility of obtaining residence permits, and therefore the possibility of permanent stay in the future”. While Poland’s statement did not mention it directly, earlier this year Spain’s government launched an amnesty that allowed undocumented migrants to apply to legalise their stay in the country. Over one million people had signed up for the scheme by the time it closed at the end of June. In its statement, Poland’s interior ministry warned that “migration must be fully controlled”, as otherwise it can “be used against the values that guide the EU”. It also called for the “official recognition of migration as a challenge directly linked to security”. It added that during Tuesday’s meeting it had “presented its own experiences with border protection in the context of the instrumentalisation and weaponisation of migration and adapting law to migration challenges”, including restrictions on asylum claims. “The example of Ceuta clearly demonstrates that absolute access to asylum is impossible to maintain in the face of such real threats,” wrote the interior ministry, which said that it “welcomed the shared perspective on migration among a growing number of member states”. In a statement of its own, the European Council noted that there had been a “common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight.” It added that member states “were united in expressing strong solidarity with Spain”, appreciated its “swift and effective efforts” to deal with the crisis, and had also expressed their condolences for the people who died while attempting to cross from Morocco to Ceuta. ESPAÑA: CEUTA PIDE CERRAR LA FRONTERA POR LA LLEGADA MASIVA DE MIGRANTES DE MARRUECOS Más de mil jóvenes marroquíes se congregaron en la frontera con Ceuta para intentar ingresar al enclave español, y cientos lograron superar las barreras de protección, que en ese momento no… pic.twitter.com/Mx0LuQwMW2 — Clarín (@clarincom) July 30, 2026 When the migration crisis on its border with Belarus broke out in 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings that year. Despite efforts to discourage and prevent crossings, the figures remained high, with just under 30,000 attempted crossings recorded in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have fallen dramatically this year, with only 235 attempted crossings recorded in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the estimated number of successful crossings has been falling, from 12,000 in 2023, to 5,000 in 2024, 1,700 in 2025, and zero in the first half of this year, according to the Polish interior ministry. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. World.title: Construction Disrupts Prague Tourists and Businesses During Peak Summer Season
World.content:
Construction projects across Prague’s historic center are proving a pain for tourists and locals alike who say the clumps of dirt, building supplies and equipment block popular sites and make it difficult to move around one of Europe’s most visited cities.



Heading down Národní to the Charles Bridge or going for a beer near the Vltava river now looks more like a vast construction site where tourists need to look out for more than the cobble-stone streets and baroque spires.

“It’s their first time here too, [they’ve] never seen it and now it’s torn up,” said Sherryl, a tourist visiting from the United States with her friends.

A major source of the disruption are upgrades to the public transport system. The central tram route delivering travelers to the heart of the city near the Národní Divadlo stop has been shuttered for weeks.

The disruption has taken a heavy toll on surrounding businesses like Aggeo, an Italian grocery store along the corridor. Its manager, Irena Kumpová, noted a sharp drop in foot traffic from travelers and regular local customers, who stroll by the National Theater on their way to gaze at the artist David Černý’s famous Kafka head.

“I’d rather stay closed… it’s a catastrophe,” remarked Kumpová.

With tourism growing every year in Prague, the widespread construction is making its mark this summer. So far this year, 1.7 million people have visited Prague, marking the strongest start in 15 years, according to Prague City Tourism and the Czech Statistical Office.

Tram services are suspended through the city center, clogging the streets and forcing many to find another way to work or home. For businesses that rely on heavy foot traffic during the busiest months of the year, that means less earnings.

“I have a table outside, but mainly just to signal to people that we’re open, but no one sits there right now,” said Kumpová.

The reconstruction is part of Prague’s broader effort to modernize its transport network, including long-term investments such as the future tram connection to Wenceslas Square and the expansion of Metro Line D as the city seeks to expand public transport.

Not everybody minds the disruption. The loud machines, dusty air, and obstructed sidewalks offer a certain charm for some who view the construction as part of the sightseeing experience.

“Despite the construction, it’s still beautiful,” said Raluca Costachescu, a traveler from Romania.

Written by: Mae Bryant, Bilyana Spasova, Milica Petrušová, Zuzana Kormančíková, Zhanna Bekiryan

World.title: Live Nation and PPF to Run Three Major Prague Venues
World.content:
Live Nation and PPF Group are forming a joint venture that will operate three of Prague’s major event venues — O2 Arena, O2 Universum and Forum Karlín.

The companies plan to invest in the venues and upgrade their facilities, with Live Nation set to hold a 51 percent stake in the new company.

The agreement will bring together one of the world’s largest live entertainment companies and PPF, the investment group that owns O2 Arena and O2 Universum through its subsidiary Bestsport.



PPF has also operated Forum Karlín, which has been owned by Patria Investment Company since last year.

The companies announced the planned partnership in a joint statement. Financial details of the transaction and the amount of the planned investment have not been disclosed. The deal remains subject to the required regulatory approvals.

Under the agreement, the new operator will be responsible for the day-to-day running of all three venues, including event planning and programming. The venues themselves will remain under their existing ownership structures, and their names will not change.

The partners said they intend to invest substantially in the facilities over the coming years. The aim is to improve conditions for audiences and performers while expanding the number of events held in Prague and strengthening the city’s position on the international concert and entertainment circuit.

PPF said the cooperation with Live Nation is also part of its strategy of developing the long-term value of its assets alongside major international companies.

Live Nation Entertainment operates across several areas of the live entertainment industry, including concert promotion, ticketing and sponsorship. Its businesses include Live Nation Concerts, Ticketmaster and Live Nation Sponsorship.

PPF Group is an international investment company with holdings across Europe, North America and Asia. Its portfolio includes telecommunications, media, financial services, real estate, e-commerce, industry and biotechnology.

World.title: Prague to Restore Tram Service Between Holešovice and City Center
World.content:
Residents of Prague 7 will regain a tram connection between Holešovice and the city center from September, with tram line 5 set to operate through the district and continue toward Wenceslas Square.

The change follows months of pressure from Prague 7 officials and local residents, who have called for better tram connections since the cancellation of line 14.

The district had previously requested either the return of line 14 or the introduction of an equivalent service and organized a petition supporting the demand.



The new arrangement will initially be temporary. According to the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) system, two trams will operate on the route at least through December 2026.

Line 5 to replace temporary route

The new service is linked to planned transport changes in Žižkov. Because of a traffic closure there, tram line 34 will be replaced by line 5 in Holešovice.

At Holešovice train station, line 5 will connect with line 6, effectively creating a continuous service between the two routes. Trams will run from the station through the Holešovice area, past the market and across Vltavská Street before continuing toward Wenceslas Square and other parts of central Prague.

For passengers in Holešovice, the move restores a connection that was lost when line 14 was discontinued.

Service could change again next year

The situation between January and June 2027 has not yet been fully settled. According to PID, the final arrangement will depend in part on discussions between the incoming leaderships of Prague 3 and Prague 7.

Maintaining the additional tram service in Holešovice during that period could require limited reductions elsewhere in Prague 3. Another option would be to temporarily return to the existing arrangement using combined tram lines 6 and 34.

PID has warned that permanently combining lines 5 and 6 could also create delays at both ends of the route. Such a change could affect passengers travelling through Prague 2 and Prague 5, even though it would provide the direct connection sought by Prague 7.

World.title: “Ivan, Go Home!” Rally to Take Place Outside Russian Embassy in Prague
World.content:
A Czech-Ukrainian rally will take place outside the Russian Embassy in Prague on August 20 to mark the 58th anniversary of the Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The event, titled “Ivan, Go Home!”, is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. on Thursday, August 20, at Boris Němcova Square in Prague 6.

The rally comes one day before the anniversary of the night of August 20-21, 1968, when troops from five Warsaw Pact countries entered Czechoslovakia to crush the Prague Spring reform movement.



The invasion brought an end to the country’s attempt to pursue a more liberal form of socialism and was followed by two decades of political repression and Soviet military presence.

The event is being organized jointly by People in Need (Člověk v tísni), Memory of the People (Paměť národa), Million Moments for Democracy (Milion chvilek pro demokracii), and the European Congress of Ukrainians.

Organizers say the rally will connect the historical experience of the Soviet occupation with Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Participants will gather to remember those killed or persecuted following the 1968 invasion and the people who lived under the communist regime that followed. The organizers also plan to express support for Ukraine and draw attention to what they describe as the continuing use of imperial violence by Russia.

The choice of the rally’s name refers to one of the best-known slogans associated with the 1968 invasion. “Ivan, go home!” appeared on posters, walls, buildings and military vehicles as Czechoslovaks protested against the foreign troops occupying the country.

The invasion halted those reforms. Soviet troops remained in Czechoslovakia until the end of the communist era, while the subsequent period of “normalization” brought censorship, political purges and restrictions on civil liberties.

World.title: World of Warcraft Film Ibelin to Shoot in Prague
World.content:
Production of Ibelin, a new film based on the life of Norwegian World of Warcraft player Mats Steen, is moving to Prague this summer.

Filming is expected to take place at Barrandov Studios from early August through early October, following the production’s spring shoot in Norway.

The film is not connected to the 2016 Hollywood movie Warcraft. Instead, it tells the real-life story of Steen, who lived with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and built friendships, relationships and a social life inside the online world of World of Warcraft.



The Prague production is reportedly seeking extras for roles including blacksmiths, guards and innkeepers. The casting suggests that parts of the film set in the game’s fictional world could be filmed in the Czech Republic. The producers have not yet officially confirmed which scenes will be shot in Prague.

Charlie Plummer leads the cast

American actor Charlie Plummer will portray Mats Steen. Toni Collette and Stephen Graham will play his parents, while the supporting cast includes Bill Nighy, Isabela Merced, Maisy Stella, John Bradley and Ivanna Sakhno.

The film will be directed by Norwegian filmmaker Morten Tyldum, whose credits include The Imitation Game and the science-fiction film Passengers.

At the center of the story is the difference between Steen’s increasingly restricted physical existence and the freedom he experienced online. His character, known in World of Warcraft as Ibelin, became an important figure to people he met through the game.

One of Norway’s largest film projects

The Prague shoot is part of an international production with a reported budget of CZK 1 billion.

According to the Norwegian Film Institute, the project received 20 million Norwegian kroner in production support.

Ibelin is being produced by Vendôme Pictures, Pathé and Neby-Tyldum as an international co-production. The Norwegian Film Institute describes it as an English-language drama with a planned running time of around two hours.

The film is being developed for theatrical release, with its premiere currently expected in the third quarter of 2027.

World.title: GALLERY: Time Capsule Buried Beneath Prague’s Wenceslas Square Tramline
World.content:
A time capsule containing different items, newspapers and messages documenting life in 2026 has been buried beneath Prague’s reconstructed Wenceslas Square.

The capsule was placed on Wednesday, August 5, near the statue of St. Wenceslas as work continues on the upper section of the square.

The Prague New Town Association, which is involved in activities around the statue and the surrounding area, organised the ceremony.

The date was not originally chosen for its historical significance. Construction work ultimately determined both the day and the location of the burial. But the association later discovered that August 5 also marks the 60th anniversary of the release of the Beatles’ Revolver album.

“We were wondering what made August 5 go down in history. Then we found out that it was 60 years ago that the Beatles released their famous album Revolver. So now we are leaving a message here for future generations,” said Monika Vlková, the association’s executive director.



The box, measuring 60 by 40 by 23.5 centimetres and weighing about eight kilograms, was then taken to a prepared pit beside the statue. Workers had excavated the hole to a depth of around 1.7 metres, where the capsule was placed before the site was covered.

The container had been wrapped in transparent protective film, as had its contents.

The collection includes coins, newspapers published during the first week of August 2026, T-shirts, badges and written messages. It also contains proposals submitted by architects during the competition for the redesign of Wenceslas Square.

The box reportedly also holds a hammer and a beer glass.

The objects are accompanied by a 20-page report describing everyday life in the Czech capital in 2026. The capsule also contains USB drives with digital material documenting the period of the Covid-19 pandemic and its effects on life in central Prague.

The capsule is intended to remain underground for decades. The association estimates that Wenceslas Square could undergo another major reconstruction in roughly 50 years, although nobody can predict when the next intervention will actually take place.

World.title: Czechia Tightens Temporary Protection Rules for Ukrainian Men Aged 23 to 60
World.content:
New rules affecting Ukrainian men seeking temporary protection in the Czech Republic will take effect on August 5, 2026.

Under the changes, men aged 23 to 60 applying for temporary protection will have to demonstrate that they are exempt from military service in Ukraine.

The requirement will apply to new applications and certain other applications for protection, but not to people who already hold valid temporary protection.



The Czech Interior Ministry says the new rules follow an EU Council decision published in the Official Journal of the European Union on August 4. The decision also extends temporary protection for people fleeing Russia’s war in Ukraine until March 31, 2028.

For applicants aged 23 to 60, military registration documents will be checked as part of the application process. Applicants will use Ukraine’s Reserv+ system to demonstrate their military status, with the electronic military registration document showing whether they are exempt from military service.

The rules are different for younger applicants. People aged 18 to 22 will only need to demonstrate that they are registered in the Reserv+ system.

The new requirement concerns people applying for temporary protection for the first time, as well as repeat applications and applications connected with family reunification. It does not apply to people who already have valid temporary protection.

The military-service requirement will also not be introduced as part of the regular extension process. Ukrainians whose temporary protection is already valid will therefore not have to provide this additional documentation when extending their status through March 2028.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the Czech government had pushed for stricter conditions for new applicants. According to the ministry, the change is expected to reduce the number of new arrivals and ease pressure on public services, including health care and social security.

World.title: Filming of American Spy Series to Bring Restrictions to Prague 7
World.content:
Filming for the American series Birdwatcher will take place at the Prague 7 tax office on Kapitána Jaroše Embankment from August 8 to 24, bringing temporary restrictions to the area.

The production will use the tax office building at Kapitána Jaroše Embankment 1000/7, while part of the sidewalk outside the building will be closed to accommodate filming equipment.

The restrictions will not affect the normal operation of the tax office.



Drivers should also expect temporary parking restrictions on nearby Na Ovčinách Street. Vehicles will still be allowed to pass through the street, but parking will be prohibited during the designated filming periods.

The restrictions will not be in force continuously throughout the filming period. They will apply only on specific dates, with Prague 7 publishing a map showing the affected areas and individual dates on its website.

Prague has become a major filming location

Birdwatcher is an American spy fantasy series set during the Cold War. The production is being led by Legendary and Apple TV, with Andy Goddard directing. Wyatt Russell plays the lead role.

The story follows Colonel Lee Shaw as he embarks on a covert mission behind enemy lines to prevent the Soviet Union from unleashing a new Titan capable of devastating the United States and altering the balance of the Cold War.

The series is set in the 20th century against the backdrop of the Cold War, and parts of the production are being filmed in Prague.

Czech production company Stillking Films is handling the local production. The company has previously worked on major international productions filmed in the Czech capital, including The Gray Man.

World.title: 18-year-old Hungarian man suspected of killing Austrian man in anti-gay attack
World.content:
An 18-year-old Hungarian man is suspected of killing a 29-year-old Austrian man in Lower Austria, with investigators examining the possibility that the attack was motivated by the victim’s sexual orientation.

The victim was found dead early on Thursday in a house in Langenzersdorf, north of Vienna. The Hungarian suspect was arrested at the scene and reportedly gave a full confession on Friday. According to Austrian newspaper Krone Zeitung’s report, the two men had met online and arranged to meet at a house in Langenzersdorf while its owners were away.

Police investigate possible hate crime

The Korneuburg Public Prosecutor’s Office has confirmed that the case is being investigated as a possible hate crime. Spokesperson Gudrun Bischof told Austrian media that investigators believe the victim’s perceived sexual orientation may have been a motive for the killing.

The suspect reportedly lured the 29-year-old man to the house, which he was looking after in the absence of the owners. According to reports, the victim suffered severe injuries to his face and died at the scene.

Krone reported that the suspect practised taekwondo and allegedly used his martial arts skills during the crime. No weapon has been found, according to the report. Police were called to the property after an emergency alert. When officers arrived, the older man was lying on the floor with severe facial injuries and could no longer be saved.

The 18-year-old was arrested without resistance.

Links to ‘paedophile hunter’ groups

Austrian media have reported that the Hungarian suspect was allegedly associated with so-called “paedophile hunter” circles.

These groups claim to target paedophiles, but authorities have previously linked some of them to attacks on gay men based on the false equation of homosexuality with paedophilia.

According to reports, members of such groups have used social media to identify and lure men they believe to be gay before confronting, humiliating, assaulting or robbing them.

Austria has previously investigated similar attacks

The case comes amid wider scrutiny in Austria of groups accused of carrying out attacks under the guise of “paedophile hunting”.

A series of raids launched at the request of prosecutors in Graz last year across seven Austrian provinces resulted in numerous arrests. Those targeted included people suspected of hate crimes and individuals allegedly involved in attacks against members of the LGBTQ+ community.

Investigators in those cases reportedly uncovered allegations of victims being robbed, humiliated and physically assaulted, in some cases seriously.

According to HVG, following the death in Langenzersdorf, Austrian LGBTQ+ rights organisation HOSI Wien, the Social Democratic Party (SPÖ) and the Greens have called for the country’s national action plan against hate crime to be fully implemented as soon as possible.

The case is being investigated as a suspected murder and possible hate crime.

World.title: New Hungarian foreign-policy priorities set out for relations with Putin’s Russia, MAGA world, EU, V4, NATO and Balkans
World.content:
What is underway at the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs may prove to be more than a simple change of leadership: it could amount to a restructuring that reaches to the institution’s foundations.

The institute has been transferred from the Prime Minister’s Office back to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Its new director-general is Botond Feledy, while András Rácz has been appointed his deputy, responsible for research and academic affairs.

Botond Feledy (l) and András Rácz (r) Photo: Prtscr/Youtube

Both researchers have been outspoken critics of the Orbán governments in recent years, condemning their confrontational approach towards the EU and conspicuously close ties with Russia. In an interview, they have now outlined the priorities they believe should guide Hungary’s foreign policy — and the role they envisage for a revitalised Institute of International Affairs.

A complete break with Orbán’s foreign policy

Feledy told InfoRádió that the institute was being rebuilt “from the ground up”. The aim is to create a background institution that does more than communicate political decisions after they have been taken. Instead, it would support the Foreign Ministry with analysis and expertise before decisions are made, bringing perspectives into the process that are less prominent within the ministry’s own structure.

In an interview with 444, also published yesterday, the pair said they were planning a complete break with the American- and MAGA-focused foreign policy direction associated with Balázs Orbán, the Prime Minister’s political director. Rather than operating along ideological lines, the new leadership wants the institute to focus on preparing decisions and to draw a clear distinction between professional analysis and political propaganda.

Orbán and Trump in the White House. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

The changes could also involve staff. Feledy said some employees would remain at the institute, while others would be asked to leave. The organisational structure would not simply be imposed from above, however: the new system would be developed together with the institute’s staff.

The leadership also intends to retain the institute’s status as a non-profit private limited company, arguing that this could provide greater flexibility when testing new technologies, including the use of artificial intelligence in public administration.

The EU may once again become a central concern

One of the most significant shifts in foreign policy is likely to concern Hungary’s relationship with the European Union. Feledy said that the institute had accumulated little expertise on EU affairs in recent years, and that this would have to change.

Hungary is a member of both the EU and NATO, he noted, meaning that advancing the country’s interests within the Union is not an ideological question but a fundamental national interest. Some 80 per cent of Hungary’s trade is conducted in that direction, he said.

The institute therefore plans to build new research capacity, primarily in EU affairs. Greater attention could also be paid to issues that have received less prominence in Hungary’s foreign-policy debate, including digital sovereignty, cyber and economic security, the protection of critical infrastructure, migration and the geopolitical consequences of climate change. Water management could also become a priority, given both the climate crisis and the current water-related emergency.

At the same time, the institute would retain its traditional strengths, including research into the Balkans and the post-Soviet space. It also plans to develop new expertise on China and East Asia.

Rebuilding relations in central Europe — particularly with Poland, Austria, the Czech Republic and Slovakia — could likewise receive greater emphasis.

Hungary’s foreign policy strategy may also be renewed. The current strategy, drawn up in 2011, would be replaced by a new document, in the preparation of which the institute would play a role. The leaders said civil-society organisations and other professional bodies would also be involved.

No break with Russia, but servility is over — and Ukraine must be rebuilt

In the case of Russia, the proposed shift would involve a change in the style of the relationship rather than a complete foreign-policy reversal.

Rácz said there was no short-term alternative to maintaining pragmatic relations, primarily because of Hungary’s energy dependence. But he argued that there was no need to maintain such a close and “servile” relationship with the Russian leadership as that demonstrated by the ties between former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó and Sergei Lavrov in recent years.

Szijjártó and Putin. Photo: Facebook/Szijjártó

The researcher added that the relationship between Szijjártó and Lavrov, Russia’s foreign minister, had been even closer than the Hungarian public currently realised.

Have you read this one? Did Minister Szijjártó brief Lavrov during EU talks and offer to forward documents? Leaked recordings here!

The approach to Ukraine is more cautious. The new leadership does not expect a rapid breakthrough, but Rácz said that “something has already begun”.

On minority rights, the priority should be the implementation of existing agreements rather than the conclusion of new ones. They also said that the concessions secured in this area had been achieved not by the Orbán governments but through pressure from the EU.

The change, therefore, would not take the form of a single dramatic foreign policy U-turn. Instead, it points to more professional and less ideological decision-making focused on the EU, stronger regional ties and a more pragmatic approach to relations with Russia and Ukraine.

The reformed Institute of International Affairs could become one of the main centres of expertise behind that new foreign policy direction.

World.title: Sziget Festival to kick off on Sunday – everything you need to know
World.content:
Alongside its stages showcasing global superstars, Sziget Festival is placing renewed emphasis this year on cultural diversity and visitors’ comfort. Revamped festival districts, distinctive new and returning artistic productions, new food and drink venues, communal spaces and comfort-enhancing improvements will all await festival-goers. The festival will begin with two special days before its official opening, before once again operating for five days as a diverse city waiting to be explored – one in which culture, entertainment and shared experiences all take centre stage.

Sziget Festival: warming up with two special days

Sziget will launch this year with two special days before its official opening. On 9 August, the Minus One Day will host Bródy Songs Day, when more than 50 Hungarian performers – including Gábor Presser, Zsuzsa Koncz, Charlie, András Lovasi, Azahriah, Beton.Hofi, Dzsúdló, Bagossy Brothers Company, Carson Coma and Wellhello – will come together to celebrate the six-decade career of János Bródy. The evening will be a musical celebration spanning generations, culminating in a performance by Bródy himself.

The unique, unrepeatable six-hour programme is expected to draw older visitors to the festival as well. With them in mind, the organisers will provide minibus transport from the entrance to the Main Stage, while 5,000 cardboard chairs will also be available for the occasion at a cost price of HUF 600 each.

The Zero Day on 10 August will bridge Sziget’s past and present. This year, the organisers are inviting former ‘Sziget-goers’ back to the festival so that they can experience its atmosphere once again – this time, perhaps, with their children. Artists closely associated with Sziget’s history, including Faithless, Morcheeba and Goran Bregović, will return to the Main Stage. The evening will continue at the Revolut Stage, where György Korda and Klári Balázs will return to a Sziget stage after a long absence with a one-off show featuring a live band and dancers.

Afterwards, a nostalgia party led by Péter Janklovics, aka Pietro Fabuloso, will continue until dawn, recreating the atmosphere of the legendary Dance Song Festival tent. The two special opening days will both honour iconic figures from Hungarian popular music and underline one of Sziget’s central messages this year: the festival experience can be passed down from one generation to the next.

A city waiting to be explored

In 2026, Sziget will once again operate as a diverse city waiting to be discovered. Across the festival site, 12 districts – each with its own character, programme and atmosphere – will follow one another. Each could stand alone as a festival experience, yet they are organically connected, forming a series of easily accessible worlds that together create the complex, varied experience that is Sziget.

In the northern part of the festival, Wonderland will once again be a realm of creativity, self-expression and boundary-pushing experiences. It is where art, culture and unusual communal spaces meet, hosting the ArtGarden, Delko Checkout, the Museum of Applied Arts, the Kino Bizarre cinema with its distinctive cinematic world, the Light Stage, which invites exploration during the day, and the much-anticipated return of the iconic Luminárium. Wonderland will also remain home to one of the festival’s most distinctive meeting places, Magic Mirror / Magic Runway – a celebration of freedom, self-expression and diversity.

The heart of Sziget’s electronic music universe will be Delta District, where Arzenál x Turbina: Der Klub, BOLT Night Stage and Yettel Colosseum will offer all-night programmes across three venues with very different characters. The line-up includes internationally renowned names such as Peggy Gou, Sara Landry, Argy, Sub Focus, Richie Hawtin, Anfisa Letyago, Indira Paganotto, Dixon, Yousuke Yukimatsu, WhoMadeWho and Joris Voorn.

Numerous activities

Sziget is also offering discounted night-time admission this year. The Night Ticket by Revolut is aimed at those arriving only for the late-night programme. It allows entry to the festival site from 11 PM and remains valid until 8 AM the following morning. Night tickets for the festival days between 11 and 15 August are priced uniformly at HUF 29,900 and can be purchased through the official Sziget website.

Fans of hip-hop and rap will have their own district in dropYard, which will function not merely as a music venue but as a complete cultural space. The Graffiti Wall, Halfpipe and Skate Art programmes, The Cypher by Friss and the VISA Live x dropYard stage will together bring audiences closer to the genre’s musical, visual and street-culture worlds.

The Blue Zone will once again serve as Sziget’s centre for wellbeing and safety. Between concerts, festival-goers will be able to rest, take part in free health screenings, request a massage and seek support from mental-health professionals. The zone is designed to promote recovery, health and a safe festival experience. It will also host Kultúrapont, where visitors can enjoy acoustic concerts and slam poetry performances.

Epicentre and districts

Sziget’s epicentre will once again be Fő tér, where the festival’s biggest concerts and most spectacular programmes will take place. It is home to the Main Stage, which in 2026 will again host the festival’s biggest artists, including Skrillex, Bring Me The Horizon, Florence + The Machine, Twenty One Pilots, SOMBR, Zara Larsson, Lewis Capaldi, Skepta and Jorja Smith. Two Hungarian acts will also appear on the Main Stage this year: Sisi and Carson Coma. The Coca-Cola Stage will also be located around Fő tér, alongside the Grand Street Theatre, which will offer a spectacular experience every evening after the concerts.

The musical adventure continues beyond the main square. In the SZOHO district, The Buzz delivered by DHL will take centre stage, showcasing international acts who are already stars in their home countries but are still waiting to be discovered in Hungary. It will once again be one of Sziget’s most important destinations for musical discovery, giving promising artists from around the world – many on the cusp of international careers – the chance to introduce themselves. Visitors will have the opportunity to encounter the defining names of the coming years before they become household favourites.

Further music stages and entertainment venues will line Grand Avenue. These include Bacardi Stage, offering energetic programmes and tribute acts; the atmospheric Piros Pezsgő Piano Bar; and the Revolut Stage, which will host large-scale productions and international stars such as Natasha Bedingfield, Underworld, BUNT, Dijon and Ashnikko.

At the Budapest Park venue, leading figures from Hungary’s popular music scene will meet the festival audience at the Budapest Park Stage by Johnnie Walker. The programme will also offer a journey through Sziget’s history, with legendary bands such as Kispál és a Borz and Tankcsapda returning to the festival. Tankcsapda will perform songs from its era-defining album A legjobb méreg. They will be joined by Majka, Pál Utcai Fiúk, Quimby, Bëlga, Beton.Hofi, Pogány Induló, Co Lee, Mehringer and Manuel, among others.

The centre of Sziget’s artistic programme in 2026 will be the new Jardin des Arts, where the various strands of contemporary performance will converge. Visitors will be able to see the distinctive circus productions of Cirque du Sziget, the spectacular audiovisual performances at Le DÔME, the large-scale circus and theatre productions at Le Grand Theatre, and the immersive experiences of Mobilis, which actively involve the audience.

The district will also be home to The Joker, one of Sziget’s more playful and entertaining venues. Moving into a new building in 2026, it will offer board games during the day, followed by stand-up comedy and magic shows in the evening.

The We are Family district is designed for festival-goers arriving with children. From family camping and childcare facilities to a playground, everything is intended to ensure that parents and children alike feel comfortable at Sziget. Vándor Vurstli, which offers entertainment for every member of the family, will once again take visitors on a journey through time. Its world evokes the atmosphere of a 20th-century fairground, with games, performers and unusual productions providing carefree entertainment.

Visitors looking for nostalgia, playfulness and a little innocent escapism will find target games, magicians, puppet theatre, fortune-tellers, jugglers and a mini Ferris wheel. Vándor Vurstli is one of Sziget’s most colourful attractions – a place where the imagination can run free and everyone can rediscover the joy of childhood curiosity.

In the southern part of the festival site, Impact Village will serve as a hub for community initiatives, social responsibility and active participation. It will include Bartók-negyed, Civil Sziget, EU Meeting Point, Green Sziget Center, Sziget Changemakers, Szitizen Center, Wedding Garden and XS Land, which offers accessible experiences designed to promote awareness of disability and inclusion.

At Sziget’s southernmost point, the focus will turn to exercise and active recreation. In addition to sports pitches, the Field of Sports will feature a running club, the Hottie Pilates Tent and the Padel Zone / Workout Zone for those wishing to enrich their festival experience with sport, movement and relaxation alongside the concerts and cultural programmes.

Major comfort improvements

To tackle the increased risk of dust caused by the dry conditions, the organisers installed a temporary irrigation network at their own expense several weeks ago, in response to the earlier heatwave. Main routes without a permanent hard surface, as well as the audience areas in front of the stages, have been covered with ground protection, while several large continuous areas have been fitted with temporary flooring.

The routes will be watered continuously, and substantially more dust-binding material will be used this year than in previous years. In a record for Sziget, a total of 89,600 square metres – almost nine hectares – of ground protection has been laid, connected to the paved roads of Hajógyári Island. This is nearly 20,000 square metres, or almost two hectares, more than in 2025, making it the largest ground-protection project in the festival’s history.

One of the most important elements of the development is an increase of more than 5,000 square metres in the ground-protected area around the Main Stage. A second protected route will also be created alongside the Revolut venue, following the line of the flag road, further improving ease of movement around the site.

Sziget is also taking extensive measures to deal with the summer heat. Around 2,500 square metres of air-conditioned indoor space will be available for visitors seeking relief. The cooled venues include Magic Mirror, Joker, La Dôme, Luminárium, Sziget Ville Camping Wellness and the Skyboxes in the VIP area.

The amount of shaded space will also increase significantly. This year, festival-goers will have access to 14,000 square metres of shaded areas – around 3,000 square metres more than in 2025. The festival’s largest covered venue will remain Revolut, whose almost 6,000-square-metre space is one of Sziget’s principal communal areas.

In addition, more than ten hectares of tree-covered, shaded audience space will be available. As part of the heat-protection measures, the number of misting arches will be increased. Several areas were also closed during the construction period to preserve green spaces, which help cool the festival site naturally.

An extensive drinking-water network will ensure that visitors can stay hydrated. The site will have six drinking fountains, ten single-tap drinking points, three nine-tap drinking points and seven three-tap drinking points. Subject to the results of water-quality tests, drinking water will also be available in all toilet facilities.

Sziget 2026: food and drink elevated

Sziget will welcome visitors in 2026 with a revamped food and drink concept. Across the festival site, a broad selection of Hungarian and international flavours will be available, from street-food favourites to restaurant-style dishes. Alongside Thai, Italian, Japanese, Mexican, Greek and French cuisine, Hungarian food will play a prominent role.

Food courts will remain an important part of the offering, while vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, lactose-free and other special-diet options will receive more attention than ever before. The Budget-Friendly programme will also continue, with most food outlets offering at least one one-pot dish priced below HUF 3,500.

Festival-goers should also note that all drinks will be available at a ten per cent discount until 6pm on festival days. New this year is Food Paradise, combining premium gastronomy with daytime programmes and communal experiences. The Piros Pezsgő Piano Bar will bring together sparkling drinks, Hungarian wines, local flavours and live piano music.

For the first time, Sziget will also host a Farmers’ Market, showcasing a carefully selected range of products from local growers and craftspeople. As part of the revamped VIP experience, guests will be served by leading gastronomic partners including Costes, Digó Nápolyi Pizza, Buja Disznók, 101 Bisztró and TOKIO.

New solutions will also make eating at the festival more convenient. A QR-code ordering system will debut in the Food Paradise area, allowing visitors to order food more quickly and easily.

ALDI will once again provide festival-goers with shopping facilities on the Sziget site. At the pop-up shop, Szitizens will be able to buy freshly baked bread, fruit, vegetables, chilled products and non-food items at the usual shop prices. In the ALDI Grill Zone, staff will cook the grill products purchased in the shop free of charge.

Visitors will be able to choose from 25 dishes, including sausages, marinated meats, fish, vegetarian products and vegan options. ALDI will offer Sziget’s most budget-friendly meal options: a breakfast can be put together from HUF 207, vegan grill products start at HUF 469, and grilled sausages at HUF 1,159. The Grill Zone will have almost twice the capacity of last year, operating 24 grills and seating up to 100 guests at a time.

Sziget will again place a strong emphasis on sustainable catering. Partners will operate under stricter environmental requirements, with waste reduction, responsible sourcing and energy-efficient operations all receiving particular attention. Cooperation with the Hungarian Food Bank Association will help reduce food waste.

Visitors will also find comfortable, shaded communal areas and a wide choice of drinks, while the DRINKiQ programme will once again promote responsible alcohol consumption.

The Green Sziget Center will remain one of the festival’s main hubs for sustainability and environmental awareness. New this year is a farmers’ market offering local, seasonal fruit and vegetables, processed products and healthy snacks. The programme will include educational events on climate change and biodiversity, while the popular Nature Walk guided tour will continue to introduce visitors to Sziget’s distinctive natural environment.

The festival is also strengthening its sustainability efforts. The tent-deposit scheme has significantly reduced the number of tents left behind, while donated tents and camping equipment will once again be passed on to the Hungarian Charity Service of the Order of Malta. Comprehensive waste-management improvements will also be introduced, with greater emphasis on prevention, recycling and the active involvement of partners.

In the spirit of sustainable transport, adventurous visitors will be able to arrive at Sziget this year on guided bicycle tours from Vienna and Bratislava.

Power and water concerns at Sziget Festival? Founder reveals what’s really going on

Prepared for extreme conditions

Following yesterday’s announcement that the country’s energy security is not at risk and that no further voluntary reductions in consumption will be required, the festival’s electricity supply can be adequately provided by the grid. Nevertheless, Sziget can switch to its reserve generators at any time should a power shortage or system failure occur.

Water supplies in the capital are also sufficient. The festival’s average daily water consumption is expected to be around 1,000 cubic metres, supplied through the public utility network and supplemented by buffer capacity. In preparation for any disruption to the network, a total reserve of 800,000 litres of water will be available, with a further 10,000 litres of drinking water held on site.

Medical cover at the festival will be provided by the National Ambulance Service through an on-site treatment centre, supported by several hundred medical assistants and security staff. A pharmacy will also operate on the site around the clock.

MÁV railway group preparing with extra services for the Sziget Festival – details

Sziget’s safe operation will be co-ordinated by the so-called Operational Control Centre, which monitors events at the festival in real time and takes immediate action if necessary. The centre’s work involves, among others, the National Ambulance Service, the Disaster Management Directorate, the police, the National Meteorological Service and In-Kal Security.

According to preliminary figures, the festival’s maximum daily attendance this year is expected to be between 70,000 and 75,000 people – well below the officially authorised capacity of 95,000. Overcrowding is therefore not expected.

Those who would prefer quiet relaxation to all-night partying will not need to leave the festival site. Several venues have been created specifically to support rest, recovery and the preservation or restoration of physical and mental balance.

The organisers’ stated aim was to make this year’s festival visibly more comfortable. Alongside cultural diversity, they believe this is another area in which Sziget can significantly outperform its international competitors.

World.title: Why is it a problem if Péter Magyar decides who can lead Hungary’s public media?
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s intervention in two public media appointments has caused debate over the independence of Hungary’s state broadcaster.

The independence of Hungary’s public media has been one of the country’s most sensitive political issues ever since the democratic transition of 1989–90. Following the change of government in 2026, it appeared almost inevitable that the operation of the Media Service Support and Asset Management Fund (MTVA) and the wider public service media would undergo far-reaching reforms.

One of Péter Magyar’s flagship campaign promises was to bring the era of political propaganda to an end and establish a genuinely independent public broadcaster.

A cleaner public media – but at what cost?

Events over the past few days, however, have opened an entirely new chapter in that debate. The controversy began when MTVA announced the appointment of Gábor Hajdú—who had previously worked for Hír TV and Echo TV—as the new editor-in-chief of M1 News. At the same time, Miklós Borsa, a former presenter of the broadcaster’s flagship news programme, was set to return to the screen.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar clearly had a different view. Remaining true to his increasingly familiar style of direct political communication, he commented on a news article covering the appointments with just 4 words (which were two words in Hungarian):

“I don’t think so…”

The following day, MTVA announced that both appointments had been withdrawn. The speed of the reversal immediately reignited a fundamental constitutional question: should a prime minister—whether formally or informally—be able to influence who occupies senior positions within the country’s public broadcaster?

The criticism once aimed at Fidesz

The episode is particularly striking because one of the strongest criticisms levelled against Fidesz for years was precisely its alleged political control over Hungary’s public media.

Opposition politicians and independent observers frequently argued that anyone who had watched the so-called “state television” during the previous sixteen years could hardly fail to notice its editorial bias.

Yet even Viktor Orbán generally avoided creating the impression that editorial decisions were being made directly from the Prime Minister’s Office. The latest developments appear considerably more explicit: a brief public comment by the sitting prime minister was followed almost immediately by the withdrawal of two high-profile appointments.

Whether this sequence reflects direct political intervention or merely coincidental timing is open to interpretation. Nevertheless, the public perception it creates is difficult to ignore.

Echoes of the Judit Polgár nomination

Many commentators have therefore drawn parallels with another recent controversy: the nomination of Judit Polgár for the presidency. The issue then was not primarily the nominee herself. Hungary’s greatest-ever chess player would likely have been an acceptable choice for many voters.

Rather, critics argued that the government had abandoned its own promise of broad public consultation and instead acted unilaterally, much as previous governments had done when filling the country’s highest constitutional offices.

A similar criticism now emerges in the case of MTVA. For many, the problem is not necessarily that the two withdrawn media executives had previously worked within what critics describe as the former government’s media machinery. Supporters of the current administration argue that figures associated with political propaganda have no place in a renewed public broadcaster.

Instead, the concern centres on the process itself. If the prime minister can effectively overturn appointments through a public social media comment, questions inevitably arise about where institutional autonomy begins, and political authority ends.

A question that goes beyond Péter Magyar

The debate extends far beyond the current prime minister, Péter Magyar. If it becomes accepted practice that a head of government may informally reverse senior appointments with a single public remark, the same precedent would inevitably be available to every future administration, regardless of political affiliation.

That is precisely why democratic institutions are designed to function according to transparent rules rather than the preferences of individual office-holders. Supporters of Péter Magyar naturally offer a different interpretation.

In their view, this was not political interference but a necessary correction. They argue that leaving individuals who had played leading roles in what they regard as the previous government’s propaganda system would have fundamentally undermined the credibility of efforts to rebuild public service broadcasting.

From this perspective, the intervention was intended to restore institutional independence rather than weaken it.

Good decisions also require the right process

That argument, however, addresses only part of the issue. In a constitutional democracy, legitimacy depends not only on whether the final decision is correct but also on whether it is reached through a fair and transparent procedure.

If senior appointments are made through an established professional process only to be withdrawn immediately after a prime minister’s public intervention, many observers will inevitably conclude that political will ultimately overrides institutional decision-making. Ironically, this is exactly the type of governance that Fidesz’s opponents criticised for years.

The independence of public media is not strengthened simply because a different political force now exercises influence over it. It becomes stronger only when no governing party is able to shape its day-to-day operation according to immediate political interests.

If Péter Magyar genuinely intends to open a new chapter for Hungarian public broadcasting, the long-term objective should be to ensure that senior appointments are made through transparent, institutional procedures that remain as independent from political actors as possible.

Such an approach would not only reinforce confidence in the public media today. It would also establish a democratic standard that every future Hungarian government would be expected to follow.

World.title: A taste of summer at Axis Café & Lounge: a lunch well Spent
World.content:
There’s a particular kind of relief that comes from stepping out of Budapest’s midday summer heat and into somewhere cool, calm, and quietly beautiful. That’s exactly what I found on a recent lunch visit to Axis Café & Lounge, tucked inside the Crowne Plaza Budapest, where the kitchen has rolled out a new summer menu built around a simple idea: real nourishment, real flavor, and a bit of a reset for the senses. I went in curious and left genuinely impressed — here’s how the lunch unfolded.

First Sip: ISLA DE PIÑA

I started, as any reasonable person should on a scorching midday, with a cocktail. The ISLA DE PIÑA arrived pale gold and glistening, a blend of rum, passion fruit purée, lime, and pineapple juice. It was tropical without tipping into syrupy — the passion fruit gave it a tart, almost floral edge, while the pineapple juice rounded everything out into something that tasted like vacation in a glass. It was the kind of drink that makes you slow down immediately, loosen your shoulders, and start reading the menu properly instead of skimming it. A strong, breezy opening move for a midday break from the office grind.

A Rich Start: Duck Liver Terrine

Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete

Before the smoky courses arrived, I started with the duck liver terrine, and it set the bar high right from the first bite. Silky and rich, it had that melt-away texture that only a well-made terrine can pull off, balanced by a bright, slightly sweet accompaniment that kept it from feeling too heavy — even in the middle of summer. Spread onto a crisp slice of toasted bread, it struck that classic bistro-style balance between indulgence and freshness, and it was clear from this very first course that the kitchen wasn’t cutting any corners, even on a lighter, seasonal menu. A confident, elegant opener.

Photo: Dailynewshungary.com

Smoke and Sunshine: The Baba Ghanoush

Next came the smoky baba ghanoush — roasted tomato and pepper, parsley, olive oil, and warm flatbread on the side. This dish immediately transported me somewhere else: the charred, smoky depth of the eggplant felt like it had come straight off a summer grill, yet here it was, plated elegantly in the middle of the city. It’s built to be shared, and I can see why — it’s the kind of food that invites conversation, second helpings, and a bit of lingering. The vegetables, herbs, and olive oil worked together in that effortless, Mediterranean way where nothing feels heavy, but everything feels satisfying. Scooped up with warm flatbread, it was fresh, and quietly addictive.

The Baba Ghanoush. Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete

The Main Event: Creamy Salmon Tagliatelle

If the baba ghanoush was the warm-up act, the creamy salmon tagliatelle was the headliner. Silky ribbons of pasta wrapped in a rich, velvety sauce, studded with sweet green peas and tender spinach — it managed to feel indulgent and light at the same time, which isn’t an easy balance to strike. The freshness of the peas and spinach cut through the creaminess just enough to keep every bite feeling summery rather than heavy. It’s easy to see why this dish is tipped to be a crowd favorite this season — it has that rare quality of being comforting enough for a lazy terrace lunch or dinner, yet polished enough for a proper go out.

Salmon tagliatelle. Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete

A Sweet Landing: Salted Caramel Cake

I closed things out with a slice of salted caramel cake, and it turned out to be the perfect final note. Rich, buttery caramel balanced by just the right touch of salt, it managed not to feel like an afterthought — often desserts can feel like an obligatory add-on after a savory meal like this, but this one held its own. Sweet, a little smoky-toned from the caramel, and satisfying without being overwhelming, it was a fitting way to end a meal built around balance.

Salted Caramel Cake at Axis. Photo: Dailynewshungary.com

Worth Going Back For

Even with a satisfyingly full table, I couldn’t help but notice a couple of other dishes on the menu that I’m already planning to order next time. The cauliflower and white bean cream soup, finished with harissa and toasted cashews, sounds like exactly the kind of dish that’s light enough for a hot afternoon but still hearty enough to carry a lunch — the legumes promise a plant-based richness, while the harissa adds a bit of a kick without taking over.

Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete

And for anyone after something a touch more elegant, the pan-seared sea bass fillet with sautéed chard, garlic, roasted baby carrots, and salsa verde looks like the more refined choice on the menu — bright, herby, and beautifully balanced, if the description is anything to go by. Both are firmly on my list for a return visit.

If you missed it: Gordon Ramsay chooses Budapest for first Central European restaurant – opening date revealed

The Bigger Picture

What struck me most about the meal wasn’t any single dish — it was the coherence of the whole experience. Chef Csuklich Viktor’s summer menu at Axis clearly isn’t just about seasonal ingredients for the sake of it; it’s built around the feeling of stepping away from the heat and pace of the city and actually recharging, even if just for the length of a meal. Plant-forward dishes sit comfortably alongside more indulgent choices, and the cocktail list — full of citrus, herbs, floral notes, cucumber, mint, and grapefruit — reinforces that same sense of freshness throughout.

Whether you’re grabbing a quick business lunch or settling in for a longer, unhurried midday or evening meal on the terrace, this feels like a menu designed to meet you wherever you are — and to send you back out into the city a little more refreshed than when you arrived.

If you are at Nyugati, don’t forget that Axis Café & Lounge is open daily for breakfast from 8:00–12:00 and for lunch and dinner from 12:00–22:00. The service is superb – something everyone can experience for themselves.

World.title: Budapest Festival Orchestra to give free open-air concert at Heroes’ Square
World.content:
Iván Fischer and the Budapest Festival Orchestra (BFO) will give a free open-air concert at Heroes’ Square on the evening of Sept 12 to open the autumn season, the orchestra said ina statement on Friday.

The concert begins at 6.30pm and will feature Schubert’s Eighth, the Unfinished Symphony, as well as works by Arvo Part and Prokofiev. The BFO Children’s Choir will perform the Part piece in the original Estonian under Fischer’s baton.

The organisers said the concert is primarily aimed at families and the youngest music lovers. The BFO’s new children’s choir will also make its debut at the event.

The concert is free to attend, and no registration is required. The organisers ask the audience to arrive early for better seating, and cardboard chairs will be provided on site, which can be taken home after the concert.

World.title: Treasure hunt: what experts found around the German motorbike recovered from the Danube in Budapest – photos
World.content:
A Bosch W 175 T 1 spark plug and bakelite plug holder, an oil bottle, a grease tube, insulating tape, a cylinder-head spanner, a spark-plug wrench, a small wire brush and a tyre-pressure gauge were among the items recovered from the pannier of a Second World War-era German motorbike, which emerged from the rapidly receding Danube last weekend alongside the remains of a German soldier, the Institute and Museum of Military History said in a Facebook post on Friday.

Human remains found beneath the German motorbike

The glue and patch material from a puncture-repair kit had also survived intact. The institute’s experts additionally found a drive-chain link, several bolt heads, a hammer head and Y-straps when they opened the side box of the DKW NZ 350-1 German motorbike, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

Museum specialists will clean and conserve the artefacts, and restore those suitable for restoration, they added.

One comment beneath the post said the remains and identity tags of a Wehrmacht soldier and a Waffen-SS soldier had been found next to the motorcycle, along with a decoration known as the Kuban Shield. The medal was awarded to soldiers who successfully defended the Kuban bridgehead in Russia and along the shores of the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov during fighting between February and October 1943.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

A passer-by spotted the motorbike

The Institute and Museum of Military History had previously announced on social media that cleaning and urgent conservation work had begun on the Second World War motorcycle discovered at the weekend in the bed of the Danube, where water levels had fallen to a record low.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

This is how it was taken out from the mud of the Danube: Valuable WWII German motorcycle, human remains and explosives pulled from the Danube in Budapest – photos

It recalled that a passer-by had spotted the motorcycle’s front fork protruding from beneath the rocks on the embankment at Batthyány Square the previous weekend. Museum experts identified the machine and excavated it together with its associated items. The rare find was transported to the institution’s hangar on Kerepesi Road in the early hours of Monday, and work to clean and conserve the motorcycle began during the week.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

The work was inspected on Wednesday by László Kürtös, the Ministry of Defence’s parliamentary state secretary, and Colonel Roland Maruzs, commander of the Ministry of Defence’s Institute and Museum of Military History, the post said.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum
